nytimes.com.title: Democrats Win Big
nytimes.com.text:
It has been a very good night for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The party flipped several key seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, to win the Senate. After elections that were all about President Trump for many voters, Democrats are on the verge of controlling both chambers in Congress.
Stunning wins for Democrats
Democrats notched a series of sweeping victories in the midterm elections, as voters expressed their extreme displeasure with President Trump by ousting the Republicans who have backed him.
Although all results are not yet in, Democrats won control of the U.S. Senate, according to New York Times projections, and have more than a 95 percent chance of winning the House of Representatives.
Democratic candidates won Senate races in a number of Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and (for the first time in more than 90 years) Kansas.
In perhaps the highest-profile race of the midterms, for a Texas Senate seat, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator, toppled Ken Paxton, a scandal-ridden Republican state attorney general who got a crucial Trump endorsement. Democrats also won the governor’s race in Texas for the first time in more than 30 years, in a seismic upset.

nytimes.com.title: U.K. Supreme Court to Hear Challenge to Ban on Palestine Action: What to Know
nytimes.com.text:
Britain’s decision to outlaw Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian direct-action group, as a terrorist organization has been challenged in a succession of legal hearings since it was imposed last year. Now, the country’s Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge against the ban and decide its future.
The British government accused Palestine Action of orchestrating “a nationwide campaign of direct criminal action,” putting national security at risk. According to the government’s independent adviser on counterterrorism legislation, it was the first time a protest group that did not call for violence against people was proscribed under counterterrorism laws.
Here’s what to know.
What is Palestine Action?
Palestine Action was founded in 2020 as a pro-Palestinian protest group that largely focuses its efforts on demonstrations against corporate and military targets linked to the sale and export of defense equipment to Israel. The group says it does not promote violence against individuals.
It was co-founded by Huda Ammori, an advocate who had previously worked for a Palestinian rights organization, and Richard Barnard, an activist linked with other grass roots movements, including Extinction Rebellion, a global environmental group.
During legal proceedings challenging the ban, Britain’s High Court said that the group claimed to have a mailing list of some 20,000 people but that the “extent and nature” of Palestine Action’s membership and organization was “largely unexplained.” Analysts said that before it was disbanded, Palestine Action was run by a relatively small, committed group of activists.
The group’s actions have drawn international attention. President Trump criticized it after activists were accused of vandalizing one of his Scottish golf resorts by defacing the clubhouse and spraying “Gaza is not 4 sale” across a green. Mr. Trump called the demonstrators “terrorists” and said he hoped they would be “treated harshly.”

nytimes.com.title: As Trump’s Midterm Deadline Looms, Gulf Countries Brace for Possible Renewal of Iran War
nytimes.com.text:
In the marble-floored atria of a five-star hotel in Manama, Bahrain’s capital, military officers in full regalia mingled with ambassadors and political analysts last weekend, swapping business cards and chatting over plates of tiramisü infused with Arabic coffee.
The smiles and the warm handshakes at the gathering — the Manama Dialogue, an annual security conference — belied the grim topic underpinning much of the conversation. The possibility that the United States might, within days, reignite its war with Iran, prompting a barrage of Iranian missiles and drones on the very city where they were meeting, hung over the event like a dark cloud.
As President Trump weighs a renewed attack on Iran sometime after the midterm elections on Tuesday, Gulf Arab officials fear that their countries — which host American military bases, Western companies and valuable oil and gas facilities — will be the hardest hit, as they were after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. They also fear that the fighting will be worse this time around.
The Iranian and American positions on a potential deal to stave off a crisis are still “far apart,” Anwar Gargash, a senior official from the United Arab Emirates, told the conference audience. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.”
The U.S. military carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, according to U.S. officials. Still, Mr. Trump told Fox News on the same day that “there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”
American and Israeli military officials have drawn up an expanded list of targets to strike, including energy infrastructure and other sites vital to the Iranian economy. Iran has warned that it would retaliate fiercely, targeting critical infrastructure and underwater communications cables in the region.

nytimes.com.title: A Test for Israeli Democracy: Should Jews Ask Arabs to Join the Government?
nytimes.com.text:
Israel’s democracy is facing a huge test after Arab political parties made historic gains in last week’s election.
And opponents of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are facing an enormous dilemma over whether Arab lawmakers should now be given a share of power in a new government.
Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents secured a clear majority in the Parliament by winning 67 out of 120 seats. But 19 of these were won by the Arab parties, and their inclusion in a governing coalition is seen as so problematic by many Israeli Jews that opposition leaders are putting themselves through contortions looking for ways to form a government that would not rely on Arab lawmakers.
The aversion to building a government with the two main Arab factions — the United Arab List, or Raam, and the Joint List, which comprises three smaller parties — is enormously frustrating to political activists who helped drive Arab turnout to a near-record high of 77 percent last week.
“Why is it so complicated? A vote of an Arab citizen of Israel should equal no less than the vote of a Jewish citizen,” said Alon-Lee Green, a founder of the Jewish-Arab organization Standing Together.
The efforts to sideline the Arab parties also fuel complaints among many Arab citizens, who represent about 20 percent of the country’s population, that Israeli Jews welcome their participation in the political process only up to the point where they might wield real power.

nytimes.com.title: Anthrax Outbreak in Africa’s Oldest National Park Is Killing Hippos
nytimes.com.text:
An anthrax outbreak in a park in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been killing hippopotamuses, threatening vulnerable wildlife and raising concerns about human exposure to the disease.
The outbreak at Virunga National Park — Africa’s oldest national park — has killed 30 hippopotamuses since September, when observers first started noticing suspicious carcasses, Laura Parker, who leads the park’s conservation programs, said in an email on Tuesday. The cause of the animals’ deaths, and the outbreak, has since been confirmed by laboratory analyses, she noted.
This is the second outbreak of anthrax in the park since last year, and it comes as Congo is contending with an Ebola epidemic that has killed more than 4,800 people since May and strained the country’s resources.
Doctors who have analyzed anthrax outbreaks in the region say that the disease represents a significant public health challenge, intersecting with issues like food insecurity, conflict and poverty, and disproportionately affecting rural populations with limited access to health care.
Park officials have been raising awareness among local communities to ensure people do not touch or consume meat from any affected carcasses and report any such finds to the authorities, Ms. Parker said.
“Virunga’s response is focused on surveillance, safe carcass management and reducing risks to both wildlife and people. Teams are monitoring the affected area, documenting new mortalities and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses,” she said.

nytimes.com.title: ‘This Hour Has 22 Minutes,’ a Canadian Sketch Show, Beats American Late Night to the Punchline
nytimes.com.text:
Hours after Katie Zacharia was fired as White House press secretary five days into the job, the Canadian satirical series “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” captured the chaos in a sketch posted online — beating American late-night comedy shows to the punchline.
Some 48 hours later, and a week before the rapper Nicki Minaj traveled on Air Force One to rally for President Trump in Michigan, “22 Minutes” imagined the MAGA darling as Ms. Zacharia’s successor.
In both cases, the creative team on the show, Canada’s version of “Saturday Night Live,” did not wait for their weekly broadcast. The polished sketches went straight to the show’s TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, attracting nearly 24 million views.
For the last 34 years, this sketch comedy show has reliably roasted Canadian and American politics, culture and quirks. But “22 Minutes” is having a renaissance buoyed by Mr. Trump — in particular his trade war, tariffs, threats and insults toward Canada. Television audiences are up, and social media viewership is growing rapidly.
“Social media has opened up our show beyond what I thought was capable,” said Stacey McGunnigle, a cast member and writer who has created and portrayed many MAGA women, most memorably Karoline Leavitt, Natalie Harp and, ever so briefly, Ms. Zacharia.

nytimes.com.title: Helicopters Collide Over Everest Trail, Killing 1 and Injuring 3 Others
nytimes.com.text:
A midair collision of two helicopters near Mount Everest on Tuesday left one Indian tourist dead and a visitor from New Zealand and two pilots injured, according to Nepal’s civil aviation authority.
The helicopters collided as they were attempting to land in the Pheriche area of the Solukhumbu district of Nepal around 8 in the morning, the aviation authority said in a statement. Pheriche is a village at an altitude of about 13,900 feet along the Everest Base Camp trekking route.
Video of the accident showed that, in apparently clear weather, the propellers of a lower helicopter made contact with a second aircraft that had been flying higher nearby and swooped downward rapidly. Both helicopters fell to the ground not far apart and appeared to have been destroyed in the collision.
The crash cast a pall on the popular tourist destination during the autumn climbing season and highlighted the dangers that some locals and government officials have warned of as flights in the region have proliferated.
The Nepali authorities identified the dead tourist as Vasanth Kumar Balaramaramadu, 44, of India and the injured visitor, who was being treated at a hospital in Kathmandu, as Shailesh Kisan Patel of New Zealand. The aviation authority’s statement expressed hope for a speedy recovery for the injured, including two unnamed pilots.
In a post, the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu expressed “its deepest condolences on the unfortunate demise of an Indian national” and said it was working “in close coordination with Nepali authorities for early repatriation of the mortal remains of the deceased.”
The aviation authority in Nepal said it was investigating the collision and would take any actions or corrective measures needed to address potential issues. “Preliminary reports suggest miscommunication between the pilots, as the area is outside the coverage of Lukla Airport’s air traffic control tower and pilots have to communicate with each other,” Mukesh Dangol, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, told The Kathmandu Post.
The perils of heavy helicopter traffic in the mountainous region are well known, and the Nepali government has struggled to strike a balance between the needs of a thriving tourism industry and the demand for better regulation to ensure safety and preservation of the natural environment.
In 2023, five visitors from Mexico and a Nepali pilot were killed when their helicopter crashed during a sightseeing trip over Mount Everest.
Local officials and those at the Sagarmatha National Park, home to Mount Everest, have clashed with government regulators over helicopter restrictions in recent years. In 2024, the park authorities said they would begin restricting helicopter sightseeing tours and some other flights in 2025, a rule that civil aviation regulators initially said the park had no authority to enforce.

nytimes.com.title: More Iranians Call for Nuclear Weapons After War With U.S.
nytimes.com.text:
From pulpits at Friday prayers to street rallies, Iranian clerics and officials are increasingly urging the country’s leaders to reverse their longtime pledge not to pursue nuclear weapons.
This demand, once seen as a fringe position held by hard-liners, is moving into mainstream public debate, and the shift could have dramatic consequences for Iran, whose government has for decades argued that its nuclear program was solely for peaceful purposes.
“We must be equipped with nuclear weapons — so that we can fight the criminal America with strength, God willing,” Ali Sepahvand, the Friday prayer leader in Iran’s western city of Kuhdasht, said last week, according to a widely distributed video.
As his voice echoed through a prayer hall, covered in photographs of commanders killed in the war with the United States and Israel this past year, the congregants chanted: “Nuclear deterrence is our inalienable right!”
The growing calls for Iran to pursue nuclear weapons come as the country’s leaders engage in diplomatic efforts to stave off renewed war with the United States and Israel, an outcome widely considered likely after the American midterm elections on Tuesday.
For decades, Iran’s officials have publicly endorsed the fatwa, or religious edict, from its supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, which forbade the development and use of nuclear weapons. Issued in his capacity as the head of Iran’s theocratic state, his decree barred Iranian institutions, including the military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, from pursuing a nuclear bomb.

nytimes.com.title: U.S. Assisted Venezuela in Deadly Drone Strike, Officials Say
nytimes.com.text:
For years, a Colombian rebel army operated freely across the border in Venezuela, allowed to traffic cocaine and oversee illicit gold mines under Nicolás Maduro, the country’s former president.
But with Mr. Maduro forcibly removed by the United States and Venezuela’s government under the thumb of the Trump administration, Venezuela’s military last week launched a deadly attack on the group, the National Liberation Army, better known by its Spanish initials, ELN.
The attack, according to four U.S. officials, was carried out on Friday with the help of U.S. intelligence and drones. It was not previously public who had been responsible for the attack.
The joint operation underscores how the Trump administration is increasingly enmeshed in Venezuela’s domestic affairs and how it has embraced a militarized strategy to combat drug trafficking in Latin America.
The attack was not the first joint operation in the country. In June, a strike by the United States and Venezuela killed a leader of Tren de Aragua, the transnational gang.
The New York Times reported this week that the Trump administration is aiming to establish a long-term U.S. military presence in Venezuela.

nytimes.com.title: Spain’s Transport Minister Resigns After Deadly High-Speed Rail Crash
nytimes.com.text:
Spain’s transport minister announced his resignation on Tuesday evening, nearly a week after the deadliest train crash in a decade killed nearly 70 people and raised doubts about the country’s once-vaunted rail system ahead of national elections.
“A transport minister cannot remain in office after two accidents of such severity in less than a year,” the minister, Óscar Puente, told lawmakers on Tuesday evening after days of resisting calls for his resignation.
Mr. Puente’s resignation came at the end of a bruising day of questioning for the minister, who gave lawmakers a detailed account of the events leading to the accident, in which one high-speed train rear-ended another on the same tracks.
“You’re so good at explaining why people die on trains, and so bad at preventing them from dying on trains,” said Ester Muñoz, the spokeswoman for the main opposition conservative party, the Popular Party.
Mr. Puente’s resignation reflected his increasingly untenable position ahead of snap elections on Nov. 29 and suggested that he had become a liability to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who had stood by him. Many political parties had demanded his resignation, and recent polls showed that a majority of Spaniards believed Mr. Puente should step down.
“Óscar Puente has faced up to his responsibilities, offered solutions and then stepped aside,” Mr. Sánchez said on social media after the minister’s resignation. He added, “Politicians like him bring dignity to our country.”

cnn.com.title: Too big to rig? How Trump’s voter fraud crusade crashed into a Blue wave
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration’s unprecedented crusade to hunt for voter fraud spurred widespread fears of federal election interference but ultimately never materialized on Election Day – thanks to resistance from local election officials and federal courts. In what quickly became a wave election for Democrats, voters delivered a sweeping midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, with few issues reported at polls across the country. The Justice Department’s surge of voting monitors seemingly did not lead to disturbances. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were not sent to polling places. The US Postal Service did not refuse to deliver mail-in ballots. And on Tuesday night, Trump indicated that he would not challenge the results of an election that delivered control of the House and Senate to the Democrats. Just like in 2020, institutional guardrails of the American electoral system largely blocked the Trump administration from carrying out some of the drastic steps that it pursued. The Supreme Court blocked Trump’s March Executive Order that would have severely restricted states’ mail-in voting. Local election officials brushed off threats from the Justice Department that they could face prosecution over noncitizen voting. And the federal courts rejected the Justice Department’s 11th-hour attempt to force California to segregate 20,000 ballots from being counted. Election experts who spent months gaming out worst-case scenarios with tabletop exercises and trainings for election workers said that all of the preparation helped ensure the election was carried out lawfully and that any federal government attempts to overstep its authority was quickly halted. “For all of the handwringing and speculation about how the federal government might interfere, how foreign adversaries might attempt to interfere … we’re seeing elections go very normally with only minor problems,” said David Becker, founder of the Center for Election Innovation & Research. “It’s largely due to the preparation of those local and county election officials, who worked so hard with their state officials, despite attempts at federal interference,” added Becker, who advises local election officials in both parties. The day was not without problems. There was a ballot scanner “debacle” in Westchester County, New York, that delayed counting; bomb threats were reported in several states; and various isolated allegations such as voters being incorrectly turned away from the polls or poll watchers not being allowed proper access. But those were all typical issues that tend to arise on Election Day, and nowhere near the widespread chaos that some had feared. At least in the immediate aftermath of Tuesday’s rout, Trump told the New York Times in an interview that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results of the midterms. Several prominent election deniers also appeared to be accepting the Democratic wins on Tuesday. Aggressive steps Trump’s Justice Department is still aggressively investigating claims of widespread noncitizen voters on the rolls in California and the two Daniel Sullivans on the ballot in Alaska. Many of the extreme steps Trump took in his efforts to overturn the 2020 election came weeks after Election Day. But for months, election officials and Democratic lawmakers have been guarding against what they warned could become a constitutional crisis that would upend voting in the midterms if the White House tried to seize control of the US voting process that’s largely delegated to the states in the Constitution. The president and his administration took aggressive steps – and suggested they might go further. Trump officials tried to prove the president’s false claims the 2020 election was stolen from him. The FBI seized 2020 ballots from Fulton County in Georgia earlier this year, while intelligence officials tested voting machines from Puerto Rico in an unsuccessful attempt to prove baseless conspiracy theories about voting machines being hacked by foreign adversaries. Trump said in February Republicans should “nationalize” the elections, while his allies pushed him to use the federal government’s powers to declare a national emergency to take control of the electoral process with steps like blocking certain voting machines from being used. Trump officials repeatedly refused to rule out sending ICE agents or other law enforcement officers to the polls. Voting rights groups reported smooth operations at polls across the country on Tuesday – crediting the months-long campaign that included trainings and education of local election officials and judges for ensuring that the federal government wasn’t allowed to overstep its authority. “When it comes to federal agents at the polls and so many other issues, it’s really important to remember … that today could have looked very different,” said Andrew Walchuko, a policy director and counsel at Common Cause, a non-partisan good government group. “I think we really put them on notice that we are watching.” Throughout Tuesday, FBI field offices across the country operated command posts focused on monitoring any election issues that would require federal attention. While there were a small number of false bomb threats and disruptions that temporarily impacted some polling places, there were no actual significant threats, according to one senior law enforcement source. Steps the Trump administration took that threatened to disrupt the election in the leadup to Election Day were blocked by the courts or rebuffed by states. Trump’s March executive order to restrict mail-in voting would have prevented the US Postal Service from mailing absentee ballots unless the states sent USPS its list of eligible voters. The Supreme Court blocked the administration from implementing it in September. Last month, the Justice Department sent California a list of 20,000 voters it claimed could be noncitizens, demanding the state and county officials segregate those voters’ ballots and threatening prosecution of officials who didn’t stop noncitizen voting. But California election officials rejected those demands, and the federal courts quickly put a stop to the effort to set the ballots aside. “Like Americans across the country, we know the federal government does not run our elections. States and counties do. And at every turn, California has pushed back,” Aarti Kohli, executive director of the Asian Law Caucus, which deployed monitors in California with Common Cause-California, told reporters on Tuesday. A debunked claim Some conspiracy theories still circulated on social media during the election on Tuesday. But in a twist, the Republican National Committee — which long amplified Trump’s false claims of a stolen 2020 election — helped debunk at least one of the incorrect claims. The RNC’s Election Integrity team, which encouraged voters to flag irregulates or potential fraud, addressed a viral video that raised concerns about ballot handling in San Diego, explaining that election workers filmed loading ballots into an “unmarked minivan” were doing their jobs. The video showed workers collecting ballots from an overflowing drop box. The RNC responded that its own “special monitors” flagged the full box to election officials and that workers were simply moving the excess ballots to the central voting site. “And the ‘unmarked van’?” the RNC Election Integrity account wrote in the post on X. “It’s a County vehicle used to transport ballots.” CNN’s Josh Campbell contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Trump reacts to Republican losses and declines to take blame
cnn.com.text: By the time the House and Senate had been called for Democrats on Tuesday, a consensus among members of both parties was forming: voters had rejected President Donald Trump’s record in office, and he would face a starkly different political reality for the remainder of his term. Trump, however, sees it very differently. “But I don’t view it as a hit on me,” Trump told Fox News in a live phone interview. “We’ve had the greatest two years in the history of the presidency in terms of the economy, in terms of all the things that we’ve done.” The stunning results across a swath of America were not primarily the fault of the Iran war he began eight months ago — he told the Wall Street Journal that was only a “piece” of it — or the tariffs that drove up prices or his fixation on topics far from voters’ minds, Trump insisted. It was the candidates who were to blame, he argued, helped along by favorable coverage of Democrats on his once-favorite channel, Fox News. The results were only a “little surprise,” he would later tell that channel. The winds of history were always against him, he’d long warned. He neglected to mention that he had selected many of the candidates himself. “I thought they’d do better,” he told Fox, referring to Republicans in the third person rather than the party he is currently leading. Later, he attributed the losses to a “mood in the air.” He also insisted Tuesday night that his governing agenda would continue apace, despite the dramatically altered political conditions in Washington. The election results were the punctuation on a long and often frustrating campaign season for Trump, who spent the bulk of the last month flying aboard Air Force One to red states with the task of encouraging supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” The gambit did not work, but Trump saw fault not in his own performance but in that of the people he was trying to help. “They just didn’t inspire the people to get out and vote,” he told Fox. “And I wasn’t on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, they would have got out.” Many of the candidates who lost on Tuesday — including Darline Graham in South Carolina, Ken Paxton in Texas, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Mike Collins in Georgia — were hand-selected by Trump himself, in some cases over the objections of other Republicans. He did not mention that as he bemoaned the candidates’ inability to translate his support into votes. “I had no choice,” he said of the decision to support Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued candidate in Texas he endorsed over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. “When it wasn’t fashionable, he kissed my ass.” How intensively Trump wanted to pin blame on his party’s candidates seemed to vary by the minute. “I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!” he wrote, ominously, on Truth Social a few minutes before midnight. His first target was Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, the Republican incumbent who lost re-election to Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Trump deemed him a “Republican in name only” and claimed “He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!” But in a phone interview with Politico around the same time, he insisted he wasn’t interested in assigning blame. “I don’t want to blame anybody,” he said. “I just want to say, you know, it was a very interesting period of time. I watched with great interest, learned from it.” Trump sounded more conciliatory toward Democrats, who he will now be forced to rely upon if he wants to pass anything through Congress. He made similar pledges after Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms, but the offers of bipartisanship did not materialize. “You know, I have a lot of friends that are Democrats. Believe it or not, I’ve already spoken to some of them,” he said, without naming them. He spoke vaguely of trying to find areas of compromise, but insisted he had no regrets about the issue many Republicans blame most for Republicans’ woes — the war in Iran. “I don’t think about it. I did the right thing,” he told the Wall Street Journal when asked if he had regrets about the war. “I would have done it again.”

cnn.com.title: Former elementary school teacher becomes newest paper billionaire in China
cnn.com.text: A former elementary school teacher has been propelled into the ranks of paper billionaires in China after the stock debut of his company selling tape and other adhesive products to tech giants, according to Forbes. Michael Mai, chairman and CEO of Crown New Materials Technology, entered the rarefied financial heights on Tuesday when the company, which produces binding agents for major brands like Tesla and Apple, made its trading debut on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange. Shares shot up as much as 787%, from 16.98 yuan ($2.55) per share in its stock filing to a height of 150.58 yuan ($22.57) per share at one point, according to the Shenzhen bourse, mainland China’s second-largest stock exchange. Mai, an Australian citizen and permanent resident of Hong Kong, has an estimated net worth of $2.5 billion, based on his stake in the firm, Forbes reported. The 62-year-old was reportedly an elementary school teacher in the southern Chinese city of Zhongshan – where the company, founded in 2000, is based. His sister, Mai Huixia, 64, who serves as vice-chairperson, joined him in the billionaire ranks, with Forbes reporting that her stake gave her a $2 billion fortune. Shares eased to about 77 yuan ($12) per share Wednesday morning following the peak a day earlier that prompted the company to call on investors in a statement to “invest rationally.” CNN has reached out to the company for comment. With four manufacturing plants across China and one in Vietnam, the company specializes in products that bind components found in a range of retail products, from vehicle roofs to semiconductors in smartphone, according to its website. China’s stock markets have taken a hit in recent months amid weak consumer spending and concerns over a possible bursting of the AI bubble. Since peaking in June, key Chinese indexes have fallen more than 20%, crossing the threshold for a bear market. Beijing responded two weeks ago by pumping $19 billion into exchange-traded funds, according to Bloomberg data, its biggest intervention since early 2025, when US President Donald Trump’s tariff offensive roiled global markets.

cnn.com.title: The historic firsts of the 2026 election
cnn.com.text: Winners up and down the 2026 ballot will make history this year, CNN’s Decision Desk projects, including the first Black woman governor and the first out gay male US senator. As President Donald Trump takes on the latter half of his second term, both parties will welcome a diverse group of newly elected lawmakers at the state and national level. Read more about the candidates who are projected to boast the moniker of “first.” First female Black governor Keisha Lance Bottoms is projected to become the first Black governor of Georgia, the first female governor of Georgia and the first female Black governor in US history. Bottoms, who served as Atlanta mayor between 2018 and 2022, was among the women whom President Joe Biden considered as a running mate in the 2020 election. She later joined his administration. Bottoms beat out Trump-endorsed Rick Jackson, making expanding Medicaid coverage, homeowner tax relief and increasing education funding the key pillars of her campaign. First out gay male US senator Chris Pappas is projected to become the first out gay male senator in US history with his win in New Hampshire’s US Senate race. His win means Democrats will hold on to a critical seat, in a state that Republicans previously saw as one of their best opportunities to flip. Pappas is a four-term congressman from southeastern New Hampshire. First Black governor of Florida Byron Donalds is projected to become the first Black governor of Florida. He campaigned on tax reforms, regulating data centers and supporting Trump’s agenda in a state that has become more solidly red. He was bolstered early in the race with a full-throated Trump endorsement. When Donalds assumes office there will be three serving Black governors in the US, with very different politics — the other is Democratic Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, who is projected to win reelection, and Bottoms in Georgia. First elected woman US senator in South Carolina Annie Andrews is projected to become the first elected female US senator from South Carolina, defeating appointed Sen. Darline Graham and flipping a seat that Republicans have held for nearly three decades. Trump orchestrated Graham’s appointment to the seat left vacant after the sudden death of her late brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham, in July. The president’s backing of a political unknown stirred controversy in solidly red South Carolina. In her short political career, Graham pitched herself as more conservative than her brother, breaking with some of his positions, like eliminating the filibuster or a more hardline approach to immigration, to side with Trump. Andrews painted herself as an independent-minded moderate who is concerned about affordability, quality of life and corruption. First Hispanic governor of Texas Gina Hinojosa is projected to become the first Hispanic governor of Texas, unseating Republican Gov. Greg Abbott who served almost 12 years in office. The two candidates clashed over culture issues, including abortion, during the campaign. Hinojosa, a 52-year-old state lawmaker and attorney, will be the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990 and only the third woman to hold the position. First female Black member of Congress in Colorado Melat Kiros is projected to become the first female Black member of Congress from Colorado with her win in the state’s 1st District. Kiros, a 29-year-old democratic socialist and lawyer, will also join the Generation-Z sect of Congress as one of the youngest sitting members of the House. First Muslim member of Congress from New Jersey Adam Hamawy is projected to become the first Muslim member of Congress from New Jersey after winning in the 12th Congressional District. Hamawy, a retired US Army combat surgeon and sharp Israel critic, hails from the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, supporting Medicare for All as well as canceling medical and student loan debt. First Native American congresswoman in New York Claire Valdez is projected to become the first female Native American member of Congress from New York. The one-term assemblywoman will win the state’s 7th Congressional District. Valdez’s win marks another victory for the Democratic Party’s progressive wing whose growing influence came in part from the popularity of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who championed Valdez. First out gay member of Congress in Michigan Jeremy Moss is projected to become the first out gay member of Congress from the Wolverine state with his win in Michigan’s 11th Congressional District. Moss, who served as state senator before his win, takes over the seat made vacant by Rep. Haley Stevens — who left the post to run for the US Senate before losing in the primary. First woman elected governor of Ohio Amy Acton is projected to become the first Democrat to win Ohio’s governorship since 2006 and the first woman ever elected to the office. Acton, a physician, defeats Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a race that captured national attention over a controversial attack ad. Campaigning on affordability, Acton pitched property tax cuts targeted at middle-income and older Ohioans, and a moratorium on data centers unless they cover their own utility costs. First Latino elected governor of California Xavier Becerra is projected to become the first elected Latino governor of California, maintaining his party’s control of the nation’s largest state. Becerra, the former US congressman, state attorney general and secretary of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration, emerged from a crowded, contentious primary to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom. Buoyed by California’s solidly liberal electorate and a favorable midterm political environment, Becerra repeatedly linked his opponent, Republican Steve Hilton, to Trump, hammering his endorsement and appealing to Democrats to send a message of opposition to the administration.

cnn.com.title: ‘How did we get here?’: Inside a losing GOP campaign defined by Trump
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump was in the midst of his fourth political rally in three days when he asked a close associate the question that had been troubling him for some time: How did the Republican Party get in this bad of shape? It was mid-October, and with just weeks to go to the midterm elections, the GOP was bleeding support in dozens of races across the country. The House majority was lost. Senate control was, improbably, a toss-up. And Trump had embarked on a monthlong salvage mission, crisscrossing the US to rouse apathetic voters in the kinds of blood-red districts that he’d carried easily just two years ago. “It’s a sh*t-ton of travel,” said a person familiar with the private exchange. “And the question he keeps asking is, ‘How did we get here?’” The president’s belated revelation underscored the dire state of affairs that Republicans around him had spent the last several months struggling to combat. Already facing historical headwinds and an energized Democratic Party, Trump had plunged the nation into an unpopular war with no clear exit strategy. Gas prices soared as a result, fueling widespread inflation and a resurgence of voter anxiety over the cost of living. The self-inflicted wounds sank Trump’s approval ratings to record lows. Faced with an angry and disillusioned electorate, Republican candidates were now desperately seeking ways to escape their leader’s downward gravitational pull. “People are so mad,” one glum Texas-based GOP operative said in the run-up to Election Day. “And Trump hasn’t done anything to help any of that.” In the end, the GOP paid a staggering political price. Frustrated voters decimated Republicans’ majority in both the House and the Senate, delivering a stunning rebuke of GOP governance that extended well into areas long considered conservative strongholds. By late Tuesday, House Republicans were facing an electoral rout, losing several districts that Trump won by more than 10 points just two years ago. Two Democratic sources believe the sweeping victories could give them more than 240 seats in the House, a number that would have been unthinkable just a few weeks ago. The Senate’s trajectory was, in some ways, even more disastrous for Republicans, who had entered the midterm cycle needing only to defend a handful of traditionally red seats to keep control. Instead, the chamber also flipped to Democratic control just hours after the polls closed due to losses in reliable Republican strongholds like Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina. The aftermath is likely to leave Trump dramatically weakened and girding for a final two years in office marked by an onslaught of Democratic investigations and opposition that threaten to grind his agenda to a halt. The broader Republican Party, meanwhile, suddenly finds itself adrift. Even before the results rolled in, it was awash in finger-pointing and second-guessing as GOP officials braced for a poor showing at the polls. That discord is only likely to deepen as Republicans sift through the rubble of a midterms that failed to meet their already low expectations, according to interviews with more than a dozen Trump aides and advisers, party officials and campaign operatives. Those Republicans described a series of questionable calls and pivot points over the last year, including an overly optimistic strategy, indecisive messaging and the misguided selection of a handful of extraordinarily weak candidates. But ultimately, they agreed, Republicans simply couldn’t outrun Trump. The president’s decision to go to war — then spend six months dismissing the economic fallout while pursuing his own vanity projects — unraveled his coalition and proved deeply toxic to Americans across the political landscape. “Honestly, there’s just one person to blame,” said Barrett Marson, an Arizona Republican strategist. “If the war had not happened, it would be an entirely different election cycle. And only one person started that war.” On Tuesday night, a White House official rejected any suggestion that Trump bore responsibility for the GOP’s losses, arguing it was candidates’ own fault. “President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves,” the official said. An unpredictable Trump But White House efforts to now downplay those losses as inevitable — and wholly separate from Trump — represent a major shift from this time last year, when his advisers mapped out a plan to defy history and preserve the party’s slim majorities by putting Trump “on the ballot,” as his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, termed it last December. GOP leaders at that point felt emboldened by Trump’s command of a diverse and seemingly durable coalition of MAGA voters. They were invigorated by the passage of a massive tax cut-and-spending package dubbed “The Big Beautiful Bill.” The economy looked resilient and inflation was easing, offering a potent contrast to the high-cost Biden years. Republicans also had another weapon in their arsenal: An unprecedented redistricting scheme, orchestrated by top Trump political aide James Blair, to preemptively shift more than a dozen congressional districts toward Republicans and shrink the number of seats they might have to defend come November. The smaller map of perceived competitive seats formed the basis of an optimistic midterm strategy that Blair and Wiles laid out in private meetings beginning in February, according to people in the room. They urged top GOP lawmakers and allies to advance a disciplined economic message that emphasized Trump’s accomplishments, including progress on the cost of living and popular priorities like reining in drug prices. Based on that strong start, Republicans would then ask voters to grant them two more years to effectively finish the job. The Republican Party needed to stay on the same page, they insisted — even as they acknowledged that an undisciplined Trump likely would not. The president, Blair told one group, would be “doing his own thing.” That would turn out to be a massive understatement. The war catastrophe Fewer than two weeks later, Trump launched a surprise attack on Iran, killing much of the nation’s top leadership in strikes meant to collapse its regime and deliver the president a quick and resounding victory. Instead, the offensive hardened Iran’s resolve, drawing the US into a war that within weeks had killed American service members and halted the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz, sparking a global energy crisis. Trump and his senior aides initially downplayed the repercussions, boasting that the war was nearly won and would ultimately last just four to six weeks. But even at that early stage, some of Trump’s advisers privately recognized that it could spell political disaster. “There are a lot of people who don’t know why we needed to do this,” one Trump adviser lamented at the time, adding that the decision had immediately rendered months of meticulous midterm preparation “obsolete.” “If oil hits $100 (per barrel), who knows?” the adviser said. “It’s a political risk, and there’s no ands, ifs or buts about it.” The outlook darkened further over the next couple months, as the war swamped the political conversation and Trump’s own agenda. Plans to send the president on a sustained tour to tout his accomplishments were put on hold. Major strategic decisions — like where and when to begin spending Trump’s roughly $400 million war chest — were delayed. Perhaps worst of all, allies fretted, Trump had betrayed his core political identity as a president devoted to juicing the economy and keeping the US out of foreign wars. “They underestimated the backlash in the base,” one Trump ally said of the White House as the war stretched into its second month, oil hit $100 a barrel and US gas prices neared the $4-per-gallon mark. “If we’re not plenty concerned about that in April, then we’re dead in November.” By the summer, it became clear that the war was not a “total and complete victory,” despite Trump’s repeated claims, and would instead loom over the entire midterm cycle. The June collapse of a short-lived ceasefire had left Republican candidates without a clear message on the conflict, as every economic pillar they had planned to run on melted away. Gas topped $4 and continued to rise, grocery prices were marching upward and polls increasingly showed voters revolting against a president who had promised their costs would go down “on day one.” In some GOP circles, lawmakers and their advisers privately calculated whether and how sharply to break with Trump on key issues in the campaign’s final stretch. A handful had already levied criticisms of his price-hiking tariffs or expressed displeasure with the war — though tentatively and, in several cases, not before giving the White House advance notice. But even as Trump’s approval ratings bottomed out, most declined to take such a significant step. Some concluded that, after defending and justifying Trump’s every move for the last 18 months, abandoning him now wouldn’t win much credibility with swing voters — and would assuredly tank their standing with the MAGA base. Others were simply too wary of inviting Trump’s personal ire, calculating instead that it was better to stick it out and hope his most ardent remaining supporters could pull them across the finish line. Spiraling off message Inside the White House, what had begun as an expansive plan to trumpet Republicans’ policy successes and cement the congressional majority was eventually whittled down to a last-ditch bid to turn out Trump’s MAGA base one final time. The president had remained largely disengaged from the nitty-gritty political planning, at times remarking to those around him that he had already done his job: He’d won the White House. Instead, Trump spent inordinate time overseeing construction projects around Washington that he viewed as critical to his legacy. Americans, however, overwhelmingly saw it as a waste of time and money. When he did address the issues at the top of voters’ minds, it was typically to wave them away. Trump regularly insisted gas prices would soon plummet and argued the Iran war was worth the “short-term pain.” He celebrated tariffs and unreservedly embraced the artificial intelligence sector, despite polls showing deep bipartisan skepticism of both. As for the affordability worries dominating Americans’ concerns, he’d initially dismissed them as a “hoax,” sparking a scramble among his aides to clean up his remarks, an administration official and an adviser said. To their dismay, Trump then went out and said it again and again, eventually turning it into a regular component of his stump speech. “It was a word they made up,” Trump complained during a September rally in North Carolina. “And I got hit with this affordability word for a year-and-a-half.” Trump’s hand-picked candidates The midterm map that Trump aides sought to shrink, meanwhile, had widened — in part due to the weakness of several of Trump’s hand-picked candidates for Senate. In Texas, where Trump elevated Ken Paxton over the objections of GOP Hill leaders, the scandal-plagued candidate was performing so poorly that some operatives in the state privately questioned whether he even wanted the job. Michael Whatley, a close ally of the president, got off to a slow start and never recovered in North Carolina despite the tutelage of several close Trump advisers. Darline Graham, who Trump impulsively endorsed to replace her late brother, South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, looked every bit the political novice in a state that went for Trump by 18 percentage points in 2024. And to the Trump team’s deepening frustration, several House and Senate lawmakers in typically safe seats had been caught flat-footed by their stronger-than-normal challengers. “They were coasting, even when there were signs,” one adviser griped as Republicans raced to shore up Sen. Roger Marshall’s flailing campaign in Kansas, where Democrats are now projected to win for the first time in nearly a century. As gas and diesel prices spiked, dragging down Republicans across the country, the White House searched for any policy levers that might assuage voters facing fresh economic strain. Trump endorsed access to cheaper forms of gasoline and cleared the way for truckers to use tax-free diesel typically reserved for off-road vehicles. He promised payouts to buoy farmers that by Election Day totaled roughly $15 billion. But those gestures largely fell flat, and at points were directly undermined by steps Trump took to try to shore up other parts of the ailing GOP base. Among the most damaging was the decision to temporarily boost beef imports — a move designed to lower grocery prices that ultimately succeeded only in enraging Republicans throughout the Midwest. The war, one Republican operative close to the White House said, was not only unpopular on its own, but had generated widespread domestic fallout that the administration could not contain. “It created an inflation issue that became directly relevant to the president, and a thousand other things cascaded from that,” the operative said. That rising threat to Republicans across the political landscape only further heightened the importance of perhaps the party’s biggest advantage: the roughly $400 million that Trump had accumulated in his super PAC, much of it from wealthy donors and corporations seeking to curry favor during the first year of his presidency. Yet for months, that PAC, MAGA Inc., declined to spend amid Trump’s reluctance to give away money he’d raised to help other candidates and Republican officials’ own difficulties in deciding how and where to deploy cash across a worsening map. After extensive wrangling, the president finally greenlit pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into contests around the nation across the final two months. It was a welcome infusion for the GOP that allowed the party’s two main super PACs to concentrate their spending on swing districts and pickup opportunities, officials said, while Trump’s MAGA Inc. focused on triaging races deeper into red territory. Yet there was still the matter of how best to utilize the president himself. Within Trump’s orbit, some allies felt Republicans’ best shot was to localize their races and keep the focus on Democrats, in hopes that GOP voters’ fears of empowering “socialism” would win out over their more immediate frustrations. Others believed that Democrats had already made the midterms about Trump and, alarmed by the lack of grassroots enthusiasm within the GOP, they argued there was nothing to lose now from unleashing the president in full. “There’s no counter message,” said another ally, “because they’re taking out ads for the [Big Beautiful Bill] and nobody gives two f**ks.” Trump on the trail Trump eventually settled the debate himself. In mid-September, after growing agitated by internal polling showing Republicans consistently trailing in races across the country, he determined he’d take the matter into his own hands, people familiar with the matter said. Trump’s team hastily organized a final-month sprint that put him in a different town nearly every day, barnstorming the nation to plead with his devotees to go vote — even if, this time, it wouldn’t be for him. “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said during one stop in Michigan, echoing an appeal he made at nearly every rally. “When I’m not on the on the ballot, people don’t show up. Please show up and vote.” At times, the near-daily travel invigorated Trump, who basked in the crowds and relished his reputation as what one adviser described as “the greatest turnout machine in the history of American politics.” In other moments, he raged at having to work so hard in the closing stretches of campaigns that were not his, people who spoke with him said. Top Republicans also viewed the tour as a mixed blessing; they hoped the return of Trump’s signature rallies could resuscitate enthusiasm within an inert GOP base, yet worked to steer him toward solidly red districts to minimize any harm to toss-up races. The rallies, GOP officials insisted in the final days, showed signs of boosting turnout — even as Trump offered an inconsistent and sometimes-baffling closing message. During several visits to Ohio, for example, the president publicly fixated on the shape of GOP Sen. Jon Husted’s “ass” — a uniquely Trumpian compliment borne from his disbelief that Husted hadn’t done more on the trail to emphasize his past as a Division III college football player, people familiar with the matter said. Yet for all the enthusiasm on the ground among Trump’s diehards, it did little to assuage voters’ concerns about the war and high prices, or visibly move polls that increasingly showed Republicans being overtaken by a blue wave. As Trump approached the end of his tour, his mood had darkened significantly, those who spoke with him said. So with less than 24 hours to Election Day, Trump returned to a topic that he’s often described as “relaxing” to him: Construction. Standing in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday, Trump devoted much of his final pre-midterm speech to detailing his battles with the pool’s algae and the key decision points involved in repairing pipes and replacing grass. It was a bizarre decision, GOP officials said, but not a fateful one. Trump had set his party on this path eight months ago — all that was left to do now was brace for impact.

cnn.com.title: A 3,200-pound NASA observatory is careening back toward Earth. Here’s what to know
cnn.com.text: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to meet a fiery end early Wednesday morning, nearly 22 years after it launched to study the most powerful explosions in the universe. While most of the 3,200-pound spacecraft is expected to burn up as it blazes through the thick inner band of Earth’s atmosphere, NASA predicts some pieces of the vehicle will hit the ground. “The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely, approximately 1 in 2,100,” NASA said in a statement Monday. The agency also anticipates that Swift’s debris could land somewhere between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude — or about 1,420 miles (2,285 kilometers) below and above the equator. That band encompasses much of Central and South America, Central Africa, southern India, Southeast Asia and northern Australia, as well as vast stretches of ocean. It’s not yet clear exactly when Swift will make its final descent to Earth. Prediction models typically have a margin of error of at least a few hours. An estimate from the nonprofit Aerospace Corporation put reentry 5:19 a.m. ET, plus or minus two hours. A more recent US Space Force projection predicted reentry for 7:42 a.m. ET with the same margin of error. A risky reentry If Swift were launched today, it would likely have to adhere to far stricter safety guidelines regarding end-of-life planning, according to The Aerospace Corporation, which is a federally funded research and development center. Current orbital debris mitigation standards, which were updated in 2019, mandate that “uncontrolled reentries have an expected casualty of less than 1 in 10,000,” said Parker Wishik, a spokesperson for The Aerospace Corporation. He noted in an email that, in this context, “casualty” refers to “serious injury or death.” While NASA has long known that Swift would likely have to make an unpredictable plunge back to Earth, the agency had hoped that a daring rescue mission launched in July could latch on and boost the Swift Observatory as atmospheric drag gradually pulled it from a once-stable orbit. It could have extended Swift’s operating life by a decade or more, but ultimately the effort failed. The spacecraft eventually dropped down to just 171 miles (275 kilometers) above the planet, and the observatory officially stopped gathering scientific data. “At this point, the spacecraft was no longer able to compensate for the effects of the increased drag and entered safe mode,” NASA said in a news release. A team of researchers at Penn State — NASA’s partner on the project and home to the observatory’s Mission Operations Center — sent the final kill-switch command to Swift on October 20.  Swift’s demise was hastened by an increase in solar activity over the past couple of years as the sun reached the peak of its 11-year cycle in 2024. Intense flares and coronal mass ejections caused Earth’s atmosphere to expand, which intensified the drag on Swift, leading scientists to predict it would descend toward our planet this fall. Arizona-based Katalyst Space Technologies scrambled to put together the last-ditch effort to stabilize the Swift observatory earlier this year, getting the rescue mission off the ground in only nine months. The company rapidly produced a spacecraft called LINK, which aimed to grapple the telescope and lift it back into a stable orbit. But the mission failed a few weeks after LINK’s launch in July as the satellite spun out of control in space before reaching the Swift observatory. Another rescue attempt As Swift’s fate was sealed, mission scientists slowly turned the telescope’s instruments back on to collect data and observations right up until the end. The instruments had been shut off for months to save power and mitigate how quickly the spacecraft sank out of orbit. The Swift Observatory, which does not have an established observational replacement waiting in the wings, has served as an astrophysics multi-tool in low-Earth orbit since it launched in November 2004. Named after fast-flying birds, the telescope could quickly pivot to observe blink-and-you-miss-it cosmic events such as flaring black holes. The telescope was originally designed to study the most powerful explosions in the universe, called gamma-ray bursts, but scientists have also used it to monitor other types of cosmic flashes as well as asteroids and comets. Despite the failed attempt to rescue Swift, NASA has signaled it may try similar lifeline-extension missions for other valuable space-based instruments. Last week, the agency issued a solicitation — formally called a Request for Proposals or RFP — to commercial companies, asking how they might boost, service or otherwise prolong the life of the iconic Hubble Space Telescope. NASA’s analysis shows that there’s a 10% chance Hubble will plunge out of orbit by 2032 and a 50% it will deorbit by 2033, according to the RFP. The beloved telescope, launched in 1990, has delivered some of the most recognizable images in astronomy and has transformed scientists’ understanding of the cosmos. There is no replacement for Hubble expected before the 2040s, the RFP states.

cnn.com.title: Trump’s personal push of Darline Graham in South Carolina comes back to bite his party
cnn.com.text: In a stunning upset in typically reliably Republican South Carolina, CNN’s Decision Desk is projecting that Democrat Annie Andrews will defeat President Donald Trump’s hand-picked candidate Sen. Darline Graham. Andrews is flipping a seat Republicans have held for nearly three decades and a state that voted for Trump by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024. But the result has been building since Graham became the GOP nominee in late August. Pushed by Trump, the governor appointed Darline Graham to finish her brother’s term after his sudden death, and she decided to run for the full term. Graham eventually made it through a bruising special primary and runoff to become the GOP nominee after several personal interventions by Trump, including a rally in the state before the primary and dedicated spending from his PAC, MAGA Inc. But the party didn’t immediately unite behind Graham and her campaign struggled, needing help from outside groups. Concerns about her lack of experience persisted, especially after she said “national security is not my thing,” during a primary runoff debate. Andrews, a 45-year-old mother of three, launched her Senate campaign last year, acknowledging the uphill battle she faced running as a Democrat in South Carolina. She was originally running against GOP incumbent Sen. Lindsey Graham until he suddenly died in July. The day after the GOP primary, Andrews was up with a statewide ad, “White Coat,” introducing herself as “a mom to three kids and pediatrician” who will work with Republicans “to cut taxes and keep your family safe.” She ticked off priorities like cutting healthcare costs and taking on insurance companies. Like several other Southern Democrats this cycle, Andrews painted herself as an independent-minded moderate who is concerned about affordability, quality of life and corruption. The Democrat also tapped into lingering Republican frustrations with their candidate, calling Graham “unserious and unqualified” and noting the Senate race is “a job interview, not a coronation.”

cnn.com.title: A blue wave, a rejection of Trump and other takeaways from the midterms
cnn.com.text: The Democratic wave is here. The party claimed control of Congress and won governors’ races across the country on Tuesday – and now, as votes are counted in more key states, the question is how many more Republicans will be wiped out. Across the political map, the blue shift has been enormous. In rural Middle America, the huge margins of victory that Donald Trump posted two years ago have plummeted. In heavily Latino congressional districts, the president’s 2024 gains have evaporated. And though the White House is already deflecting blame, Trump’s interventions in his party’s attempts to hold its House and Senate majorities seem to have only hurt the GOP’s chances. Trump’s recruiting efforts and endorsements were backfiring. Candidates he’d backed over other prominent Republicans had lost or were trailing in Senate races in North Carolina, Georgia, Texas and South Carolina. His redistricting gambit also appears to have fallen flat. In Florida, Democrats won several districts that were redrawn to guarantee Republican victories. In Texas, long the country’s biggest red state, Democrats are in contention to break their decadeslong lockout from statewide office — not just in the high-profile Senate race, but also potentially in the gubernatorial contest and other statewide races. Millions of votes remain to be counted, and it’s far too early to know the full implications of Tuesday’s elections. What’s clear already, though, is that Americans broadly rejected Trump — and Democrats stand to make huge gains because of it. Democrats flip six Senate seats — and aim for more Democrats have already flipped six Republican-held Senate seats the party needed to claim the majority, winning races in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina — and doing so by defeating several candidates who were hand-picked by Trump. State Rep. James Talarico ushered in a generational moment for Texas Democrats as he defeated Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Republican state attorney general who was endorsed by Trump, in what became the most expensive Senate race in US history. In Iowa, state lawmaker Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson — one of the GOP’s star recruits of the 2026 cycle — in the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Turek made the case that the  state was bearing the brunt of Trump’s tariffs and high diesel prices resulting from the war with Iran. In Ohio, two years after losing the state’s other Senate seat, Democrat Sherrod Brown completed a political comeback by defeating Republican Sen. Jon Husted. In Kansas, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall — the latest reminder that though it’s barn red at the presidential level, voters in the state are willing to elect Democrats. In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper trounced former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley — an outcome that was widely expected by strategists in both parties. South Carolina, though, was a stunner. Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — claiming a seat that’s been in GOP hands since Strom Thurmond switched parties in 1964. A Democrat hasn’t won a Senate race in the Palmetto State since 1998. A roster of South Carolina political veterans had been interested in running for the seat after Lindsey Graham’s death in July. But Trump asked Graham’s sister — a political novice — first to occupy the seat temporarily and later pressured her to run for a full term. She struggled in debates and on the campaign trail. South Carolina was nowhere near the top of the Democrats’ list of the most winnable GOP-held seats. And a victory there is a good sign for the party’s chances in states that were expected to be more competitive — including Maine, Iowa and Alaska. Further buoying the Democrats’ hopes of a Senate majority was an early, decisive win by Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff. The race was another example of Trump’s failed midterm maneuvering: His endorsement boosted Rep. Mike Collins to a primary win over a more moderate alternative backed by popular two-term Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. Ossoff’s strengths and Collins’ struggles helped Democrats win the governor’s race in Georgia, as well, with Keisha Lance Bottoms now set to become the nation’s first Black female governor. Florida House races showcase Dem momentum and offer signs of a big Latino swing In Florida, the results offered evidence of a potentially enormous swing among Latino voters in Democrats’ favor. Democrats held onto three seats that Republicans had redrawn in an effort to guarantee victories this fall. CNN has projected that Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz will win in redrawn districts, as will Democrat Pia Dandiya in the 22nd District. In another heavily Hispanic district in central Florida the GOP had redrawn, Democratic Rep. Darren Soto narrowly leads his Republican challenger in the 9th District. Democrats capitalized on President Donald Trump’s historic unpopularity Tuesday, flipping control of both the House and Senate in a resounding and historic midterm victory, CNN’s Decision Desk projects.Only twice in the last 50 years had control of both chambers changed in the same cycle.The exact sizes of the Democrats’ majorities are still yet to be determined as the final election results are counted. But Democrats appear set to have some room for error in both chambers.History was also made in some gubernatorial races on Tuesday. Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will become the first Black female governor in US history, CNN projects. US Rep. Byron Donalds, a Republican, is projected to become the first Black governor of Florida. And Gina Hinojosa is projected to become the first Latina governor of Texas. But the biggest eye-opener might come in South Florida’s 27th District, which is based in the overwhelmingly Latino Miami-Dade County. Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar released a buzzy ad this year standing in front of the White House, criticizing Trump’s immigration policy. She won by 20 percentage points two years ago. She might hold on this year — but she leads Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez by just over a thousand votes. But a swing of that size means the gains Trump made with Latino voters in 2024 have effectively evaporated, at least in Florida. Trump drags down Republicans, but appears unlikely to accept the blame Trump watched returns come in from the White House East Room, where the mood was described as tense. Notably, he went silent on Truth Social for three hours Tuesday night as Democrats kept winning races before posting just after 10:30 p.m.: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.” Left unsaid was that Trump had spent weeks telling his supporters to pretend he was on the ballot — and that he hand-selected many of the candidates who have been suffering tonight. Candidate weakness in South Carolina, North Carolina and Texas in particular became a major headache for national Republicans, who were forced to spend millions contesting races they never expected to be close. Officials have stressed that Trump “left it on the field” — doing what he could to retain congressional majorities but also seeding the ground to pin any Republican losses on the candidates themselves. Trump has been aware that he was likely to catch blame if Republicans lose. That was part of his rationale for carrying out a frenetic campaign blitz over the last month, which by his own admission was exhausting. He says he tried to cut it short, but was convinced to hold final events in Iowa and Kansas. “We gave this a very strong shot,” Trump said Monday at his Reflecting Pool speech, acknowledging history was not on his side. Good signs for Dems who may run in 2028 The results were full of encouraging signs for Democrats who may want to run for president in 2028. At least two potential White House contenders, Govs. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, cruised to victory in their reelection bids. Pritzker nodded to speculation about his political future in his victory speech, saying he’s been asked, “What’s next?” “The answer is simple: I’m going to ask you to continue to hope, to wrap yourself in hope, in courage,” Pritzker said. “We climbed one mountain tonight, but we are sitting at the base of another.” Another possible White House contender, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, was not on the ballot Tuesday but scored a big win when his former aide, Zach Dembo, flipped a GOP-friendly House district in central Kentucky. And in Georgia, Ossoff’s decisive victory is likely to increase 2028 buzz surrounding him, even if he has denied interest in running. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms winning the governor’s race means a fellow Democrat could pick his replacement in the Senate if he were to vacate his seat for a presidential run. This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: Hakeem Jeffries is on track to make House speaker history. But major challenges lay ahead
cnn.com.text: Soon after Hakeem Jeffries arrived in the House in 2013, one of his earliest mentors approached a group of senior Black Democrats with a message. “I think he is the one,” former Rep. Eddie Bernie Johnson told lawmakers at the time, including Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, who recalled she was seated in her long-time perch on the House floor when she made the prediction. Within months, that same bloc of Black Democrats began meeting regularly over dinner to discuss Jeffries’ future — drawing up plans to ensure that he would replace then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi when she retired and hoping to cement his place as the first Black speaker in US history, according to multiple people involved in the discussions. A decade and a half later, Jeffries is now on a clear path to be elected House speaker in January — only second to the vice president in the line of presidential succession — in a position that effectively hands him control of a newly resurgent Democratic party in President Donald Trump’s final two years in power. “A lot of people in this administration should not sleep well at night,” Cleaver said in an interview, predicting that Jeffries and their party would make life punishing for the Trump administration. Ideological and generational challenges ahead That gavel, though, is not yet a guarantee. Jeffries still needs to win over a crop of incoming Democratic socialists decrying current leaders for failing to meet the moment. Once considered a political insurgent himself, Jeffries now battles skepticism from the party’s activist wing over his more-establishment stance on issues like Medicare for All and Israel. Jeffries, a deliberative former corporate lawyer, has also drawn private criticism from some in his party for being overly hesitant. But people close to him insist that he will have a decisive and aggressive approach to wielding the speaker’s gavel in the Trump era — pursuing significant confrontations with the administration and corporate America alike. They say he plans to supercharge a new era of Democratic populism — a tax-the-rich and subpoena-the-CEOs mentality that would unravel decades of cautious party attempts to avoid controversy with big business. He wants to raise the minimum wage by much more than Democrats tried to in 2019, enact strict new ethics codes for the Supreme Court and rein in artificial intelligence. He’ll also be leading the party as it pursues an aggressive oversight agenda into the final two years of Trump’s second term. “The American people are rightly frustrated. They want disruption, they want dramatic change,” Jeffries said in a recent interview with CNN’s Manu Raju, previewing his agenda. If elected, people close to Jeffries said he sees his task as two-fold: He must satisfy a restive electorate that wants Democrats to take big swings and achieve real change — while also avoiding political overreach that could cost them seats two years from now. That means Jeffries will need to limit the whims of his insurgent left. Democrats are unlikely to vote to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement or enact Medicare for All, for instance. His allies say he will seek to avoid votes, wherever possible, on policy relating to Israel. “He’s gonna do bold and smart, not bold and stupid,” one moderate Democrat told CNN. “He’s going to try to avoid massively divisive votes. … He’s going to zero in on affordability and ignore the culture wars.” Another member, Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, added that Jeffries has been clear that Democrats will “win this at the kitchen table and we’re going to govern at the kitchen table.” For him, that includes new ways to make life more affordable, such as expanding access to government healthcare. “I think Americans are ready to move toward a universal healthcare system. There are a number of ways that we can get there,” Crow said, who has co-authored a bill to expand Medicare to Americans aged 60 and above. Another challenge for Jeffries won’t be ideological, it will be generational. Already, plans are underway inside the Democratic caucus to enact new term limits for committee chairs, according to people familiar with the discussions — a huge shift in the seniority-driven Democratic party that reflects the anti-establishment mood of this election. (Current chairs could be grandfathered in for a short time.) But there’s skepticism about whether Democrats can pass another voter priority — a stock-trading ban — as part of the House’s rules for member conduct in January. Some members prefer to pass a standalone bill sometime next year that also includes strict stock-trading rules for Trump administration officials, not just lawmakers, though it would be unlikely to become law, according to people familiar with the discussions. That stock-trading disagreement is a glimpse of one of Jeffries’ biggest challenges next year: Resistance from long-serving members who are used to far more gradual change. Then there is the issue of actually working with the administration. Democrats are expecting little cooperation, if any, with a president who recently coined himself “Mr. Veto.” And even trying to have conversations across the aisle has been a fraught endeavor for Jeffries. This summer, he faced fierce backlash from liberal Democrats after a private meeting with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. (The two worked closely on a criminal justice law in Trump’s first term.) Jeffries later told CNN of the meeting: “We have a responsibility to solve problems and sometimes that means meeting with people on the other side of the aisle.” His path to the gavel Before Jeffries landed the perch of top House Democrat, his supporters occasionally pushed him to consider other positions, according to multiple people who recalled the efforts over the years. Some Black church leaders pushed him to run against former New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio. Another group of House members encouraged him to run for the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee after the death of Rep. Elijah Cummings in 2019. Some even privately urged him to run for president in the summer of 2024 after then-President Joe Biden was forced to leave the race. But he turned down each one with what appeared to be a longtime goal in mind — House speaker. “He could have been chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. He could have been the Democratic whip early on. But he’s very strategic,” Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio said. Jeffries rose through the ranks of the Democratic caucus, in part, because of his skill on the House Judiciary Committee, including a high-profile stint during Trump’s first impeachment and, before that, dealmaking with Republicans on drug and sentencing reform. “He walks in as someone who just looks like he’s just fearless,” added Beatty, who entered Congress alongside Jeffries in 2013. The Brooklynite gained fame in the Trump-era by prosecuting the case against Trump during his 2020 Senate impeachment trial. He was handpicked for the role by Pelosi and famously quoted from the late rapper the Notorious B.I.G. on the Senate floor. (His passion for music is widely known in the party. As a teenager in Brooklyn in the 1980s, he once rap-battled under the name Kid Fresh. Cleaver refers to him as “the prime minister of hip hop.”) In the years since the first impeachment push against Trump, Jeffries has only sharpened his attacks on the president. He has called him “the dumbest person ever to sit at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue” in response to Trump’s attacks on Jeffries’ intelligence. This summer, Jeffries called him a “feeble, unhinged, conspiracy-peddling 80-year-old failed president.” “He loves to fight, he loves confrontation. He’s got that bravado and confidence,” one senior Democratic aide who’s worked closely with both Jeffries and Pelosi told CNN. There has been some friction in Jeffries’ tenure as party leader. Several Democrats recalled a nasty fight over a GOP resolution to honor the “life and legacy” of Charlie Kirk after his assassination last year. Jeffries and his leadership agreed to vote in favor, as a gesture of unity to condemn political violence targeting both parties.
