But his decision infuriated members of the Black caucus, who said the GOP’s resolution praised Kirk while ignoring his record of what they described as hate speech against Black Americans. (Kirk had called the Civil Rights Act a “huge mistake” and has claimed Black leaders like Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and Michelle Obama didn’t have enough “brain processing power” to be taken seriously in politics.) “These are not harmless words. They carry the same spirit of division that once fueled Jim Crow—when racism and bigotry were written into law to deny people their rights and dignity,” one of the Black lawmakers who opposed the resolution, Rep. Troy Carter, wrote at the time of Kirk’s rhetoric. In a meeting after that vote, some of those Black Caucus members confronted Jeffries about how he handled the GOP bill — and why he waited so long to tell his caucus about his decision, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions. “I have never seen the CBC so publicly go after Jeffries,” said one person describing the meeting. Heading into 2027, that rift between the Black caucus and Jeffries is long-healed. One person involved in the many back-and-forth conversations  between Jeffries and Black Caucus members back then said the moment actually strengthened members’ trust in him: “They expressed concerns and he met them.” And next year, the powerful bloc could see its largest-ever number of Black lawmakers — with the nation’s first Black speaker at its helm. A new guard in the Democratic party Shortly after Jeffries was elected party leader, Rep. Henry Cuellar of Texas approached his longtime colleague and urged him to get to the US border immediately. It was 2022: Democrats like Cuellar believed Biden’s border policy was a mess and the only way back to power was understanding how to speak to border communities like his. Jeffries made the trip to Cuellar’s hometown of Laredo for a nighttime border tour — where they watched smuggling attempts in real-time — in addition to more humanitarian-oriented visits with local nonprofits. “I couldn’t get Democrats to say two words: Border security,” Cuellar said, recalling his experience with party leaders up to that point. But after Jeffries’ tour of Laredo, Cuellar said he heard a key shift in his language. “I heard him say ‘border security,’ and ‘you’ve still got to treat migrants with dignity.’” People close to Jeffries say he has been focused for years on how to repair the Democratic party’s sagging brand — which, they add, is not just about defeating Trump. He saw the party’s missteps in recent elections, particularly in 2024, when nearly everyone missed the flashes of anger from Americans who later voted for Trump. Since then, he and his leadership team have been working steadily to build back that trust from voters — lighting into the Trump administration and forcing direct confrontations with Republicans whenever possible. Getting their message out was key, too. Jeffries frequently tells his members that the average American spends about four minutes a week on politics — three-and-a-half of those minutes on Trump. “We are fighting for 30 seconds a week,” he has said, according to people familiar with the remarks. For Jeffries, that looked like a nearly 9-hour floor speech against the GOP’s tax breaks bill, a historic 43-day shutdown over healthcare subsidies and “total war” over redistricting in the midterms. Some of his colleagues underscored another key trait in their leader — “a spirit of American optimism,” in the words of Democratic Rep. Madeleine Dean, at a time when most other politicians of either party have been downright dismayed about the future of the country. Dean recalled the night of the January 6 insurrection at the Capitol, where she and other members were huddled in a safe room as rioters were being removed from the building. She recalled going up to Jeffries — then, the highest-ranking Democrat in the room — and urging him to allow lawmakers to go back to the floor and resume the electoral count. “’Hakeem, they cannot run us out of here,’” Dean recalled telling him. And he agreed — later declaring, in unison with then-Rep. Liz Cheney: “We will go back and do our job.”

cnn.com.title: An electorate unhappy with Trump and the economy hands Congress to Democrats, CNN Voter Poll shows
cnn.com.text: A tide of voter dissatisfaction flooded into Republican states, CNN Voter Poll data shows, handing Democrats definitive victories and control of the House and Senate. President Donald Trump’s approval rating is below 40% among voters nationally, and three-quarters of voters say that economic conditions are bad, with most laying the blame for higher prices directly on Trump’s policies. About one-fifth of midterm voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they disapprove of his performance. What’s notable in the data is how widespread those sentiments are, with Trump’s approval rating underwater even among midterm voters in states that he comfortably won two years ago. That helps explain how Democrats are projected to win Senate races in states like South Carolina, Texas, Iowa and Kansas. The specific contours of each race, of course, played a role as well. In South Carolina, nearly two-thirds of voters said that Republican Darline Graham lacked the right experience, and in Texas and Kansas, most doubted that Republicans Ken Paxton and Roger Marshall had the right character to serve. Economic discontent was felt nationwide Another factor weighing down Republicans across the country was voters’ economic discontent. The share of voters who say inflation has caused them hardship is similar to where it stood in 2024. But while cost-of-living concerns under the Biden administration helped Trump’s path back to the presidency two years ago, many voters now lay the blame for their continued economic malaise directly on the Trump White House. Around two-thirds say they feel that Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the country. More than 60% say that higher costs are largely due to his policies, rather than factors outside of his control. That’s eroded voters’ confidence in the GOP as a whole. Nationally, voters give Democrats the advantage over Republicans to handle the economy. And the roughly one-fifth of voters who don’t trust either party on the economy largely voted for Democratic congressional candidates. The high cost of living, which has weighed heavily on many Americans’ wallets, was top of mind for voters in this election. They expressed concern about the cost of gas and diesel fuel, groceries, utilities and healthcare. The CNN Voter Poll, a successor to previous years’ exit polls, combines traditional in-person interviews at polling places on Election Day with tens of thousands of interviews conducted nationwide in the weeks before the election. That scope makes the polls a powerful tool for understanding the demographic profile and political views of voters in this year’s election. Even so, the Voter Poll is still a poll, with a margin for error — which means it’s most useful when treated as an estimate, rather than a precise measurement. But this year, many trends in the data are clear. Voters shift Democratic The blue wave was evident in the demographic breakdowns from the national results of the CNN Voter Poll, which show how voters split in their choice of House candidate for their district. Democrats consolidated support among several slices of the electorate that had shifted toward the Republicans in the 2022 midterms under President Joe Biden, and in some cases even outdid their performance eight years ago, during Trump’s first presidency. Women moved more toward Democrats Women, who supported the Democrats by about an 8-point margin in 2022, returned to support the party’s candidates in greater force this year. Similarly, male voters were split between the Democrats and Republicans this year, eliminating the double-digit advantage that GOP candidates held in 2022. The youth vote went overwhelmingly blue Voters of all ages also shifted toward the Democrats in comparison with 2022, with voters younger than 30 voting Democratic by an even broader margin than they did during Trump’s first term. Democrats made a dent in GOP’s hold on White voters Democrats narrowed the advantage that Republicans had held with this demographic in previous midterms in 2018 and 2022. White college voters favored Democrats by a wider margin than in either of the past two midterms Both White voters and voters of color with college degrees supported the party by double-digit margins. Meanwhile, Republicans saw some erosion of their 2022 advantage among White voters without a college degree. Self-identified Republicans were more likely than Democrats to cross party lines And political independents who voted this year favored the Democrats by a double digit-margin. The double haters went to Democrats While voters with unfavorable views of both parties split about evenly in 2018, and voted Republican four years ago, in 2026 they were a decisively Democratic voting bloc. This group — often called “double haters” — made up about 15% of this year’s electorate.

cnn.com.title: Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump is arguably the most pro-Israel president of modern times. So his Election Day announcement that the United States would end nearly $4 billion in annual aid to Israel was stunning. But as is often the case with Trump, the announcement — made on Fox News — was short on details and difficult to pin down. It could end up being less seismic in practice than the shock announcement might suggest. Still, Trump’s move was yet another intriguing twist in his relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — his partner in the Iran war, which threatens GOP hopes in Tuesday’s midterm elections. And it comes at a critical political moment, with Israel in political limbo after there was no clear winner in last week’s election and uncertainty over Netanyahu’s future. The political dynamic in the US is also impossible to ignore. In a sense, Trump seems to be conceding a point to Democrats such as Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed in implying that aid to Israel is becoming politically unsustainable in US politics. This underscores an extraordinary fracture in the long-lasting bipartisan pro-Israel consensus in Washington. And it goes beyond the question of how a new Democratic House or Senate would handle the issue after Tuesday’s midterms. The announcement points to an uncertain new era for Israel: Netanyahu has been aligned with Republicans in Washington through several administrations, but there has been significant domestic backlash to Netanyahu’s response in Gaza to the October 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks, not only among progressives but also activists on the right of Trump’s MAGA movement. Growing uncertainty over whether there will be a congressional majority to back Israel and arms sales to its military will create huge future geopolitical implications for the Jewish state and US Middle East policy. Trump ignites an Election Day furor Trump loves to shock, to create news around himself and to distract. So perhaps his announcement in an interview on Fox News was a political play on a day when many Republicans fear a stinging rebuke from voters. He certainly seemed to surprise the Fox anchors. “I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping …. they’re fine with it because, you know, they’ve become a very successful country,” he said. Trump added that the US would help the Israelis if they needed it. “But by end of this year, we won’t be paying Israel.” The president appeared to be referring to annual US military aid to Israel, which amounts to just less than $4 billion a year under a deal made under former President Barack Obama in 2016. That arrangement is due to run through the end of 2028. Most of the funds are spent on buying weapons and equipment for the Israeli armed forces from exclusively US manufacturers, so the deal has significant implications for US businesses and employment. Attention is turning to what US and Israeli military cooperation will look like in future. Netanyahu told the Economist in January he wanted to “taper off” US military aid to Israeli within 10 years and that the shift was “in the works.” It’s hard to know whether Trump’s statement on Tuesday means that the US aid would stop immediately, a step that would be intriguing but would not amount to a strategic fracture between the allies. Foreign policy analysts who have served in both Republican and Democratic administrations have argued Israel is now such a powerful economy that it doesn’t need US aid to buy military equipment. The nexus between US arms manufacturers and Israel is expected to remain strong, and the militaries of the allies have recently worked together more closely than ever. That was the case even before the Iran war — for instance, when the Biden administration staged massive air and naval defensive operations to repel Iranian cruise missile and drone attacks in 2024. Brett McGurk, who was a senior White House and State Department official for four administrations, said the issue of US aid to Israel is deeply misunderstood. “I wouldn’t overstate the significance” of Trump’s remarks Tuesday, McGurk said. “Whether he’s talking about, we’re going to end the MOU when it ends in 2028, or we’re going to stop it right now, I don’t know,” added McGurk, a CNN global affairs analyst and author of the new book “Brink” about his role negotiating hostage releases in the Gaza crisis. Israel and the Palestinians are now a domestic US issue Trump’s announcement came as tens of millions of Americans are voting after an election campaign that showcased the new intertwining of the issue of Israel and the Palestinians in domestic US politics. It was extraordinary to hear him apparently reacting to opposition to US aid to Israel from Democrats like El-Sayed, whom he’s subjected to a torrent of anti-Muslim rhetoric. The Michigan Democrat has argued that Americans are paying more for groceries because of a war the US is fighting at the behest of Israel. “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they (Israel) don’t need it?” Trump told Fox and Friends. “It’s a bad talking point because you’d say — ‘Why don’t we give everybody $4 billion?’” The Israel issue caused a weekend clash between El-Sayed and his former Democratic primary foe Haley Stevens, who then endorsed his GOP rival, Mike Rogers. Stevens objected to an ad by a left-wing influencer featuring a couple in a supermarket blaming higher prices on Israel. El-Sayed denounced the ad, which his team said was not affiliated with the campaign. But the showdown encapsulated the schism over Israel that could complicate any new Democratic congressional majorities. Progressives may interpret Trump’s shift as a validation of their positions. “Even a broken clock can be right twice a day,” El-Sayed said Tuesday, according to the Wall Street Journal. Others, however, argue that critiques of Israel’s government too often cross over into antisemitism — a charge candidates like El-Sayed deny. Trump may also be seeking a political win for himself. Ending US aid to Israel would speak to Trump’s “America First” instincts and hostility to the use of American wealth to support foreign nations. His argument that he’d use unspent cash to pay down the deficit is less convincing, given ballooning national debt in his two terms. While progressives are outraged at Israel because of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, anti-Israel sentiment has also been rising to Trump’s right in the Republican Party, fanned by influencers and podcasters with huge audiences. CNN’s Donie O’Sullivan, who has spent months speaking with Trump supporters, found many believe the US is fighting Israel and are skeptical about the US relationship with its government. In a Quinnipiac poll published in June, 48% of respondents said the US is too supportive of Israel; 38% said US support was about right; and only 7% said the US was not supportive enough. This was the highest percentage of voters thinking that Washington was too supportive of Israel since Quinnipiac first started asking the question in January 2017. In a sign of how sentiment on Israel has shifted among Democrats, former Obama White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, who may run for president in 2028, has argued against unconditional US military aid to Israel and called for a new US relationship with the country in a speech in Tel Aviv earlier this year. In one sense, it might make sense politically for Israel to try to separate its military decisions and purchases from polarizing US domestic politics. It would be free to make its own choices about what to buy, although in practice it’s unlikely to turn to Europe’s manufacturers because of huge public anger there over Gaza. The idea that it would purchase Russian or Chinese equipment seems a long shot given certain US opposition. But such scenarios point to another headache for Israel if it remains a flashpoint in US politics. Presidents can authorize arms sales to foreign states; lawmakers can seek to block them, but in this case, the chances of veto-proof majorities seem slim. But there’s another worrying possibility for Israel’s supporters: that political hostility produces a president from either party who is less committed to its national security needs than Trump, former President Joe Biden or their predecessors. As Emanuel put it in an interview with CNN’s Fareed Zakaria in July, Israel could pay a price because of its own actions. “That’s not a Democratic Party problem. That’s an America problem,” he said.

cnn.com.title: Justice Department sends criminal target letters in Alaska probe to people aligned with Democratic party
cnn.com.text: The Justice Department sent target letters to more than a dozen people it believes helped recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent, in Alaska — an indication that the department is working towards bringing federal charges, according to two sources familiar with the investigation. The recipients include the leadership of the Elias Law Group, the law firm that represents both the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign, the sources said. In a statement posted online, its chairman Marc Elias said, “No one should be surprised that President Trump’s Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day. “We will not be intimidated by a sham investigation,” Elias said. “We are going to keep working around the clock to support our clients and make sure President Trump and his party enjoy a well-deserved beating at the ballot box.” The target letters, which were largely sent to individuals aligned with the Democratic Party, are a remarkable move so close to Election Day. Typically, the letters are sent to warn individuals that they may imminently face charges These letters also warn that the people must preserve documents, records, and communications while the investigation continues, a law enforcement official told CNN. A New York Times report alleged that Peltola’s campaign worked with senior aides at the committee — which directs the party’s campaign strategy in Senate races — to find another Dan Sullivan to stave off votes from the Republican incumbent. The incumbent is Dan S. Sullivan. The man running against him is Daniel J. Sullivan. The Justice Department has dramatically accelerated the criminal probe since the report, CNN previously reported. The story provided investigators new material, US Attorney Michael Heyman said in a press conference Friday. Heyman and other department officials say their election-related efforts in Alaska and other states are intended to safeguard votes, not sway the election as critics have alleged. The department has also issued more than 100 grand jury subpoenas and preservation letters, one law enforcement official said, and investigators have begun conducting witness interviews. Among those interviewed is Matthew Salisbury, a one-time candidate for the US House of Representatives. Salisbury said an operative attempted to recruit him to run as a spoiler candidate against Sen. Sullivan. Salisbury told CNN that he reached out to the bureau and was subsequently interviewed at the local field office. He provided agents with information on the political operative who approached him in December. The interview had “no pressure, no leading questions or allusions to what they were investigating,” Salisbury said. Salisbury did not enter the race, telling CNN that “I just felt as if this was never intended to support me. It was intended to split the ticket, and I didn’t want to be a part of that because it just didn’t feel right. It felt unethical and it felt like it would be deceptive.” FBI agents have also begun visiting the homes of Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign donors in the remote Alaska island he lives on, CNN previously reported. The agents are asking people if they knew which Dan Sullivan they donated to. CNN’s Curt Devine contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Spanish transport minister resigns after two deadly train crashes in one year
cnn.com.text: Spain’s Minister of Transport Óscar Puente announced his resignation after two deadly train crashes occurred in a single year, including one last week that killed 69 people and injured more than 200. “I made the decision about my future in the first few minutes after the tragedy,” Puente told lawmakers in Madrid. “A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this severity in less than a year, however different they may be and regardless of whether or not they bear direct responsibility for them.” Puente resigned six days after one train plowed into another after what authorities say was a combination of human and computer errors along a high speed railway line connecting Madrid and Andalusia. One train, operated by Spain’s national rail service, crashed into a stationary train at high speed during a safety system failure that had halted all rail traffic along the line. “There was a red signal prohibiting movement, yet the train was authorized to proceed,” Puente said last week. “It is a decision made under inexplicable circumstances.” Last week’s crash was preceded by another serious rail accident in January, where two high-speed trains collided head-on in the town of Adamuz, killing at least 41 people. At the time, it was the deadliest crash Spain had seen in more than a decade. Numerous politicians and Spain’s transport workers’ union had called on Puente to resign in the aftermath of last week’s collision. The night of the crash, police scuffled with a hundreds of protesters outside the transport ministry headquarters, some of whom carried placards demanding that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez resign. Puente’s announcement arrives just three weeks before the country’s general elections, in which the minister said he would not be standing as a candidate. Sánchez called those elections early in the wake of several corruption scandals, a controversy over housing affordability and numerous setbacks for his socialist PSOE party in municipal elections. Sánchez praised Puente in a statement on social media, saying that the former transport minister stepped aside “out of respect for the victims and the progressive project.” “Politicians like him dignify our country and show us that not all of us are the same,” Sánchez wrote. “While some only give lessons, others give everything.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

cnn.com.title: Google will let schools turn off AI, but they may also lose Search
cnn.com.text: Google is rolling out new controls for schools to limit students’ access to the company’s AI tools. But if schools opt out of AI altogether, they’ll also lose access to Google Search. The policy change could mark a major shift in how students and educators interact with one of the biggest providers of education technology in the world. Google’s Chromebook laptops are used by tens of millions of students, sometimes starting in kindergarten. The move comes as many communities have pushed for stricter limits on screen time and AI use in schools, amid growing fears that the technology could stunt students’ learning and development or pose safety risks. A number of school districts, including New York City and Los Angeles public schools, banned generative AI tools for many or all students this school year. Google on Tuesday said its products that use AI, like its Gemini assistant and Google Search, will be off by default for K-12 student accounts, until school administrators “explicitly turn them on.” The change reverses an earlier move by Google in August to turn on Gemini by default in its Google Classrooms app. But now, if schools want to turn off AI entirely, they’ll also lose access to Google Search. The company said the changes are in response to calls from educators and policymakers for more control over AI tools. Chris Phillips, vice president of education at Google, told the New York Times that “search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” and that schools that ban AI “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” Google has made AI central to Search in recent years — adding “AI overviews” summarizing answers at the top of many results pages and expanding the size of the search bar to accommodate longer queries. Google’s Tuesday blog post does not offer specifics on how these controls will work, or what students might see if they tried to access Google Search from a school that has banned AI. Phillips wrote in the post that the company will “share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition.” In response to questions from CNN about how the new controls would work, Google pointed to a Tuesday afternoon post on X in which the company said the policy change would give schools “more choice, not less.” It added that schools would be able to toggle on Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search individually. But the post still implies that schools will not be able to use Search without AI features, saying: “AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.” The policy change came as part of a larger announcement by Google about a slate of updates to its AI tools for learning, based on the idea that the technology should help students work through problems rather than simply giving them answers. Under this new “guided learning” principle, Google says that when its systems detect, for example, that a student is using Search for homework help, they’ll be prompted to walk through the problem or topic step-by-step rather than receiving a single answer. It’s an approach also being taken by other AI companies, as they seek to convince educators and parents that their products are valuable learning tools, and that experience with AI in school is essential to success in the workforce later. OpenAI in August announced “ChatGPT for Teens” which, in addition to safety controls, focuses heavily on learning, allowing parents and teens to turn on “Study Mode” to work through questions. Many tech companies have also provided funding to train teachers in AI. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who announced the New York Public Schools AI ban this year, responded to Google’s policy change by accusing the company of trying to “force” AI into schools. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children,” he said in an X post Tuesday.

cnn.com.title: Supreme Court prepared to rule that publicly funded religious schools can reject children of same-sex couples
cnn.com.text: A majority of the Supreme Court signaled on Tuesday it would allow Catholic preschools receiving taxpayer money to deny enrollment to children of same-sex couples, potentially delivering another significant win for religious rights in schools. The court’s conservative majority was unconvinced that a Colorado law, which bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender in publicly funded preschools, could be squared with recent high-profile precedents that expanded the ability of those religious schools to receive public money. Broadly, the case represents a clash between First Amendment religious protections and laws intended to protect gay and transgender Americans from discrimination. When those conflicts have come to the Supreme Court in recent years, religious claims have won time after time. And there was no indication over the course of two hours of an Election Day oral argument that the Colorado dispute would be any different. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, at one point, questioned why Colorado had “provoked” the confrontation and missed a “win-win” by enforcing the discrimination provision and not allowing Catholic schools to opt out to “respect religious rights.” “It seems like this is a would-be solution in search of a problem,” Kavanaugh, a member of the court’s conservative wing, told the Colorado attorney defending the state law. “I’m just trying to figure out why we’re here.” In many ways, though, the case was of the court’s own making. For years, the conservative majority has expanded the ability of religious schools to receive public funding — chipping away at a wall many Americans understood to have long separated church and state. But those decisions largely steered clear of questions about what would happen when those publicly funded religious schools declined to enroll the child of a gay couple or use a student’s preferred pronoun in the classroom. Sensing that Colorado’s argument was likely a lost cause, the court’s three-justice liberal wing repeatedly leaned into an attorney representing the Catholic parish and a Colorado family that sued to challenge the state’s anti-discrimination law. “What you’re basically saying is, ‘We can exclude people merely because the exposure to them would cause us harm’ — that’s really what you’re saying,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor told the attorney for the Trump administration, which opposes Colorado’s law. “That is completely what you’re saying: We can exclude children of same-sex marriage, we can exclude children who might have transgender feelings or beliefs because exposing other children to them creates a problem.” Sarah Harris, arguing for the Justice Department, rejected that framing. Instead, she said, the Catholic schools were exercising their religion by “requiring parents to agree with a school that they’re going to adhere to tenets of the Catholic faith and act consistently with them.” Colorado enacted a ballot provision in 2020 that provides state funding for a universal preschool program, allowing both public and private schools to take part. The program includes a nondiscrimination provision that requires each school receiving public money to provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll, regardless of race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity and other factors. The appeal, filed by the religious public interest firm Becket, appeared ready-made for a 6-3 conservative court that has repeatedly sided with religious interests. In one series of decisions, the court has made clear that when the government opens educational funding programs up to public and private schools, it cannot bar religious schools from taking part just because they are religious or offer religious instruction. The court in 2022, for instance, barred Maine from excluding religious schools from a tuition assistance program that allows parents to use vouchers to send their children to public or private schools. Maine responded to that decision by embracing language like Colorado’s, technically allowing religious schools to take part but imposing anti-discrimination language the Catholic Church says it cannot bear. Colorado’s history of cases involving religion and LGBTQ issues At least some conservative justices seemed frustrated with the idea that states could be using such anti-discrimination provisions as a pretext to bar religious participation. “If you know that the effect of choosing that requirement will push out those with contrary beliefs, how is that different?” conservative Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Colorado’s deputy solicitor general, Helen Norton. Norton said there is “zero evidence” that the state targeted religious schools with its anti-discrimination language. She noted the state encouraged religious schools to take part, and that some religious schools — including Catholic schools — were engaged in the program. And Colorado’s anti-discrimination provision, she said, was enacted before the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in the Maine case. A decision in the Colorado dispute is expected by the end of June. A few conservative justices noted that many claims pitting religious rights against LGBTQ Americans had come from Colorado in recent years. Justice Samuel Alito, among the court’s most ardent defenders of religious rights, pressed Norton about her “state’s record in recent First Amendment cases,” ticking through a list that included an opinion this year endorsing a religious counselor’s challenge to Colorado’s ban on “conversion therapy” and a 2018 decision in which the court ruled in favor of a Colorado baker who refused to bake a cake to celebrate the marriage of a same-sex couple. “What should we make of all of this?” Alito asked. “Your honor,” Norton said, “there is no evidence of any sort of any religious hostility or animus” in the state’s preschool program. Justice Elena Kagan, a member of the court’s liberal wing, seemed concerned about the long-term consequences of a loss for Colorado. She speculated that the next case could involve a family whose child was enrolled in a public school and who argued that allowing their child to attend classes alongside a gay or transgender peer burdened their religion. “It’s going to be pretty easy for religious groups or religious individuals to come forward and say this would be a substantial burden on my religious beliefs,” Kagan said. “With respect to public schools alone, these inquiries could go on forever.”

cnn.com.title: Melania Trump to bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to White House this week
cnn.com.text: First lady Melania Trump will bring representatives from Russia and Ukraine to the White House on Thursday, after announcing a ceasefire in the city of Oleshky last month. “First Lady Melania Trump will personally bring representatives of Russia and Ukraine, two nations actively at war, together at the White House,” the first lady’s office said on Tuesday, touting the limited ceasefire as an “unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American First Lady.” Trump, who will also deliver remarks on the limited ceasefire, has kept a much lower profile during her husband’s second term. But while she’s eschewed some of the more traditional roles of the job, she’s engaged behind the scenes in more substantive policy work. Trump announced on October 23 that she had secured a localized ceasefire to facilitate the humane evacuation of elderly residents from Oleshky. The limited ceasefire began on October 27 and concluded on Sunday. Hundreds of people were evacuated from Oleshky and returned to Ukraine, including one man who hadn’t seen his wife for 1,711 days. The humanitarian situation had become so dire in Oleshky that some residents were forced to eat grass and weeds without access to medicine, clean water or electricity, Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, said last month. Trump’s office said that she worked directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership as the “exclusive intermediary” through channels she previously established while working to reunite children separated from their families during the war. “The mission was a success, delivering critical aid to the region and enabling the evacuation of nearly 800 people,” Trump posted on X, adding that she hoped Oleshky “serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.” The first lady’s office said last month that the circumstances of Oleshky came to her attention during a private discussion at the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. CNN previously reported that Pope Leo discussed the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky on a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier in October while in the hospital recovering from lung cancer surgery, according to the Vatican. The Kremlin said that Putin “supported” the Vatican’s intention to help alleviate the conditions.

cnn.com.title: Trump says US is cutting off aid to Israel at year’s end because ‘they don’t need it’
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the United States is cutting off $4 billion in aid to Israel at the end of the year because “they don’t need it.” Trump, speaking to Fox News on the morning of Election Day, suggested that US aid to Israel has become a powerful political talking point for Democrats and questioned why Republicans should “suffer the slings” from candidates like Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed when Israel isn’t in need of assistance. “It’s a bad talking point because when you say, ‘Why don’t we give everybody $4 billion?’ Israel’s our number one; we give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it,” he said. The US provides Israel $3.8 billion of military aid a year under a 10-year memorandum of understanding that began in 2018. It is set to expire in 2028. Trump appears to be suggesting he would terminate it at the end of this year. Israel is allowed to use that aid to purchase US weapons, so the money ultimately goes to American arms manufacturers. Trump said that if Israel needed the money, he would keep the aid going but added that he “reached an agreement” with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. CNN has reached out to Netanyahu’s office and the White House for additional details. The announcement — and Trump’s explicitly tying it to US politics — speaks to how polarizing US support for Israel has become for both Democrats and Republicans. However, former US officials expressed skepticism that the news would make a difference for voters at the ballot box on Tuesday. They also questioned whether the administration would actually follow through with the military aid cut, particularly if the US resumes military operations against Iran. It is also the role of Congress to appropriate funding. Still, the sudden news that Trump plans to end aid to Israel appears to be a major about-face, removing one of the major pillars of US military support for Israel. Aaron David Miller, a former Middle East negotiator for several US administrations, said that “the Israel issue has become a hugely polarizing issue in the Republican Party.” “You have MAGA outliers like Tucker Carlson, Marjorie Taylor Greene, and others, and the Vice President himself, who probably does represent a significant constituency of those who don’t see the value in in this sort of close relationship with Israel,” he said. The announcement also comes one week after Israel’s election during which the US president offered his full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu. Trump called Netanyahu “the kind of partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a country for which it has done so much.” Vice President JD Vance did not echo that endorsement. Miller called the timing of the announcement “awkward,” given Netanyahu is attempting to form a coalition to remain in power. “In the middle of coalition negotiations, here you have the president of the United States announcing unilaterally that a major element of the US-Israel relationship is going to be zeroed out,” he told CNN. Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main political rival, who is also trying to agree a coalition deal to take over as prime minister, reacted strongly to the news. “The special relationship with the U.S. is a central component of Israel’s national security. The fact that the defense establishment is learning, together with the citizens of Israel, about a change in the fabric of the strategic relationship through the media, shows just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct is a real danger. He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced,” Eisenkot said in a post on X. The last reported call between Trump and Netanyahu was on Saturday. It’s unclear if they have spoken since then. Netanyahu has spoken openly about the need to end US military aid to Israel, but never on such a short timeline. In May, the US and Israel began formal talks on a new agreement to replace the memorandum of understanding, though it’s not clear if there is any framework in place. Just days before last week’s election, Netanyahu told an Israeli news channel that the end of US aid was coming. “If you think we’re going to continue receiving what I secured twice, tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget, get used to the fact that we won’t,” he said. Pressed on Fox whether he was cutting of $4 billion in military aid or $4 billion as a check, Trump said, “Any way you want to define it.” “You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash. What we give them — $4 billion of things and money — and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money,” Trump said. He said Israel “can buy whatever they want.” Under Democrat and Republican administrations, the US has provided significant military support to Israel. That has continued in Trump’s second term, including as recently as September, when the administration authorized a $2.8 billion sale of heavy bombs to Israel. Miller noted that although Israel can militarily defend itself without US assistance, he doubted the US will “turn off the spigot now” with the threat of renewed war with Iran. There has been growing congressional pushback, primarily from Democrats, against continued US military support for Israel. However, a provision in the annual defense bill, which passed the House in July, would codify and deepen cooperation between the US and Israel on defense technology. The head of Israel’s left-wing Democrats party lambasted Netanyahu after Trump’s announcement, calling it a “huge failure.” Yair Golan, a retired deputy chief of staff in Israel’s military, said in a statement on X, “A responsible prime minister would have fought to increase America aid, not eliminate it. Netanyahu is deepening the security and economic crisis and endangering Israel’s future.” Netanyahu biographer and journalist Anshel Pfeffer said Trump’s sudden declaration that US aid to Israel would abruptly stop at the end of the year was a personal failure for Israel’s longest-serving leader and for Ron Dermer, a member of Netanyahu’s inner circle who managed the relationship with the Trump administration. “Netanyahu and Dermer, who both claim to be the biggest experts in American politics, have together overseen the most dramatic decline in Israel-US relations,” he said on X. This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: Scientists say they’ve found the strongest evidence yet of red blood cells in a dinosaur bone
cnn.com.text: Traces of prehistoric blood could reveal unprecedented clues about dinosaur biology, but they’ve been notoriously difficult to confirm. Now, researchers studying a 115 million-year-old dinosaur bone say they’ve found the strongest evidence yet of red blood cells in a fossil. Tissues, cells and other soft biological samples rarely ever survive the fossilization process and thus make for controversial discoveries. A few previous studies, dating back to the late 1990s, have reported structures resembling red blood cells in dinosaur and other reptile fossils, but researchers have fiercely debated their legitimacy. The new study, published Monday in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, used a combination of new microscopic imaging and chemical analyses to find not only microscopic structures resembling red blood cells preserved within the dinosaur bone, but also chemical evidence of heme — a molecule in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. According to the study’s authors, it is the first time heme has been detected in situ, or within the structures themselves, in a dinosaur fossil. The well-preserved Early Cretaceous bone and new research approach bolster the argument that biological structures and molecules can survive in prehistoric fossils, said lead author Kliti Grice, organic geochemist and John Curtin Distinguished Professor at Curtin University in Perth, Australia. “The exciting implication is not just what we have found in this dinosaur. It is that we now have approaches that can be applied to other fossils to ask how much original biological information may still be hidden within them,” Grice said in an email. However, not all experts are convinced that the microscopic structures are truly red blood cells. If researchers find similar evidence of red blood cells in more fossil specimens, it “could potentially help us ask much more sophisticated questions about the physiology of extinct animals,” Grice said. Identifying red blood cells in dinosaurs The fossil is a partial hind limb of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a theropod dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous. Paleontologists dug up the leg bone in 2008 at the geological site Mina Pedra Branca in northeastern Brazil within the Romualdo Formation, a rocky area known for its exceptionally preserved fossils. Scientists believe stagnant waters limited oxygen and slowed the decomposition of remains buried in this region. Within the bone’s vascular canals — microscopic tubes that carry contain blood vessels and nerve fibers — the study authors found an abundance of oval-shaped microstructures that looked similar to red blood cells. The team then used a combination of imaging and chemical analysis to identify whether the structures contained signatures consistent with red blood cells. Past research may have separately described red blood cell-like structures and possible remnants of blood chemistry in dinosaur fossils, but this study brings together multiple lines of evidence, including the structures’ location, appearance, mineral composition and associated chemical signals, Grice said. The researchers suggest that low-oxygen burial conditions at the site may have limited the breakdown of organic material, helping the structures survive. Along with heme, the study authors found the bone contained traces of manganese oxides, minerals that may have further helped stabilize and preserve the cells. “Bones provide extraordinary information about anatomy, growth, locomotion and evolution. But cellular and molecular preservation potentially gives us access to a different layer of biological information: the chemistry of the living animal and its tissues,” Grice said. However, she emphasized that it is too early to draw conclusions about the physiology of Aratasaurus based on one specimen. “One of the first questions is whether this is an extraordinarily rare occurrence or whether similar preservation has simply been overlooked in other fossils,” she said. “There may therefore be fossils sitting in museum collections around the world that contain molecular and cellular information that has simply never been investigated.” What lies ahead Grice and her team plan to expand their research to other fossils from different species, geological time periods and environments to better understand how widespread this type of well-preserved molecular evidence might be. In the future, more molecular clues could help researchers investigate how dinosaurs transported oxygen through their bodies, how their tissues functioned and how their biology compared with that of animals alive today. But does finding red blood cells from a dinosaur bring scientists any closer to recreating its DNA, as seen in books and movies like “Jurassic Park”? Not necessarily, said Timothy Cleland, a physical scientist at the Smithsonian Institution’s Museum Conservation Institute. Heme and DNA are different molecules, and they would fossilize in bone in different ways, he explained. Finding evidence of one does not mean the other has survived. “This study opens new research avenues to explore heme b preservation within bone, especially in exceptional sites like this one,” Cleland said in an email, referring to the most common form of heme. “Additionally, this study begs the question, does this kind of preservation extend beyond this single dinosaur to other species within the Romualdo Formation as well as to other locations with exceptional preservation?” The structures also differed in size and shape from red blood cells in living birds and crocodilians, the authors noted in the study. But they cautioned that modern species may not be the best comparison for non-avian dinosaurs — and that the cells they found in Aratasaurus museunacionali may not retain their original shape from when the animal was alive. Cleland, who was not involved in the new study, said future research could help scientists better understand how red blood cells might change after an animal dies, which could possibly explain Aratasaurus’ odd cell shapes. It’s also possible that the structures might not be remnants of red blood cells at all. The findings do not meet established standards for identifying fossilized blood cells, said Mary Schweitzer, professor emeritus in the department of biological sciences at North Carolina State University. She was not involved in the study. She questioned whether the structures’ shape and size sufficiently match red blood cells in living relatives of dinosaurs as well as the significance of hausmannite, the type of manganese oxide the study authors predominantly found. Schweitzer noted that this substance is not detected in living red blood cells. But Grice said the team does not consider hausmannite an original component of the cells. Rather, they believe it formed during fossilization and may have helped preserve the structures and associated molecular evidence. Still, Schweitzer said in an email that the authors’ use of multiple analytical techniques is an exciting advancement for the field. Based on the data, she said she is hopeful that some molecules from the dinosaur itself remain preserved in the bone. “The usability of fossil molecules preserved in deep time is only just beginning to be explored, as conventional wisdom states preservation like this is not possible,” Schweitzer said. “The more studies we can do on very old fossils, the more we can learn about the interaction between the burial environments and the degrading organism.” Further research could eventually help scientists answer much bigger questions, including what prehistoric molecules can reveal about disease, biological processes and how molecules have evolved over time, she added. “If we can get beyond ‘It can’t’ to ‘What if it can?’, there is no telling what may lie ahead!” Schweitzer said.

cnn.com.title: Exit polls have become the CNN Voter Poll. Here’s what that means
cnn.com.text: CNN’s Election Night coverage has for decades featured the results of surveys, known as exit polls that aim to explain how and why voters made their decisions. This year, those surveys are changing and they have a new name. The CNN Voter Poll incorporates traditional in-person exit polling techniques alongside a robust, large-sample nationwide survey fielded before Election Day. The two sample sources combined will yield an in-depth look at the electorate nationally as well as in the 45 states holding US Senate or governor elections this midterm. The earliest results from the Voter Poll will be reported after 5 p.m. ET on Election Day. Data that could characterize the outcome of a race is not reported until after the polls have closed. And as in the past, the results of the survey will change throughout the night as additional interviews are conducted and, later on, as the data is adjusted to reflect the results of the election. The Voter Poll is based on interviews with roughly 100,000 voters and is conducted by SSRS on behalf of CNN and other major news organizations, including ABC, the Associated Press, CBS, Fox News, MS NOW and NBC. Like the exit polls that CNN has relied on in the past, the Voter Poll helps us better understand who came out to vote, how different groups of people voted and how they feel about some of the biggest issues of the campaign. It incorporates several different survey techniques to represent voters regardless of how or when they choose to cast their ballots. Nearly 80,000 voters participated in the pre-election survey, which was conducted between October 19 and November 3. These voters came from several sources. Some were chosen randomly from a list of registered voters across the country, and were contacted by postcard, telephone, text message or email and invited to take the survey. Others came from online panels of people who are signed up to take surveys through SSRS or Verasight, but were also matched back to the same voter file. Since all survey participants were connected back to the voter file, researchers conducting the poll have the same basic information about whether they’ve voted in the past as well as demographic and political traits for all people who took the poll. They can use that information to assess how likely each respondent is to actually turn out to vote and to ensure the surveys are representative through a process called weighting. Those voters who participated in the survey but were not verified as having cast a ballot before Election Day are then recontacted on Election Day or just before to confirm that they did indeed cast a ballot and to check whether their vote choice remains the same. In 15 states with highly competitive races, those pre-election interviews are then combined with Election Day exit polls conducted in-person, by distributing paper questionnaires to a randomly selected set of voters chosen from voting locations around each state. The polling locations were themselves selected through random sampling, meaning the resulting interviews should be representative of Election Day voters across the state. Roughly 22,000 voters are expected to be interviewed this way. Respondents to both pre-election and Election Day surveys were able to complete the poll in either English or Spanish. Results for the full national sample have a margin of error of plus or minus 0.6 percentage points; it is larger for subgroups and in individual states. More details on the methodology of the Voter Poll are available here.

cnn.com.title: Bomb threats on flights in Europe cause disruption, no devices found
cnn.com.text: At least seven flights and a cruise ship in Europe received bomb threats on Tuesday, causing disruption at airports although no devices were discovered. At least two flights to Warsaw, two to Sofia, two to ​Rome and one to Murcia airport in Spain were subjected to the threats on Tuesday, and another flight to ‌Sofia had been threatened a day earlier. An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian Air Force accompanied one of the flights to Rome while an Israel-bound cruise ship was searched for bombs in Greece. There was no claim of responsibility and officials did not attribute blame. None of the affected airlines responded to Reuters’ requests for comment. Rhys Jones, Analysis Output Manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, ​said that seven confirmed bomb threats in a single day impacting flights was exceptional. “The lack of clear target state, airline, or route indicates that general ​disruption to aviation operations is the aim,” Jones told Reuters. Authorities diverted a LOT flight from London that was meant to land at ​Warsaw’s Chopin airport to nearby Modlin airport, which was closed and then reopened after the plane was searched and ​no device was found. Another Warsaw-bound flight, an SAS flight from Copenhagen, ​landed at Chopin as scheduled. Chopin airport said no device was found and the airport remained operational. Two flights to Sofia threatened Bomb threats were made against planes traveling from ​Milan/Bergamo and Dublin to Sofia, Bulgaria’s transport ministry said in a statement to Reuters. Both landed safely and no explosive devices were ​found on inspection. The Bergamo flight was operated by Wizz Air and was carrying 176 passengers, the statement said. The Dublin flight, operated by Ryanair, had 186 passengers on board. BTA had earlier quoted an Interior Ministry official as saying a flight from Israel had been impacted, but authorities later said this was ​not the case. A day earlier, a Wizz Air flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Budapest airport after receiving a bomb threat, Hungarian ​Defence Minister ​Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said ⁠in a Facebook post. In Murcia in southeastern Spain, parts of an airport were cordoned off on Tuesday after a ‌bomb threat ⁠was reported on a Ryanair flight from Manchester. Officials said the report proved to be a hoax, and the airport resumed normal operations after authorities found no explosives on board. Ryanair declined to immediately comment. Two other Ryanair flights – one from Lisbon and another from Dublin – were searched at Rome’s Fiumicino airport following bomb threats, said a source from airport operator ADR. The Dublin flight was escorted by the ​Italian Air Force until it landed. The ​alert was cleared and the ⁠airport continued to operate as usual with no effects on other flights, the person said. An ⁠explosives detection dog and a diver searched the Panama-flagged Crown Iris cruise ship on the Greek island of Syros after an unknown person said an explosive device had been attached to the boat’s hull, authorities said. Initial checks found no explosive device with coast ​guard specialists expected to carry out further inspections before the ship could resume its voyage. While no country pointed fingers over the bomb threats, they come at a time when European officials have been ​blaming both Russia and Iran for what they describe as “hybrid attacks” and acts of sabotage. Moscow ​and Tehran both ⁠deny any such campaign. This week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several European countries. Some experts said hoax bomb threats could be part of a similar pattern of low-cost, deniable disruption efforts. “From railways to the food infrastructure that you see happening with the fridges being hacked ⁠and all ​kinds of other operations, it does fit the narrative of Russian state actors ​who want to disturb Europe,” said Eric Schouten, the head of aviation security group Dyami.

cnn.com.title: ‘Mogging’ is Collins’ word of the year, but what does it mean?
cnn.com.text: “Mogging,” a tongue-in-cheek term jovially used by members of Gen-Z and Gen Alpha to suggest an outperforming or outshining of someone or something, has been crowned 2026’s word of the year by Collins English Dictionary. Staving off tough competition with inimitable rizz, internet slang “mogging” seized the top spot after a staggering 210% surge in usage in 2026, Collins said in a press release Tuesday. But this is not the word of the year’s first rodeo. In fact, “mogging” has been in circulation for around a decade, but its meaning has shifted throughout this time, according to a separate blog published by Collins. Believed to be born from the acronym “AMOG,” or “alpha male of the group,” it was previously used as a noun in bodybuilding culture to describe the strongest, most physically dominant man in a gym, the blog says. Later, it was transformed into a verb and briefly adopted by the manosphere. In the last 12 months, “mogging” has had something of a glow-up, coming to define the act of outdoing. Were you proud of the wonky homemade cupcakes you brought to the dinner party until your friend rocked up with a three-tier masterpiece? You’ve been mogged. Had you been feeling pretty good about your thrifted outfit until you stood by the effortlessly cool commuter donning designer clobber on the subway? You’ve been mogged. Collins lexicographers monitor an astonishing 27 billion words annually. Not only do the experts track how frequently a word is used, but they also analyze patterns of use, managing director Alex Beecroft said in the release. “The selection of ‘mogging’ as Collins’ Word of the Year shows how each generation leaves its mark on language,” Beecroft said. “It’s a great example of how Gen Z and Gen Alpha have adopted a word and turned it into humorous slang, making the language their own and ‘mogging’ the rest of us.” So, which words were mogged for the coveted title this year? Close contenders As they often do, many of the shortlisted words have grown from a response to an event that dominated culture or current events. “Firewave” refers to several wildfires occurring during a short spell in town and cities after sustained periods of hot, dry weather. Meanwhile, “hydration break” dropped into the global lexicon during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, where soccer games were punctuated with pauses for players to take a drink. Organizers said the new habit was to keep athletes hydrated amid the sweltering heat across host nations US, Mexico and Canada, but fans scoffed at what they said were ad breaks in disguise. And British politics had its moment this year, as “Manchesterism” claimed a place on the shortlist. Referring to a political philosophy spearheaded by UK prime minister and former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham, “Manchesterism” involves regional power devolution and ties economic growth to social progress. But Burnham has been responsible for a little “mogging” himself this year, managing to nudge former Labour leader Keir Starmer out of the top job and taking the role himself.

cnn.com.title: At least 33 dead after Russia drops nine bombs on a Ukrainian school building
cnn.com.text: Dozens of people were killed when Russia dropped at least nine bombs on a school building in southeastern Ukraine where they had taken shelter, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, describing it as “one of the deadliest attacks of this war.” At least 33 people have been confirmed dead and another 50 are still unaccounted for after the attack on the building in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, which local governor Mykhailo Semikin said was being used as a shelter and a humanitarian aid distribution center. Semikin said they were in a newly-built, EU-funded reinforced basement designed to withstand most strikes, but the massive force of the bombs caused the concrete structure to collapse and a fire broke out. The shelter was built last year in an effort to keep classes going during wartime, but many civilians have since left as the fighting got closer to the village, and it is not currently used as a school. Instead, local authorities are using it as an administrative center and humanitarian hub. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine highlighted in a statement on Tuesday that the attack took place just as civilians from the area gathered to receive humanitarian aid. “The timing and location of the humanitarian distribution was well publicized,” said Danielle Bell, the head of the mission. “Either the Russian armed forces knew that there was a humanitarian distribution taking place, or they failed to take the most basic steps to find out what was happening in this village they were planning to attack. In either case, this attack seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law.” Zelensky said the attack came just before Russia launched another massive barrage of hundreds of drones and dozens of powerful cruise and ballistic missiles targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure – despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for energy ceasefire. Ukraine’s Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said three drones were directed at a substation that is crucial for the operation of the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant. He posted to Telegram saying actions like that threaten the nuclear safety of all of Europe, and that Ukraine has informed the UN nuclear watchdog, the IAEA. “It is very telling that all of this is happening on the day of the US congressional elections. The Russians believe that America will not notice this signal from them. But such terror must be noticed and stopped,” Zelensky said on Tuesday morning. “Ukraine must be helped to defend its skies, otherwise Russia will never stop its missile strikes. It is essential to help build peace honestly and reliably, and America can do that,” Zelensky added. The latest attacks by Russia come amid a renewed push for negotiations by the Trump administration. US envoy Steve Witkoff recently held a meeting with Zelensky in Norway before flying to St. Petersburg to meet with the Russian President Vladimir Putin. Separately, first lady Melania Trump helped to secure a ceasefire in the occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which enabled the evacuation of hundreds of civilians over the weekend. Trump’s office announced on Tuesday that the first lady would bring together representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, calling it “an extraordinary moment in American history.” Double-tap strike The strike on Monday is among the deadliest since the start of the war, but the past few months have been exceptionally bloody for Ukrainian civilians. Russia ramped up its aerial attacks on towns and cities across the country over the summer, striking at all times of the day. At least 33 people were killed last month when Russia hit two civilian buses in Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv. And a mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage. The assault against Komyshuvakha on Monday followed a familiar scenario in which Russian forces launch the first wave of strikes, wait for emergency services to arrive and then strike again. At least two first responders, named locally as Denys Konovalenko and Oleksiy Sushchevsky, both 44, were killed after rushing to the scene of the first strike. The Ukrainian Police said at least four of its officers have also been killed in the attack. They were named as Mykhailo Buzhenko and Mykola Balanda, both of who had more than two decades of police service under their belts, and Mykhailo Romanov and Dmytro Besedin, both of whom have been community police officers for more than a decade. “(They) were helping local residents take shelter in an underground school. A treacherous follow-up strike trapped everyone who was trying to escape,” the police said in a statement. Semikin told Ukraine’s national TV broadcast on Tuesday that Russia used KAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs in the attack. “To put this into perspective, this is a three-ton aerial bomb containing nearly 1.5 tons of explosive material; such weapons are primarily designed to destroy heavy concrete fortifications and bunkers,” he said.

cnn.com.title: Anthropic was founded to answer to humanity. Soon, it will also answer to Wall Street
cnn.com.text: In 2021, a group of employees at OpenAI left to start a new company focused on the safe development of artificial intelligence. They named it Anthropic, a word that means “relating to humanity.” Later this month, that company is expected to make its debut on Wall Street in what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in history. But the move raises a fundamental question: Can a company put humanity first while also answering to Wall Street? The IPO is a monumental development for the AI boom and will put a spotlight on how investors feel about the maker of the Claude chatbot. The stock market debut also marks a new chapter for Anthropic that will test whether it can balance its mission of safely developing AI with the pressures of being a publicly traded company. Anthropic has a special ownership structure designed to help the company stick to its original goals, balance profit growth with its mission and keep investors from staging a takeover. The structure includes a group of trustees who have majority control of the board of directors, as well as a special class of shares that ensures the seven founders own a majority of the general shareholder voting power. With its mission for safe AI and its unorthodox corporate structure, Anthropic’s Wall Street debut can be viewed as a guinea pig for AI frontier labs and how they are received by investors. Public benefit corporation Anthropic is registered as a public benefit corporation, or PBC. These types of companies are legally required to balance the interests of shareholders with the company’s stated mission. It’s different from a traditional company that focuses primarily on maximizing shareholder value. “The governance structure for Anthropic is very unique,” said Gil Luria, head of technology research at financial services firm D.A. Davidson. “They spell it out. They’re very upfront about it.” Anthropic described its “tripartite goals” as a PBC in its S-1 filing: “the pecuniary interest of our stockholders, the best interest of those materially affected by our conduct and the Company Purpose.” Just a fraction of publicly traded companies are PBCs. Patagonia, which is privately held, and eyewear retailer Warby Parker (WRBY) are both PBCs. PBCs can choose what they want to do with corporate profits and invest as much as they want in safety measures. And investors have little power to do anything about it. Anthropic rival OpenAI became a PBC in 2025. “Anthropic is explicit about that, that they believe that there will be instances where they choose not to maximize shareholder value because of the judgments that they make, the board and the leadership team,” Luria said. “Growing the company and enjoying profitability are part of the goal, so it’s not that it’s contrary to the goal,” he added. “It’s just that they’re saying that there may be some cases where that is not the goal, or they seek other goals, even at the expense of growth and profitability.” Anthropic’s seven founders collectively have 50.1% of the voting rights at the company, which means regular shareholders won’t have any say in its operations. This is a variation of a trend in Big Tech companies in recent years that have had structures where the founders retain majority control, like Mark Zuckerberg at Meta and Elon Musk at SpaceX. Long-Term Benefit Trust It’s not just that the founders have majority control. Anthropic in 2023 established the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), which is composed of five subject-matter experts who have no financial stake in the company’s stock. However, they have special non-financial shares with the authority to appoint four directors to the seven-person company board. The LTBT members include Neil Buddy Shah, CEO at the Clinton Health Access Initiative; and Ben Bernanke, a former chair of the Federal Reserve. There is one vacancy in the LTBT that has yet to be filled. “The LTBT may have interests that differ from yours, and it may exercise its power in a way with which you disagree or in a way that may be adverse to your interests,” Anthropic says in a filing with the SEC, referring to shareholders. When a company goes public, there can be more pressure to grow profits and deliver strong results for shareholders. But Anthropic and CEO Dario Amodei have also talked about the risk of AI causing tremendous harm to humanity if placed in the wrong hands. Anthropic’s IPO filing includes more than 90 pages of risk disclosures, varying from how AI can be misused by bad actors to the possibility of existential risk to humanity. “While this Long-Term Benefit Trust has a lot of power, the founders also have a lot of power. But, you know, in both cases, public shareholders don’t have the power,” said Jay Ritter, professor emeritus at the University of Florida and an expert in IPOs. What does this all mean? If there are growing concerns about AI, the founders and LTBT can make decisions for the company that impact the value of shares without any consideration for investors. In theory, it can help the company stick to its mission — but it remains to be seen how the structure will function until an event forces the company to act. Anthropic’s ownership structure won’t matter as much if profits are strong and it follows its mission of developing safe AI. But it will be stress-tested if earnings aren’t as strong as expected, safety issues arise, or disagreements fester between the board, founders or trustees, Luria at D.A. Davidson said. “The strangest aspect of Anthropic’s filing is its corporate governance structure,” Jay Goldberg, senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, wrote in a note. “We believe this is the largest PBC and the full implications of this structure will take time to become apparent.” “We believe this structure gives the LTBT and the founders effective permanent control of the company,” Goldberg added.

cnn.com.title: It’s a go-to luxury bag across the globe. Yet few know where in the world it’s made
cnn.com.text: In Europe this summer, it was a sight almost as ubiquitous as the sun: fashionistas weaving their way down Mediterranean beach promenades, London high streets and haute couture centers in Paris carrying earthy-colored, basket or crochet-patterned bags. The rise of raffia bags was first ignited by 1960s fashion trendsetters like Brigitte Bardot and Jacqueline Kennedy. Once a casual holiday accessory, raffia totes and clutches have blossomed into mass-market must-haves and cornerstone items for luxury fashion houses; Prada, Saint Laurent and Loewe represent just a few of the designer brands to curate raffia products that retail with four-figure price tags. Yet ask buyers where the intricately arranged palm fibers draped over their shoulders come from, and many might struggle to answer. Though 80% of global raffia demand is sourced from Madagascar, according to the country’s Economic Development Board, the East African country’s age-old connection to the natural material is relatively unknown globally. In Madagascar, the perception could not be more different. Raffia is woven into the cultural fabric of Malagasy life, explains multidisciplinary designer Domi Sanji, an organic embodiment of the national concept of “fihavanana” — enshrined into the country’s constitution — that emphasizes kinship, community and mutual respect. “It (raffia) is the root of our identity, that’s the reason why it is very present in our everyday life,” Sanji, based in the country’s capital Antananarivo, told CNN. “It is an expression of how to make society, how we live in society, and the way that the fibers are linked together. It is something from the spirit of Malagasy people: a wish to make society be together, to link each other.” Raffia is a fiber harvested from the colossal leaves of raffia palms, a tree native to Madagascar and other regions of tropical Africa, as well as parts of Central and South America. Fronds as long as 20 meters (66 feet), among the largest found anywhere, are pruned before their underside epidermal layers are peeled off. These supple green strips are sun-dried, cultivating the tan and beige colors synonymous with many eventual products, with the resulting strands then bundled and passed on to the central cogs in the raffia supply chain: the artisans. Weaving or crocheting fibers into bags, hats, home decor and a range of other goods is a skilled, labor-intensive process for specially trained craftspeople. It can take days and tens of thousands of stitches for an artisan to handmake one raffia hat. Yet there are concerns that raffia, some of those who weave it, and its surrounding landscapes are being exploited amid global demand for the fiber. Roughly 75% of Madagascar lives below the poverty line, according to the United Nations, a vulnerability that has contributed to overharvesting and an opaque supply chain marked by poor working conditions, explains Eileen Akbaraly, an Italian Indian social entrepreneur who grew up in Madagascar. Concentrated harvesting along Madagascar’s east coast contributed to 4.85 million hectares (12 million acres) of tree cover loss since 2000, a Global Ecology and Conservation report found in 2023. “Everyone is there and everyone is exploiting it,” Akbaraly told CNN. “It’s pretty horrible.” Chain tracing Seeking to remedy two problems in one fell swoop, Akbaraly founded Antananarivo-based fashion brand and social enterprise Made For A Woman in 2019 to spotlight and empower the artisans propping up raffia’s global success while implementing a traceable, sustainable supply chain for the natural fiber. Today, more than 90% of the company’s roughly 1,000 employees are women, with the majority coming from vulnerable communities, including domestic abuse survivors and sex workers, Akbaraly said. B Corp certified, a verification based on adherence to high social and environmental standards, Made For A Woman trains artisans in the skills needed to craft made-to-order products while also offering access to healthcare, education, social services and childcare, on top of equitable wages. “My job here is to give opportunities to other people and show them how incredible they are,” Akbaraly said. “My biggest moment where I’m just like, ‘Wow, I’ve done it,’ is being able to be in meetings with people or surrounded by people where I’m listening to them and I can feel that they feel empowered … that they’re starting to understand their gift and what they’re capable of.” That commitment underpins the brand’s effort to develop Madagascar’s first fully transparent and trackable supply chain for raffia. Traceability did not exist when Made For A Woman launched, said Akbaraly, who — after much searching — found what she believed to be the only supplier with social certification: Kalfane Fils, based in the northern city of Mahajanga. Under World Fair Trade Organization verification, the brand’s entire business — supply chain included — has been independently audited and deemed committed to fair trade. Akbaraly hopes it can serve as a blueprint for the wider industry. “It’s so important to know where your materials come from because they become who you are,” she said. “They are a representation of everything that you do. I don’t understand how people can work on materials and not understand where they come from.” Made For A Woman applies the same principle to its worldwide consumer base. Each handmade product, from a bag made exclusively from recycled raffia (£667/$891) to a cotton-raffia dress that takes months to weave (£1,283/$1,714), ships with a QR code on the label that buyers can scan to find out more about the Malagasy artisans, raffia harvesters and ecosystems that sculpted their purchase.
