The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

bbc.com.title: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.
"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."
He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.
There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".
Meanwhile, the Associated Press cited two regional officials as saying that, during a weekend phone call, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran following the midterms.
On Tuesday, Iran's chief negotiator with the US, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, stated: "The ball is now in America's court to prevent war."
"Just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised speech.
It was not immediately clear what Ghalibaf was referring to, but Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Irna on Monday that "very intensive" talks to try to end the war were under way with the US via Qatari and Pakistani mediators.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
"Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process... We are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," Majed al-Ansari told reporters in Doha.
Last week, Iranian negotiators discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions. They reportedly include lifting a naval blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

bbc.com.title: Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.
The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.
De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT.
Reuters reported on Tuesday that police in Spain have opened an investigation for possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true" Tenerife said.
"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."
'There are no words'
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.
The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.
Tenerife's president, Felipe Minambres, says the club's players will need "professional assistance" to help deal with the ordeal of one of their team-mates dying.
"We are all feeling vulnerable and deeply saddened right now. It's hard to even believe what has happened," said Minambres.
"We know, especially the players and the players' partners, that we will need support. We've already begun receiving offers of help today, and that support will continue.
"We will need professional assistance, but we also need the support of all our fans, because they are likely feeling the same way we are today."
Minambres added it had been a "truly unbelievable situation" and "an enormous tragedy that we have had to endure".
Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, issued a statement later on Tuesday which spoke of the club's shock and expressed condolences to De Miguel's family, club "and all those who were close to him".
"We are deeply affected by what has happened and we share the pain that the club is experiencing," it continued.
"From the very beginning we have maintained contact with them and we are at their disposal for anything they may need.
"What has happened has had a huge emotional impact on our players, the coaching staff and everyone at FC Andorra. These are particularly difficult times for everyone and we want to make sure that no one has to face them alone. That is why the club is providing psychological support to anyone who needs it."
Former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, who co-owns Andorra, said: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesus."
De Miguel's former club, Castellon, said: "It's hard to find words when reality strikes in such an unfair way.
"We join with all our affection in the grief of his family and loved ones, whom we embrace in these terribly difficult moments and to whom we extend our most heartfelt condolences."
Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, said: "Today, we all share the terrible pain of an irreparable loss.
"My deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates and the whole club."
Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe wrote on his social media: "Much sadness, there are no words."
Inter Miami and former Barcelona forward Lionel Messi said: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends."
The Spanish football federation announced following De Miguel's death that Tuesday's Spanish Cup fixtures had been postponed.
Two fixtures in the first round of the men's Copa del Rey were due to be played, while Espanyol were set to take on AS Celtas in the women's Copa del Reina competition.
A lower-league player with an eye for goal
De Miguel, who was born in Madrid, started his career at Leganes in 2015 and went on to play for eight different clubs in Spain.
After spells with Lugo Fuenlabrada and Internacional Madrid, he returned to Fuenlabrada before stints at Union Adarve, Navalcarnero and Unionistas.
He joined Castellon in 2023 and scored 16 goals as the club achieved promotion to Spain's second division a year later.
The Spaniard joined Tenerife on a three-year deal in 2025 and scored 11 goals in 29 appearances for the side.
De Miguel is survived by his daughter, Carla de Miguel Fernandez, who was born in 2025.

bbc.com.title: Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.
The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.
The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.
Here is what you need to know.
Why is Western Sahara disputed?
Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.
Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.
Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Algeria became Polisario's main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.
The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.
Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.
What was the UN's mission role?
After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.
The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.
The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.
In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.
The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.
Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.
The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.
But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.
What happened at the UN?
The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.
It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.
The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.
Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.
Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.
The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.
Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.
Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.
Why is Morocco celebrating the end of the UN mission?
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.
"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.
Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.
"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.
Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.
He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."
Could this lead to a renewed war?
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.
In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.
Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

bbc.com.title: Asian Cup postponed in wake of attacks on Saudi Arabia
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia has been postponed because of a series of deadly attacks on the host country.
The 24-team tournament was scheduled to take place from 7 January to 5 February but has been rescheduled to run from 23 December, 2027 to 21 January, 2028.
In October, a missile attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
A statement from the the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), external said the decision to reschedule had been taken "in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions".
It added: "The new dates of the tournament will be presented to Fifa for approval."
The Saudi Pro League has postponed this week's round of fixtures following the rescheduling of the Asian Cup.
It says the rescheduling creates "additional flexibility" in the calendar to allow for a "more balanced distribution of fixtures" across the rest of the season.
A number of events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled recently, including the Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition event, which was scheduled to be in Riyadh.
The Asian Tour has also indefinitely postponed it's season-ending golf tournament, which was scheduled to take place from 18-21 November.
This is the second successive Asian Cup to be postponed after the 2023 tournament was moved to 2024 and to Qatar from China because of the Covid pandemic.
The decision to postpone the 2027 Asian Cup means a number of Premier League players will not have to miss part of the current season.
Some of the players that would have been expected to be called up were Japan's Zion Suzuki of Aston Villa, Wataru Endo, who plays for Liverpool, and Daizen Maeda of Ipswich Town.
Leeds United's Ao Tanaka, Crystal Palace duo Takehiro Tomiyasu and Daichi Kamada, and Hull City's Hidemasa Morita also play for Japan.
Japan would have been one of the favourites for the tournament and Villa, who are in the Champions League, might have had to do without Suzuki for at least seven games if his country had reached the final.
Liverpool are also in the Champions League but Endo has yet to play for the Reds this season.
Brighton winger Kaoru Mitoma is currently injured but is expected to be back later this year and is also likely to have been called up by Japan.
Manchester City defender Abdukodir Khusanov, of Uzbekistan, and Hull City and Australia defender Lucas Herrington would also have expected international call-ups for the Asian Cup.

aljazeera.com.title: Photos: Champions League and Tenerife fans pay tribute to De Miguel
aljazeera.com.text:
In Pictures
Fans of Spanish football club CD Tenerife gathered outside the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez in Santa Cruz de Tenerife as tributes poured in for forward Jesus de Miguel, who died after an on-field collision.
De Miguel died on Tuesday from injuries sustained in a clash with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a Spanish second-division match, leaving Spanish and European football in mourning.
Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter.
Santa Cruz de Tenerife chief prosecutor Jose Luis Sanchez-Jauregui told the Spanish news agency EFE that criminal charges were unlikely because the collision happened in the course of play.
Tributes were held before Champions League fixtures on Tuesday, with Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and Villarreal opting not to play the competition’s anthem before kickoff in honour of De Miguel, 30, who went into cardiac arrest after being struck in the chest.
Moments of silence were observed in those stadiums and others across Europe, including at Old Trafford, where Manchester United were playing Roma. Images of De Miguel were shown on giant screens inside the grounds.
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta and midfielder Mikel Merino also began their news conferences on the eve of Wednesday’s match against Slavia Prague by paying tribute to De Miguel.

aljazeera.com.title: Democrats dominate NYC races, Hochul re-elected New York governor
aljazeera.com.text:
Progressive candidates endorsed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani have won decisive victories in their campaigns to join the United States Congress.
On Tuesday, New York City politicians Brad Lander, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez secured their seats in the 120th Congress, representing the 10th, 13th and 7th districts, respectively.
All three were considered shoo-ins following the state’s June 23 party primaries. Their districts lean heavily Democratic.
But their wins in the 2026 midterm election solidify a political shift in the New York City area, ushered in by Mamdani’s own victory as a Democratic socialist in the 2025 mayoral race.
“To me, the national story is about this new generation of progressive leaders and getting excited about those who will be inspired by them just as they were inspired by Mamdani,” Adin Lenchner, progressive political strategist for Carroll Street Campaigns, a consulting firm, told Al Jazeera.
“Brad, Darializa and Claire are on their way to help lift up that same vision of progressive leadership in DC.”
All three representatives-elect spoke to the public on Tuesday, addressing, among other things, President Donald Trump’s pledge earlier in the day to cease annual military aid to Israel by the end of the year.
Cutting off such aid was central to all three candidates’ policy platforms, as part of their opposition to Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
“I don’t know that we can trust this president to make moral and consistent decisions about our military budget, so we’ll have to see,” Valdez told Al Jazeera outside a polling location in her district late on Tuesday afternoon.
Valdez will head to Congress from the state assembly. Her political career began in the labour movement, and she has pushed to make it easier for unions to organise, as part of her policy platform.
She defeated Republican community activist Melvin Rivera in a largely lopsided race.
US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive who was first elected in 2018, also handily won her House race for the 14th congressional district.
Other notable wins for the House of Representatives include Micah Lasher, a New York Assembly member who will serve his first term in Congress after defeating Republican challenger Caroline Shinkle.
Incumbent Representative Grace Meng in Queens, New York, also won her re-election bid against Republican challenger Joseph Chou. Meng told Al Jazeera that the larger Democratic sweep in the midterms is “a mandate for us, not just a promotion”.
She said that a goal for the new Congress would be to push back on Trump.
“He has not treated Congress like a third and independent branch of government and is just going around doing whatever he wants,” Meng told Al Jazeera.
New York’s Democrats are also pushing for Hakeem Jeffries — the longtime representative for the state’s 8th congressional district — to be selected by party members for the House speaker role.
Jeffries currently serves as House minority leader for the Democratic Party.
If chosen by his colleagues to lead the House of Representatives, he will be the first Black speaker in the history of Congress’s lower chamber.
“We are going to course-correct, and my good friend Congressman Hakeem Jeffries is set to wield the speaker’s gavel,” New York State Attorney General Letitia James said after her re-election on Tuesday.
Hochul re-elected
The state of New York elected a total of 26 members to the House of Representatives in this year’s midterm race.
But important state and local positions were on the ballot as well.
In the gubernatorial race, for instance, incumbent Democrat Kathy Hochul secured another term in Albany. She won her race against Republican Bruce Blakeman, a lawyer and executive for Nassau County who ran on a platform of tax cuts and immigration reform.
With Tuesday’s results, Hochul and Adrienne Adams have become the first all-woman ticket to win election as governor and lieutenant governor in the Empire State’s history.
Hochul has served in her post since 2021. Adams previously served on the New York City Council.
In her victory speech, Hochul took aim at Trump, who campaigned heavily for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.
“Just a few weeks ago, Donald Trump came to New York and told voters to pretend he was on the ballot,” Hochul said. “Well, Mr President, you got your wish.”
Hochul’s new term officially begins on the first day of January. The new congressional leaders will be sworn in on January 3, 2027.

aljazeera.com.title: N Korea fires multiple missiles, denies US claims on Binance hack
aljazeera.com.text:
North Korea has fired several missiles into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea’s military, hours after Pyongyang denied allegations that it was behind the theft of more than $6bn in crypto assets from Binance.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said on Wednesday that it had detected the launch of several missiles from the Sondok area on North Korea’s eastern coast towards the Sea of Japan.
It said authorities in South Korea and the United States were analysing the details of the launches.
The tests marked Pyongyang’s fourth such weapons launch in a month. They came a day after North Korea denied involvement in the Binance hack, dismissing an FBI announcement that North Korean hackers were responsible as “a trite provocation”.
Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Friday that hackers stole more than $6bn in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record.
The FBI later said North Korean hackers had orchestrated the theft, attributing it to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5bn hack of the Bybit exchange last year.
Early on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said Pyongyang viewed the FBI announcement as “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” North Korea.
She ruled out dialogue with Washington until the US abandoned that policy.
“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue, of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”
US President Donald Trump said in August that he plans to meet Kim Jong Un later this year, seeking to revive the bond he claims to have forged with the North Korean leader during his first term.
Trump said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.
Previous rounds of talks between Kim and Trump in 2019 abruptly ended amid disagreements over Pyongyang’s nuclear programme. In October, the US, South Korea and Japan again reiterated their call for the “complete denuclearisation” of the Korean Peninsula.
The call came as North Korea has accelerated its weapons testing this year, in what analysts say is likely a bid to increase its leverage in any future diplomacy with the US.
Its recent tests have included a submarine-launched ballistic missile, hypersonic missiles, attack drones, and cluster bombs designed to be carried by ballistic missiles.
On Tuesday, Pyongyang said it had tested a new cluster warhead for strategic cruise missiles the previous day, claiming it could destroy an area of 5 to 6 hectares (12 to 15 acres) with “high-density power”.
The latest launches followed a North Korean state media report that Kim had visited a naval shipyard building a destroyer and stressed the importance of a powerful navy.

aljazeera.com.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes Georgia’s first black governor
aljazeera.com.text:
Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes Georgia’s first black governor
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Governor-elect of Georgia becoming the state’s first black governor, and the very first female black governor in the United States.
Published On 4 Nov 2026

aljazeera.com.title: Democrat Josh Turek flips Iowa Senate seat
aljazeera.com.text:
Democrat Josh Turek has been elected to the US Senate, defeating Republican Representative Ashley Hinson.
Turek’s victory over Hinson flips a Republican-held seat and boosts Democrats’ efforts to retake control of the Senate.
A state representative since 2023, Turek competed in four Paralympics and played professional wheelchair basketball in Europe.
Hinson was endorsed by Trump, who carried Iowa in three straight presidential elections. Turek’s victory underscored Democratic gains in a state that had initially been expected to remain safely Republican.
It’s been more than a decade since a Democrat represented Iowa in the Senate. The seat is held by retiring two-term Senator Joni Ernst.

aljazeera.com.title: Trump and Republicans trampled in the midterms
aljazeera.com.text:
Trump and Republicans trampled in the midterms
Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher says Republicans are facing a worse-than-expected midterm performance, with the party’s internal polling having failed to anticipate the scale of potential losses in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.

aljazeera.com.title: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes
aljazeera.com.text:
Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process“.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
Attack on Qeshm Island
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
Tanker struck in Hormuz
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
Separately, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed four tankers had struck mines and caught fire after switching off navigation and identification systems and using what it described as unauthorised routes through Hormuz, and said its forces had seized two other vessels.
That account could not be independently verified or linked to the incident reported by UKMTO.
The IRGC also claimed it had destroyed two US LUCAS attack drones over Bandar Khamir, according to Iranian state broadcaster Pars Today.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

aljazeera.com.title: Kansas elects first Democratic senator in almost a century
aljazeera.com.text:
Democrat Adam Hamilton has become the first member of his party to win a Kansas Senate seat in almost a century after beating incumbent Republican Roger Marshall, according to Associated Press news agency projections.
The race was considered consequential to control of the US Senate.
The highly competitive contest between Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, and Marshall stunned political observers given the state’s long history of Republican wins. A Democrat has not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932.
The founder of the largest United Methodist church in the country, Hamilton campaigned as a man of faith while pushing core Democratic positions on affordability. Like other rural states, Kansas has seen its agricultural and transportation industries hit by record-high diesel and fuel prices.
“We’re always told to not talk about politics or religion but this is one time we’re trying to save our democracy. The next two years are a pivotal time for our country,” Hamilton said on Monday.
Marshall is a staunch supporter of US President Donald Trump, who campaigned for the Republican candidate.
Marshall pushed Trump’s agenda during the campaign and pledged to expand rural healthcare, despite voting for Trump’s funding cuts, and to support agriculture. A physician, he has stirred controversy by supporting Trump’s Make America Healthy Again policies, which critics say undermine public health, and by opposing mask mandates during the pandemic.
Marshall’s campaign was also dogged by a New York Times report that he had sued about 700 of his former patients for medical debt during his years as a doctor, which Hamilton’s campaign used in attack ads.
The Associated Press reported that the $110m race was the most expensive in the state’s history.

aljazeera.com.title: Democratic Party flips US Senate in 2026 midterm elections
aljazeera.com.text:
The Democratic Party has regained control of the upper chamber of the United States Congress in the 2026 midterm elections, according to Associated Press news agency projections.
The Senate was called in the party’s favour late on Tuesday night, marking a dramatic shift in legislative power.
Democrats needed a net gain of four seats in the 100-member chamber to wrest control from the Republicans. As of late Tuesday night, they had wrested control of at least seven seats.
Some of those gains were dramatic. In South Carolina, for instance, Democrat Annie Andrews, a paediatrician, took a seat held by Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late longtime Senator Lindsey Graham. The last time a Democrat won a Senate seat in the state was 1998.
Neighbouring North Carolina saw a similar flip, with Democrat Roy Cooper, a former governor, beating his Republican rival Michael Whatley.
In Texas, a Republican stronghold, Democrat James Talarico, a state legislator and seminary student, delivered an upset against state Attorney General Ken Paxton. The last time a Democrat won a statewide election in Texas was 1994.
Democrat Sherrod Brown also defeated incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted in Ohio, flipping that seat as well. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, the Democratic pastor of a megachurch, beat another sitting senator, Republican Roger Marshall. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson unseated longtime Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins. And in Iowa, paralympic gold medalist Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson in a race that drew hundreds of millions of dollars in ad spending.
In the outgoing 119th Congress, Republicans hold a 53-seat majority. The Democrats have 45 seats, with two independents in their caucus.
With Tuesday’s results, Democrats have secured at least 53 seats, enough to take the majority, with a handful of races still being counted.
The outcome is also set to end the Republican “trifecta” achieved in the 2024 election, when the party won control of the three main levers of power in Washington, DC: the Senate, the House of Representatives and the presidency.
US President Donald Trump acknowledged the Democrats “did a good job” and had “fought hard” in the elections. Speaking to Fox News, he said he thought the war on Iran played a role in the Republican losses, as voters probably weren’t ready for “the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline”.
But in a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump distanced himself from the results, saying “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”.
‘We’ll work together’, says Trump
The Senate was projected to be harder to flip than the House in Tuesday’s midterm elections, given the smaller number of seats on the ballot.
Senate terms last six years, unlike the two-year terms of members of the House of Representatives. And elections for senators are staggered, meaning that only about a third of all Senate seats are voted on at a time.
This midterm election cycle saw 35 Senate races: 33 regular elections and two special elections, in Ohio and Florida. Those two states were left with Senate vacancies when Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio joined President Donald Trump’s second administration in 2025.
At least seven Senate races on Tuesday were considered key toss-ups. They included contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, Texas and Michigan.
States like Texas and Kansas, however, rarely fall within the toss-up category, as they are considered Republican strongholds. The last time a Democratic senator was elected in Kansas was 1932.
“How did this happen? How did a Democrat win in Kansas, a deeply red state, for the first time in nearly a century, especially in a state where only 25 percent of the people are Democrats?” Senator-elect Hamilton said in his victory speech.
“First of all, I think the people in Kansas – Republicans, independents and Democrats – were saying what’s happening in Washington is not OK.”
The Democratic Party also successfully defended several seats, including Jon Ossoff’s in the swing state of Georgia. Mark Warner, who has represented Virginia in the Senate since 2009, won a fourth term.
Trump said he would work with Democrats in the next Congress, even though he expected them to propose legislation he called “insane”.
“They’ll send over things that are insane, and I’ll veto them,” said Trump. “And after a couple of months of vetoes, they’ll call and they’ll say, ‘How do we get this stuff done?’ And we’ll work together.”

aljazeera.com.title: Democrat Amy Acton beats Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio governor’s race
aljazeera.com.text:
Democrat Amy Acton has been elected as the US state of Ohio’s next governor, delivering a stunning defeat to Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a race that captured headlines across the country.
Acton, a physician who served as outgoing Republican Governor Mike DeWine’s top health official, faced countless attacks over her response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Spending in the hotly contested race topped an unprecedented $100m.
In the final weeks of the bitter campaign, a controversial television ad featuring her estranged mother sparked fierce backlash against Ramaswamy, who claimed responsibility for it and refused to take it down off the airwaves.
In the ad, Acton’s mother accused her daughter of lying about her childhood and suggesting she has a mental illness. But it failed to mention that Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at the age of 12 after her stepfather was charged with raping her.
Acton is the first Democrat to become governor of Ohio since 2006. She’s also the first woman ever elected to the office.

aljazeera.com.title: Sherrod Brown, an Ohio Democrat, wins return to US Senate
aljazeera.com.text:
Democrat Sherrod Brown has mounted a successful return to the US Senate, handing a stinging defeat to Republicans who had hoped to hold on to the seat, according to Associated Press news agency projections.
Brown, who was ousted from the Senate two years ago, overcame a costly challenge by incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted.
More than $500m was spent on advertising in the race, with US tech companies contributing tens of millions to defeat Brown. It was the second most expensive race of this midterm cycle and among the 10 costliest non-presidential races in US history, according to The Hill.
Husted, a strong ally of US President Donald Trump, was appointed to the seat in early 2025 to replace its previous holder, US Vice President JD Vance. He has supported a host of Trump’s second-term policies, including tax cuts, the Iran war and tariffs.
The Ohio race was seen as central in deciding which party controls the Senate. Both of the state’s seats are currently held by Republicans, one of whom helped secure the Senate for Republicans by beating Brown in 2024.
The cost of living was a major issue in the US Midwest, which is home to struggling former industrial cities and rural communities.
Brown championed his strong ties to labour unions and working-class communities in his bid to regain the seat. He will serve the remainder of Vance’s term, which runs until January 2029.

aljazeera.com.title: Talarico wins Senate race, ending decades of Republican dominance in Texas
aljazeera.com.text:
Houston, Texas – James Talarico has won the United States Senate race in Texas, the first time a Democrat has won state office since 1994.
Tuesday’s victory marks a seismic shift in Texas, which has become a standard-bearer for the Republican Party’s staunch conservative policies.
“We just took back Texas,” Talarico said during a victory speech in Austin. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.”
“We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love,” he said. “And we just sent a message to every billionaire mega donor, every trillionaire mega donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country – power belongs to the people.”
The win comes after an intervention in the Republican primary by President Donald Trump, who endorsed scandal-ridden Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn.
But Paxton failed to generate enthusiasm, even among his party, despite record-breaking spending topping half a billion dollars.
The largest share came from trillionaire donor Elon Musk, who spent at least $212m supporting Paxton.
Musk’s SpaceX company is based in Texas. He has also spent heavily across the country as Democrats are expected to investigate Musk’s role as head of the federal cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency if they take control of Congress.
“It’s historic,” said Taylor Bell, a 27-year-old law student, who attended an election watch party in Houston.
“Hopefully, we see money coming back to the people of Texas and not more of the same we’ve seen – well, my whole life at this point.”
US Congressman Christian Menefee, a Democrat who represents Houston, told those gathered: “Tonight, Texas has restored the hope of a nation.”
“Tonight, I believe firmly that we can accomplish anything in this country if we just stand together and we fight back against hate and bigotry,” he said.
Yvonne Nunga, a 29-year-old who works in the technology industry, said the election represented a generational shift.
“The younger generation and all the people who want a better future came out and made their voices heard,” she said. “This party, this fight right now, is not about left or right. It’s about top vs bottom, and I’m so glad that we have candidates that are making this a pivotal point in their messaging.”
“The current politics of the current administration is not working for the people,” she added. “It’s not for the people, by the people; it’s for the billionaires bought by the billionaires.”
No ‘puppet governor’ for Trump
Tuesday also saw the surprise victory of gubernatorial Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, whose challenge had been considered a long shot even into the final days of the race.
Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in the history of Texas despite Latinos making up 40 percent of the state’s population.
“Now I stand before you, humbled and grateful, and in awe of the incredible grace and power of God and of Texas,” Hinojosa said during a victory speech on Tuesday night.
Alejandra Peimbert, a regional communications director for Hinojosa’s campaign, said the victory should be seen as a rebuke to the hardline immigration policies enacted during 10 years under outgoing Governor Greg Abbott.
Abbott has cooperated closely with the Trump administration in its mass deportation campaign, spearheading policies that saw local law enforcement officials conduct immigration enforcement.
“I think the Latino community and our vote has been underestimated by politicians constantly,” Peimbert told Al Jazeera.
“The economy is so bad, and the horrendous things that ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] has done to our community, tearing apart families, … I think my community finally had enough,” she added.
“President Trump will no longer have a puppet in a governor.”
The state has long been a Republican bastion in the US. But Abbott’s tenure has been defined by a more hardline conservative lurch, with tough approaches not only on immigration but also to social welfare programmes, abortion rights, education and religious freedom.
Abbott’s supporters have touted rapid economic growth in recent years, spurred by tax cuts and regulation rollbacks.
Critics have argued that the economic growth measured by these metrics primarily rewards corporations and the wealthy while middle- and lower-class Texans see little benefit. Texas’s poverty rate sits above the national average, with little in the way of a social safety net.
Mandalyn Salazar, a 58-year-old Houston resident, said she was in awe following the surprise victory.
“I’m just like, right now, like, in the moment, like I just can’t believe this is happening,” she said. “We have families, and we’re all paying so much for our gas and our groceries, and I just felt like our governor – he just wasn’t getting it. I think a lot of us felt like, you know, our state, like, had been taken over by big money.”
Dylan Sutter, 21, was among the revellers on Tuesday night.
“It’s one of the biggest things Texas can ever experience, because these are two strong candidates that took their time, they took their dedication and focused with every community in Texas, and so they deserve this position,” he said of Talarico and Hinojosa.
“Everything is blue. It’s like the ballot itself was painted blue by the time we were done with it.”

aljazeera.com.title: Democrat Annie Andrews flips South Carolina’s Senate seat
aljazeera.com.text:
Charleston, South Carolina, US – South Carolina has elected a Democrat to the US Senate for the first time since 1998, according to the Associated Press news agency. In a major upset for the Republican Party, Annie Andrews won in a state seen as a solid Republican stronghold.
“I think we just made some history,” Andrews said on Tuesday night after results came in.
Andrews outraised Republican candidate Darline Graham by more than $22m, according to Federal Election Commission filings, primarily with grassroots donations. She had pledged to take no money from corporate political action committees (PACs).
Andrews campaigned on lowering costs for working families, expanding affordable healthcare and protecting reproductive rights, and on opposing endless wars.
South Carolina flips
Despite South Carolina being reliably conservative, many voters, including Republicans, believed Graham to be unqualified.
After Republican Senator Lindsey Graham died suddenly in July, his younger sister, Darline, was appointed to serve out the remainder of his term. She went on to win a special primary runoff for the Republican nomination with US President Donald Trump’s endorsement.
Despite Trump’s endorsement, Graham struggled to unite conservatives behind her candidacy. During a primary debate, she said she was “not that informed on national security” and that “national security is not my thing”.
In the final month of the campaign, Trump made multiple appearances alongside Graham, an unusual investment of presidential time in a state Republicans normally win comfortably.
On Tuesday night, Andrews said Graham had called her and congratulated her on her win, which Andrews said she thanked her for.
In a victory speech, Andrews said, “This Senate seat doesn’t belong to one family, one party, or to Washington, DC. It belongs to you and it always will.”
“Nobody in Washington recruited me to run. Nobody handed me a seat in the United States Senate. And nobody wrote me a script,” Andrews said. “I owe no one in Washington anything.”
What does the win mean for South Carolina?
A South Carolina motto is, “While I breathe, I hope”. It appears on the right side of the South Carolina state seal. Many invoked this phrase as the results came in, claiming that this was their moment of hope
A group of medical students who attend the same medical school as Andrews were celebrating her win at the election watch party. They also volunteer at the free clinic in Mount Pleasant that provides free healthcare to uninsured people.
“Having a scientist in that space means a lot to us,” Daniel Newlands, one of the students, told Al Jazeera.
Lela Ali, a regional voting advisor in the South, told Al Jazeera that Andrews’s win could signal a change not only in South Carolina, but also for southern states.
“I think this victory and the gains across the region today gives people across the South a renewed sense of possibility,” Ali said. “We can’t turn our backs on the South.”
Toni Reale, 48, a mother and small business owner, teared up after Andrews win.
“In order for Annie to win, people would have had to change their typical votes, and that, to me, signals that people in my community have really thought about the options and put South Carolina first,” she told Al Jazeera.
She added, “We have a very smart and very hard-working electorate here in the state. And some really salt of the earth people that often vote against their best interests. And today, what I saw is people not just voting along party lines, but actually thinking about what’s best for our state.”
Holly Griffin, a 52-year-old healthcare worker, told Al Jazeera that the results show things are different for the state now.
“I think this shows the whole community that we have changed in front of us,” she said.

aljazeera.com.title: EU urges action as Germany, Romania and UK report supermarket cyberattacks
aljazeera.com.text:
Hackers raised the temperatures of refrigeration systems at supermarkets in Germany, Romania and the United Kingdom during Monday’s cyberattacks, officials said, bringing the number of European countries affected in the hacking spree to at least 11.
The announcements on Tuesday came as the European Union promised a collective response, warning that the attacks, which have spoiled tonnes of food across the continent, were “not isolated”.
The motive for the cyberattacks is unknown, and no one has claimed responsibility. A Romanian official said he did not suspect a state actor.
Problems were reported in at least nine EU countries on Monday: Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden. On Tuesday, officials and company representatives said four supermarkets in Germany and six in Romania were affected.
The UK, which is not in the EU, was also hit.
Thomas Regnier, a spokesperson for the EU, said the bloc’s agencies were talking with national authorities to develop a joint response.
“These are not isolated incidents, and of course, we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said.
But he refused to point the finger at any potential culprits.
No state actor
Romania’s top cybersecurity official played down the threat.
“It seems semi-amateurish,” Dan Cimpean, the director of Romania’s National Cyber Security Directorate, told the AFP news agency. “We do not suspect, under any circumstances, that it is a state actor.”
He added that “no other infrastructure was compromised”.
Belgium was among the hardest-hit countries on Monday, with dozens of stores across several grocery chains reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors there have opened an investigation.
In Italy, about 20 supermarkets were affected.
Giuseppe Spadaro, director of a group that runs Coop supermarkets in Sicily, said four of its 300 stores were hit, causing thousands of euros in damage.
“We had to throw away everything. The shelves are empty,” he told Italy’s Corriere della Sera newspaper.
Italy’s government held talks with the heads of the intelligence services and the National Cybersecurity Agency on Tuesday after the attacks, and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s office said the incident had a “limited” impact.
“There is no cause for alarm, although all the relevant institutional bodies remain on high alert,” it said in a statement.
In the UK, hackers tried to target small meat-processing firms, but the impact was minimal, said Richard Horne, chief executive of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).
Horne told the BBC the issue affected “the whole food supply chain”, and that there had been a couple of instances where “vulnerable technology had been exploited”.
The second wave of attacks mirrored the cyberattack that swept hundreds of supermarkets across France in October, which also affected stores in several other European countries.
In Sweden, the supermarket chain Coop said that refrigerators and freezers affected overnight at seven of its stores had been connected to “old 4G networks”, and that the stores had since resumed normal operations.
Carlos Cancinos, a spokesperson for the chain, said Coop had accelerated an upgrade, begun after the October attacks, to move its connected refrigeration equipment onto 5G networks and modern modems.
“This helps to solve a large share of problems of this kind,” he said.
Danfoss, a Danish maker of refrigeration controls whose systems were again among those targeted, said it had been in close contact with customers for the past three weeks. It recommended that the systems not be directly accessible from the internet.
Frank Groenewegen, a cybersecurity expert at Deloitte in The Hague, urged retailers to check whether their refrigeration controllers were connected to the internet and running the latest security updates.
“And if they don’t even know, then remove them from the public internet immediately,” he told the Reuters news agency. “With disconnecting, you haven’t fixed the root cause, but you’ve at least isolated those systems so that an attacker is not able to do this anymore.”

aljazeera.com.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as first Black woman elected US governor
aljazeera.com.text:
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has made history as the first Black woman elected governor of a US state, according to Associated Press news agency projections.
The former Atlanta mayor emerged victorious in Georgia over her billionaire opponent, Republican Rick Jackson, who spent more than $200m of his personal fortune in an attempt to succeed the popular outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp.
Bottoms, a former adviser to US President Joe Biden, was propelled to victory in part by the state’s significant Black voting bloc, which turned out in large numbers during early voting.
During the campaign, she faced Republican attempts to characterise her time as mayor as a crime-ridden decline for the state’s largest city.
“It’s a longstanding playbook to paint Atlanta as this big bad place,” Bottoms told the Associated Press news agency.
Bottoms’ win marks the third consecutive time that Georgia Democrats have nominated a Black woman for governor. Stacey Abrams lost in 2018 and 2022 to Kemp, who is leaving office in January after eight years due to term limits.

aljazeera.com.title: Democrat Roy Cooper flips North Carolina US Senate seat
aljazeera.com.text:
Democrat Roy Cooper has won North Carolina’s United States Senate race, marking a significant pickup for the party as it looks to take back control of the chamber.
Cooper, a moderate former two-term governor, is the first Democrat to be elected to one of the state’s two US Senate seats since 2008, when former President Barack Obama carried it in his first White House bid.
He replaces outgoing Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek a third term in office after becoming a frequent critic of US President Donald Trump.
Since becoming the Democrats’ Senate nominee, Cooper consistently led his Republican opponent, former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley, forcing Republicans to pull funding for Whatley’s campaign.
Cooper’s win is significant in a state that has narrowly voted for Trump three times since 2016.
Cooper said in his victory speech that he wants to combat “chaos and corruption in Washington” and pledged to work towards ending the US war against Iran after winning the US Senate election in North Carolina.
“Chaos and corruption in Washington were hurting our people. Today, you said, ‘This has to stop.’ And, as your new United States senator, I am ready to take that message to Washington,” Cooper said.
“We have to work to make healthcare, housing, and groceries more affordable, to end this war and stop the pain at the pump,” the former North Carolina governor added.

aljazeera.com.title: UN elects five judges to International Court of Justice amid record cases
aljazeera.com.text:
The United Nations has elected five judges to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) for nine-year terms, as the court faces a record caseload, including South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza.
The vote was held on Tuesday at UN headquarters, with candidates requiring an absolute majority in both the General Assembly and the Security Council to win.
Dapo Akande of the United Kingdom, Francois Alabrune of France, Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud of Jordan, Rena Lee of Singapore and Phoebe Okowa of Kenya were elected to the 15-member panel.
Their terms are set to begin on February 6, 2027.
The two UN bodies initially agreed on four candidates but failed to select a fifth. The Security Council supported Ecuador’s Marcelo Vazquez-Bermudez, while the General Assembly backed Okowa, prompting further rounds of voting.
Vazquez-Bermudez later withdrew from the race, and Okowa subsequently won the backing of the General Assembly and the Security Council.
The votes were held by secret ballot concurrently, but separately.
The ICJ is based in The Hague and has 15 judges, each from a different country. They serve nine-year terms and may be re-elected. To ensure a degree of continuity, a third of the bench is elected every three years.
The election comes as the World Court faces a record workload.
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa told the General Assembly on October 29 that 24 contentious cases are pending, covering disputes over territory, human rights and the interpretation of international treaties.
Among them is South Africa’s case accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention in its war on Gaza. The court has previously ordered provisional measures but has not issued a final ruling on whether genocide occurred.
In October 2025, the court issued an advisory opinion outlining Israel’s obligations towards the UN and humanitarian organisations operating in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Separately, the court announced on Tuesday that it would deliver a judgment on November 19 in The Gambia’s case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya minority.
Established in 1945, the ICJ is the UN’s principal judicial organ, responsible for settling disputes between states and providing advisory opinions on questions of international law.

aljazeera.com.title: Jon Ossoff wins Georgia Senate race, defeating Republican Mike Collins
aljazeera.com.text:
Incumbent Democratic US Senator Jon Ossoff has won re-election in the state of Georgia, one of the midterm cycle’s marquee contests.
He has defeated Republican Congressman Mike Collins, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump who faced intense scrutiny during the campaign regarding alleged ties to people espousing white supremacist ideology.
Ossoff, who has served as a US senator since 2021, campaigned on affordability, healthcare, and government accountability.
Collins, meanwhile, focused on the president’s agenda, immigration enforcement and reducing the size of the government.
Republicans had hoped to defeat Ossoff, the first Jewish senator in a state that backed former President Joe Biden in 2020 before reversing course and narrowly supporting Trump four years later.
Ossoff, seen by some as a possible contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, will rejoin his fellow Democrat in the Senate, Raphael Warnock, Georgia’s first Black senator, who is also rumoured to be considering a run for the presidency.
Georgia’s US Senate seats were critical for building the Democratic Party’s power in Congress and in the South, a largely Republican stronghold.
Ossoff was leading Collins 63 percent to 29 percent with 56 percent of votes counted, according to the Associated Press news agency.
Trump won Georgia narrowly in 2024 after losing the state to Biden in the 2020 presidential election.
In 2023, Trump and others were charged in Georgia with attempting to overturn the 2020 election loss by pressuring a senior state official to recalculate the results in his favour. The case was dismissed after Trump returned to office in 2025.
After the results were called, Ossoff said American voters have rejected “lame duck” President Trump by handing the Democratic candidates “sweeping and decisive victories”.
“In sweeping and decisive victories the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame duck President Donald J Trump,” Ossoff said after defeating Republican Mike Collins for Georgia’s US Senate seat.
“The fact is we’ve been too long mired in small and selfish politics bought by big money, unmoored from fixed, moral principles, and resigned to intractable division,” the senator from Georgia added.

npr.org.title: Troy Jackson wins Maine Senate race over Susan Collins, in major coup for Democrats
npr.org.text:
Troy Jackson wins Maine Senate race over Susan Collins, in major coup for Democrats
Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country
Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app
Troy Jackson has defeated Republican incumbent Susan Collins for U.S. Senate in Maine, according to a race call by the Associated Press, a crucial victory for Democrats in their push to win back the Senate majority.
The Democratic Party has long tried to oust Collins, and at a moment when President Trump's approval ratings are at historic lows, Democrats saw Maine as one of their best opportunities to flip a Republican seat.
Loading...
As the longest-serving Republican woman in the Senate, Collins entered the race with a history of defying national political headwinds, repeatedly winning in a state that has consistently voted for Democrats at the state level. But that streak ended Tuesday night.
The results bring Collins' nearly 30-year tenure in Congress to a close and make Jackson the first Democrat to represent Maine in the Senate since 1995.
Jackson's win bookends a dramatic, albeit short, Senate campaign. A fifth-generation logger, he quickly became a national figure after he replaced Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee in August, after Platner suspended his campaign following an allegation of rape, which he denies.
Jackson sought to capitalize on and maintain the momentum sparked by Platner's antiestablishment, change-focused message. He ran on a progressive populist platform, emphasizing both his working-class background and deep ties to the labor movement.
He also attempted to link Collins to several Trump policies that have fueled economic concerns in the state, particularly the rise in oil and gas prices from the Iran war, as well as the financial strain on Maine businesses due to trade tensions with Canada, which borders the state.
Despite his late entry into the race, national polls showed Jackson and Collins in a virtual tie leading up to the end of voting.
Their race was one of the most expensive in this year's midterms, with Democratic- and Republican-aligned groups spending more than a quarter of a billion dollars on ads, according to data from AdImpact.
Loading...
While Collins pitched herself as a needed independent voice in the Senate, Democrats tried to poke holes in that argument. Ads repeatedly called attention to more divisive parts of her record, including her 2018 vote that was crucial in confirming Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, expanding a conservative majority that would go on to eliminate the constitutional right to abortion in 2022.
Collins has said that she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh and that she is a supporter of abortion protections.
On the campaign trail, she also touted her work as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, a key leadership position that she argued has helped her bring more federal funds to Maine.
In an October interview with Maine Public Radio, Jackson pushed back on that framing.
"She's losing more money than she's bringing in. You know I keep saying, it would be great if she just stopped doing anything. We'd be better off," he said. "We're losing a lot more; our healthcare, Iran war, tariffs. I mean, all these things are costing the state way more money than Susan Collins can ever bring in."
Collins does have a record of voting against Trump administration policies. An analysis by The New York Times found that Collins breaks with her party on votes more than any other Republican in the Senate. But the rate at which she does so has dropped considerably during the president's second term, the analysis found.
In the final Senate debate, held in October, Collins made a pitch for why having a more moderate representative is a strength for voters in Maine, rather than a liability.
"[Jackson] is going to be an automatic vote for the Democratic position no matter what," she said. "We have lost a lot of the centrists, and one of the reasons is we need people who will work across party lines."

npr.org.title: Democrats win full control of Congress, ushering in a new era of divided government
npr.org.text:
Democrats win full control of Congress, ushering in a new era of divided government
Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country
Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app
Democrats have cemented control of both chambers of Congress, according to an NPR analysis based on a tally of race calls by The Associated Press.
The twin victories in the House and Senate return the Democratic Party to full control of Congress for the first time since 2023 and deepens the level of expected friction between President Trump and congressional Democrats in a new era of divided government. After a largely unrestrained start to his second term, Trump's final two years in the White House are now certain to be hampered by congressional investigations in two chambers and legislators hostile to his agenda.
The midterm campaign was defined by Americans' frustrations with the high cost of living and perceived public corruption. Those concerns were at the heart of Democratic campaign messaging, including in the seven Senate races that flipped from Republican control: North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine. Democrats also easily held onto a Senate seat in Georgia, despite its swing-state status.
In the House, Democrats secured a number of flips in key races, including at least three Florida districts that the state's Republican legislature redrew in an effort to stymie Democratic candidates. Democratic candidates also managed to oust four Republican incumbents in swing districts across Pennsylvania, all of that state's competitive races.
Loading...
"From sea to shining sea, the American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption," said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat who is poised to become the next Speaker of the House. "They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January."
Now, Washington enters a new political moment. Come January, when the new Congress is sworn in, President Trump is certain to face an onslaught of investigations and congressional oversight. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., expected to become chair of the House Oversight committee, did not mince words in the statement he posted to X: "LAWYER UP."
Still, voters hoping to see swift policy change could be disappointed. Trump retains his veto power, meaning legislation passed by Congress will almost certainly need his support to become law. That means Democrats' affordability-focused agenda may ultimately become a messaging tool for the 2028 election season, rather than a near-term policy intervention in Americans' everyday lives.
In an interview with the Pod Force One podcast that was published Monday, Trump addressed the prospect of losing unified Republican control in Washington, saying he would block Democrats' legislation if they take control of Congress.
"I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump said, adding, "and then at some point we'll probably make deals."
Democrats will have to work with Republicans on some must-pass legislation, including the 12 annual appropriations bills needed to fund the government.
Still, the party's control of the Senate will halt the steady confirmation of Trump-nominated judges through the body. It also means that any Cabinet nominees will need the support of at least a handful of Democrats to take the posts in a permanent capacity.
When it comes to investigations, Democrats have signaled an ambitious agenda, with potential inquiries into everything from the independence of agencies such as the Justice Department and Homeland Security, to the business interests of the president and his family.
A remarkable turnaround
The Senate win marked a long-fought victory for Democrats, and an electoral disaster for Republicans, who began the year with little expectation that their 53–47 majority was at risk. But with voters frustrated about the cost of living, the GOP was forced to compete in several states that President Trump won by double digits in 2024.
By early Wednesday morning, House Democrats had secured wins in seats that long seemed to be surefire Republican districts. In Kentucky, Democrats picked up a Lexington-area district that President Trump won with 57% of the vote in 2024.
Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., will also be returning to Congress. His district in Alabama's Black Belt was redrawn to heavily favor Republicans after the Supreme Court's conservative supermajority dismantled key provisions of the Voting Rights Act.
In the closing weeks of the election, President Trump took to the campaign trail and implored Republican voters to pretend he was on the ballot. But at a moment when Trump's approval ratings are hovering at historic lows, below 40 percent, the argument was not enough to save the GOP majority.
Losing the Senate majority marks a blow for Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.
In a post to X early Wednesday morning, Thune said that "Senate Republicans have put up a strong record of accomplishment that's created safer streets, more money in Americans' pockets, and new opportunities for families and businesses to get ahead."
"I'm proud of our team and everything we've done for the American people," Thune wrote. "Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we've done"
Across the aisle, Democrats' victory represents a vindication for Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who faced criticism from some progressives early in the president's second term that he was not doing enough to stand up to Trump.
In an October floor speech, Schumer said Democrats were ready to challenge President Trump and Republicans' agenda.
"We are ready to hit the ground running to lower costs, rein in chaos and stop the corruption," Schumer said. "Republicans broke faith with the American people. We know we need to build that trust with the Americans back up, and we will."
Loading...

npr.org.title: Democrat Josh Turek wins the Senate seat in Iowa
npr.org.text:
Democrat Josh Turek wins the Senate seat in Iowa
Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country
Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app
Democrat Josh Turek has won the U.S. Senate race in Iowa, according to a race call by The Associated Press. His win ends more than a decade of Republican control of both Senate seats in the state.
Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs, beat Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson. He flipped one of the country's most competitive U.S. Senate seats, replacing retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst, who announced she would not be seeking a third term last fall.
Loading...
Turek is a two-time gold medalist playing basketball in the Paralympics. He uses a wheelchair due to spina bifida, a condition he says is due to his father's exposure to Agent Orange in the Vietnam War. He was a relatively unknown state lawmaker who beat Zach Wahls, the former state Senate minority leader, to get the Democratic nomination in June.
Loading...
Turek, who calls himself a "prairie populist," campaigned hard on healthcare reform, attacking Hinson for her support of Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which reduces Medicaid spending nationwide by nearly $1 trillion, and claims that Hinson's personal wealth has increased significantly during her time in Washington.
Both Hinson and Turek emphasized their ability as bipartisan lawmakers to try to sway the state's large number of uncommitted voters, but increased their attacks against their opponents, especially as polling data started to indicate a close race.
