But I wanted to see for myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.
I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.
Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s trickle.

theintercept.com.title: In California’s Central Valley, ICE Might Swing a Red District Blue
theintercept.com.text:
In California’s Central Valley, some surprising voters are lining up behind a progressive upstart: A law enforcement officer who calls for the abolition of ICE. A millennial who once voted for a Republican congressman.
They found themselves among supporters of Randy Villegas, a Democrat poised to oust longtime incumbent Republican Rep. David Valadao in a district dominated for decades by conservatives in California’s Central Valley.
With Democratic victories across the nation, California’s 22nd Congressional District is the kind of historically red stronghold where progressive policies may find new purchase.
Villegas’s path to the general election mirrors that of other progressive candidates charting a new identity within the party. Running on policies such as Medicare for All, addressing affordability, rejecting corporate donations, and halting the flow of weapons to Israel, the 31-year-old defeated a moderate Democratic state assembly member backed by the party’s establishment in the June primary.
Villegas’s opposition to ICE in a district that is 70 percent Latino or Hispanic marked the sharpest point of contrast with Valadao, who defended the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant campaign and famously uttered “It is what it is” on the debate stage last month when pressed on the issue. Valadao claimed “a lot” of the individuals captured by ICE in the Central Valley in recent weeks have criminal records, despite research showing the majority of those detained by ICE lack criminal convictions.
It was Valadao’s stance on immigration that most animated Central Valley voters who spoke with The Intercept.
“I’ve never seen him stand up to something I feel is egregious,” said Raul Castro, 53, a Fresno County probation officer who is upset with Valadao’s lack of willingness to oppose Trump on the ICE raids surging through the area in recent weeks. “I just don’t respect people like that.”
While standing on the front porch of his house in a middle-class suburb in northwest Fresno, Castro lamented ICE’s targeting of immigrants based on their appearance, language, or jobs. He spoke out against immigration agents pulling people from the street and into labyrinthine detention centers where civil rights advocates have reported a lack of access to basic necessities such as clean water and adequate healthcare. Though Castro once supported ICE, when asked whether he would support abolishing the agency altogether, he said yes.
“If you asked me that same question, ‘Hey would you abolish ICE?’ I’d say, ‘No, ‘cause they’re doing things to make sure our country is safe. I want to live in a safe Fresno, safe county, safe city,’” Castro told The Intercept. “But now, wait a minute, maybe that’s not what I thought it was going to be.”
Villegas told The Intercept he wasn’t surprised to hear he had won the support of an anti-ICE law enforcement officer.
“I don’t find it surprising because I think ICE has made it much more difficult for local law enforcement to carry out their jobs and their work — and everybody is seeing the indiscriminate profiling going on,” Villegas said at a Fresno park rally to support last-minute canvassing efforts.
Villegas himself does not support abolishing ICE but instead has called for wide-ranging reforms of the agency. The policy position makes Villegas somewhat an anomaly among his progressive peers, who are riding a wave of leftist energy into Congress, some of whom include “Abolish ICE” among their campaign platforms.
While holding key endorsements from high-profile democratic socialists Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Villegas has also rejected the socialist label, preferring “populist,” despite attempts by the Republican national party to weaponize the term against him. Unlike many of his fellow progressives, Villegas is also one of the few who is running in a historically red district. And he’s confident voters are not caught up in the ideological nuances and hopes to instead cut through them.
“People are fed up with an agency who is unaccountable, people are fed up with a member of Congress who is unaccountable, who doesn’t even have public town halls,” Villegas said. “We deserve better than that in the Central Valley, and I think that’s why our messaging is resonating across the political spectrum.”
Such reach across the political spectrum is also evidenced in voters like Aram Easter, 33, who was born and raised in Fresno. He doesn’t vote in every election, but cast a ballot for Valadao a decade ago when his district previously covered Fresno, largely because he bought the vision of someone with local Central Valley roots (Valadao was born and raised in the nearby Hanford). He also agrees with some aspects of Trump’s agenda, such as building the border wall. But he drew the line on immigration enforcement.
“You got people tearing people’s families apart,” Easter said. “My family immigrated here — I have Black and Mexican family — I’m not with them overly-aggressively doing it.”
Since early October, ICE raids have become more prevalent in the region, with more than 200 people detained by authorities throughout the surge, according to the local newsroom Fresnoland. Similar upticks in ICE have taken place recently throughout the state, including Los Angeles and San Diego. Voter rights organizations in the Central Valley have taken notice and are viewing the raids as an effort by the Trump administration to suppress the vote, especially in a key race in the 22nd District.
“This timing of the uptick in ICE is not a coincidence,” said Marisa Moraza, political director at PowerCA Action, which is doing independent expenditure work to support Villegas’s campaign. “It’s not a coincidence that this started at the beginning of October when voters received their ballots in the mail.”
The raids have also suppressed get-out-the-vote efforts, Moraza said. Last month, the group had to pause in-person canvassing operations for several days amid the surge in ICE activity, electing to instead do phone banking.
The ICE activity is also keeping would-be voters from dropping off their ballots, as recent arrests of U.S. citizens struck fear among voters, said Cirilo Ordaz, a canvasser with PowerCA supporting Villegas.
“With going out to vote, I think a lot of them haven’t done it yet because of that fear,” said Ordaz, who was one of dozens of Villegas supporters who fanned out across the region on the Monday before Election Day to urge residents to vote.
Sylvia Ramirez, another Fresno native canvassing with PowerCA said she’s noticed far fewer people outside in recent weeks, including a lack of crowds at the popular annual event Big Fresno Fair. For voters, she and her group offer to drop off people’s ballots for them if the fear is keeping them inside.
“Offering the services of dropping off a ballot for somebody really helps out with the fear that people have of leaving their houses,” she said, adding that she has told her family to stay at home as much as possible in recent days to avoid interactions with ICE.
The Central Valley, known for its significant agriculture production, has been the seat of high-profile Republican lawmakers, such as former Rep. Devin Nunes and former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy.
But after a Democrat-led redistricting in the state last year in response to Texas’s partisan redistricting effort, the district now includes the northwest sections of Fresno, a city with more Democrats.
Early voting across the state has outpaced recent midterm elections, according to a recent survey. It’s unclear how much of that is anti-Trump animus or having a candidate voters are excited to support.
Castro, the probation officer, was among those who voted early. In recent weeks, he said he noticed residents looking at him with concern while on the job in uniform, showing up at areas where ICE had previously conducted raids. It’s a fear he acutely understood. As a child, he lived in labor camps with his mother and father, who were both undocumented immigrants working in Fresno as farm laborers. He recalled similar indiscriminate sweeps by Border Patrol in the 1970s.
“When I was small, back then it was Border Patrol, and they used to show up in a van,” Castro recalled. “All the agents used to get out and run after these guys. And they used to round them up and take them out,” he said.
Seeing video and hearing of recent ICE raids targeting farmworkers in the area conjured such painful memories.
“I never thought I’d see that again,” he said.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

theintercept.com.title: Even Anti-Trans Panic Couldn’t Save Republicans in Deep-Red Texas
theintercept.com.text:
On an election night handing Republicans a beating in critical House and Senate races across the country, the GOP fell short even in once deep-red Texas after a campaign run on a go-to outrage tactic: fearmongering over the rights of transgender people.
Democrats escaped the political wilderness in the Longhorn State on Tuesday night, when Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton — despite the far-right attorney general’s relentless attacks on the trans community and his party’s claims that Democrats would enforce so-called “transgenderism” as a kind of ideology.
The massive upset was paired with a victory for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, who beat Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott shortly after the Senate race was called for Talarico.
In Dallas, Paxton voter Rachel Fuller told The Intercept she was alarmed by what she believed was Talarico’s support for “far-fetched” ideas, like “giving children the right to decide — and making parents, calling them abusive for not letting them have transgender changes.”
Her comments suggested some of the $78 million Republicans spent on anti-trans attack advertisements in Texas were working. But they weren’t enough to help Republicans hold onto power in Texas, which hasn’t had a Democratic senator since the 1990s.
The ads made up almost half of all ad spending in support of Paxton, according to an analysis from Puck using data from AdImpact.
By and large, the ads spread blatant misinformation about Talarico’s record.
One infamous $29 million ad created by Texas PAC, a political action committee primarily funded by billionaire Elon Musk, claimed that Talarico supported jailing parents who did not support gender-affirming surgeries for minors. “Every mom in Texas should be worried about James Talarico putting parents in jail if they do not support surgically transitioning their children,” a woman in the ad warned ominously.
That attack, which according to Puck received 1.9 billion views as of October, does seem to have caught the attention of Texans — even with voters who ultimately supported Talarico.
Julius Ishola, a canvasser for Black TOP, an operation under Texas Organizing Project that targets Black voters, told The Intercept he had frequently heard Black voters raise concerns that Talarico intended to jail parents.
“I’ve been getting a lot of bad feedback regarding James Talarico,” Ishola told The Intercept, saying many voters cited concerns of “gender sex change and possibly prosecuting parents who go against that … and allowing transgenders into female restrooms.”
As a state legislator, Talarico fought bans on transgender athletes’ participation in youth sports, and famously said that God is “nonbinary,” earning him ridicule from Republicans, who nicknamed the Senate candidate “Talafreako.” In the face of those attacks this cycle, Talarico appeared to backtrack on the issue, telling Fox News in September that he supported bans on transgender children’s participation in sports if it risks “safety or fairness” — without clarifying what that meant.
His wavering does not seem to have reached many voters.
“I voted Republican all the way. And that’s my fear of Talarico going in,” said Carol Billings, a voter who cast her ballot for Paxton at the Living Waters Church in Dallas County. Like Fuller, she cited her perception of the Democratic nominee’s trans policies as a major source for concern.
Still, many voters in Black districts, which were vital to Talarico’s victory, barely mentioned Talarico.
“At the end of the day,” said Dallas Jones, a Houston-based Democratic political strategist whose firm focuses on African American voter engagement and backed Talarico, “the results show that people care more about their everyday lives than they do about trans Americans who just want to get by.”
Some voters told The Intercept they were far more concerned with issues of affordability. “ I just hope we can get these gas prices down,” said Darryl Moore, a Fort Worth voter.
This is a developing story and will be updated. Akela Lacy reported from Dallas, Texas.

theintercept.com.title: Michigan Senate Race Closes as a Referendum on Israel Policy
theintercept.com.text:
For the left, it’s been the marquee race of the midterm cycle. Either a Republican former U.S. representative known for pushing domestic spying powers or an outspoken progressive who forced a reckoning over U.S.–Israel policy among Democrats will emerge from Election Day as the next senator from Michigan.
Abdul El-Sayed would be the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected Tuesday night, capping off a race that’s been viewed as a referendum on swing-state appeal for the Democratic Party’s left flank. If he defeats Mike Rogers, a loyal Trump ally whose campaign often peddled Islamophobic tropes against the Democratic nominee, the results will all but certainly embolden progressives ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
If El-Sayed loses, it will likely trigger a centrist backlash — and cost the Democrats a critical Senate seat as the party fights to take back the upper chamber.
Polls across Michigan closed by 9 p.m. ET on Tuesday, with anxious voters across the state awaiting the returns.
In the heavily Arab and Muslim city of Dearborn, voters across party lines said they were outraged at the Islamophobic attacks ads targeting El-Sayed that became a staple of airwaves and social media feeds in the campaign’s final days.
“I am a Muslim. And I’ve seen a lot of ads, and it’s disgusting, because we are good people,” said Gus Tarraf, a Republican running for a state House seat. “I love this country.”
Although Donald Trump carried many precincts in Dearborn two years ago due to voter frustration over the Biden administration’s support of Israel, Tarraf said his community is turning on the Republican Party this year.
“Not a lot of Arab Americans are happy with the Trump administration,” he said. “So it doesn’t matter if they know you, as soon as they know you are on the Republican ticket.”
El-Sayed’s willingness to criticize U.S. policy on Israel animated soap-opera-level drama in the final days of the race, when his former primary opponent, centrist Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, announced she would switch her endorsement to support Rogers.
After demanding an apology from El-Sayed for an outside PAC’s ad, Stevens said on social media that she came to the decision after feeling “shut out” by El-Sayed’s campaign, adding that she’s heard from “Black voters, Jewish voters, and others about how deeply these messages hurt.” Rogers, she said, gave her “the hope that he can serve in the tradition of John McCain: a senator willing to put country before party and stand up to his own side when conscience requires it.”
Stevens’s late-breaking endorsement of Rogers drew a mix of eye-rolls and outrage from voters at three precincts in Detroit and Dearborn. None of the voters interviewed by The Intercept said it had swayed them to vote for Rogers.
“People have already early voted. People have already absentee voted,” said Noora Iskander. “I don’t think many people change their minds. So I think it’s just hypocritical.”
Stevens’s decision to make the endorsement while inside a Black church in Detroit may also have generated backlash from the Black voters that Rogers was hoping to win over, according to some who spoke to The Intercept. One said the church community has been buzzing — and not positively — about the weekend’s events.
“Unfortunately, she went to a Black church to use it as a backdrop,” said Dearborn voter Dorothea Sharon. “It really was a slap in the face for the Black community that that happened.”
On election night, Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who endorsed El-Sayed and will be the senior senator from Michigan in the next Congress, asked supporters to “take a step back from all the drama we’ve had in the last couple of days,” in an allusion to Stevens. She resisted narrative portrayals of a power struggle between centrists like her and progressives like El-Sayed.
“Let me just explain to all the media that Michigan is an independently minded state, we take orders from no one,” Slotkin said at the El-Sayed watch party in Michigan. “We don’t take guidance from anyone on how to think about our vote, we make up our minds. And it’s not progressive versus moderate, it is whether you are on team fight or team flight.”
Slotkin, who is Jewish, said voters should focus on “the idea that the state of Michigan can send one Jewish senator and one Muslim senator for the first time ever in history.”
While El-Sayed has had to face intense scrutiny over accusations of conflating opposition to U.S. aid to Israel with antisemitism, little accounting has been made of the blatant Islamophobia and xenophobia from the Rogers campaign, the Republican Party, and Trump. But in Dearborn, the rhetoric had clearly hurt several voters who spoke to The Intercept.
The father of state Senate candidate Abbas Alawieh, a Democrat who played a prominent role in the 2024 Uncommitted movement, grew visibly upset when asked about the ads targeting Muslims.
“These are weak people who don’t have anything to do — they don’t have any programs for our economy, for our health, for our future,” Zouheir Alawieh said. “That’s why they are attacking us as Muslims and as human beings. It’s never been like this. This is a shame. America is a place where the Black with the white with the yellow, the Muslim with the Christian with the Jews, can live freely. Don’t try to tear up our society.”
Outside Dearborn, El-Sayed has tried to defuse the anti-Muslim smears against him by joking that he is only in favor of “shawarma law.” However, the Islamophobic attacks convinced at least one voter to cast her ballot for Rogers.
“I don’t want to live under Sharia law,” said Joann, a law firm employee who declined to give her last name after she voted in Detroit.
The fear of Islamic rule was the main issue for Joann, she said, although she also worried about El-Sayed’s campaign pledge of Medicare for All.
“I’ve worked my whole life, put all my stuff into the Medicare, but then I’ve got to let other people get it for free? It doesn’t seem fair to me when I’ve worked my whole life for it, and we’re not even sure that it’s going to be there when we really get ready to retire,” she said.
Yet it was that very messaging from El-Sayed’s campaign that excited many other residents in Michigan. Many voters who spoke to The Intercept said they were more focused on pocketbook issues.
“It’s the gas prices, the food. I mean, money is running out your pocket so fast,” Leigh James said after voting at Tabernacle Missionary Baptist Church in Detroit.
James said she had walked to the polling place to avoid using gas. “I’m trying to save,” she said. “So thank God I live in the neighborhood.”
Other voters said they were inspired by El-Sayed’s personality, with one woman describing him as a “fighter.”
Noora Iskander, who voted for El-Sayed in Dearborn, said she approved of his stance in favor of Medicare for All, his affordability platform, and his solidarity with Palestine.
“I think he’s going to make a lot of change. He’s going to scare a lot of people — which I believe is a good thing, because you can’t really change for the better if you don’t scare a few people,” she said.
This is a developing story. Matt Sledge reported from Dearborn and Detroit, Michigan.

theintercept.com.title: Troy Jackson Ousts Susan Collins in Maine, Replacing 30-Year Republican Senator With a Progressive
theintercept.com.text:
The 30-year Senate career of Maine Republican Susan Collins is coming to an end.
The powerful incumbent chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee conceded early Wednesday to Troy Jackson, a progressive challenger who was virtually unknown on the national stage until his rushed elevation as the Democratic replacement candidate just over three months ago.
“A little more than 100 days ago, I stood in front of you at our convention and asked you to put your faith in a logger from Allagash,” Jackson told supporters in Portland, referring to a rapid nominating process he went through after former nominee Graham Platner dropped out. Like Platner, Jackson came from the left flank of the Democratic Party and ran a campaign focused on the concerns of working-class people in the face of a system he presented as stacked in favor of the wealthy and corporate interests.
Collins, who has represented the state since 1997, ran as an independent force in Washington able to secure critical federal funds for Mainers. But she was brought down with the baggage of the Republican brand on a night when Democrats overperformed in critical swing states and handily seized control of both chambers of Congress.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate,” Collins said in a statement released early Wednesday. “I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years.”
While Collins often presented herself as the rare Republican who breaks ranks with President Donald Trump, an analysis by Congressional Quarterly Roll Call found that her votes aligned with Trump 90 percent of the time in both the president’s first and second terms.
“We now see her failing to stand up to a brutal, irresponsible, greedy and corrupt regime,” Maine Democratic Party Chair Charlie Dingman told The Intercept. “She has not used her seniority or her power to aggressively stand in the way of that destructive presidency, and that is a serious and fundamental difference between 2020 and 2026.”
Dingman argued that Collins faced a fundamentally different political environment than she did in 2020, pointing to her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh and the subsequent overturning of Roe v. Wade.
Still, Collins’s split support among some Democratic voters was evident Tuesday in Lewiston, where several residents told The Intercept they were supporting the Republican senator despite filling their ballots out to Democrats otherwise.
“I am Susan Collins all the way,” said Anne Marie Hastings, a voter who also expressed strong support for Matt Dunlap, a progressive running against former Republican Gov. Paul LePage in a closely watched race in the state’s 2nd Congressional District.
“I’m a registered Democrat, but when it comes to things like this, I go with what I feel is right, not the party that they belong to,” Hastings said. She also praised Collins for advocating for shipbuilding contracts at Bath Iron Works, where she said her brothers had worked.
But John Cabral III, a shipbuilder at the same shipyard, disputed Collins’s record.
“She didn’t bring any extra work,” Cabral told The Intercept. “So that’s all propaganda.”
Cabral said he supports Jackson because of his commitment to organized labor.
“I think they are going to wake up and smell the coffee,” Cabral said of Maine voters. “[Mainers] have never seen a senator fight as hard as Troy, especially for labor.”
Another Lewiston voter, Ouellette Bertram, said he voted blue across the board, with the exception of “the Republican lady,” who he said he just plain likes.
“She’s been doing a good job, I think,” Bertram said.
But other Maine residents didn’t share the sentiment toward the Republican incumbent — and the loyalty ultimately failed to secure her reelection.
Democrat-supporting voter Bryan Golay said he wished the party would move to the left but voted against what he described as the GOP’s “enshittification” of America, much of which, he said, has come during Collins’s time in Washington.
“If you can’t get shit done in 30 years, why are we gonna give you another term?” Golay said.
Mags Krantz, a master’s student of social work who works with children with disabilities, said she voted for all Democrats, including Dunlap and Jackson, citing GOP-backed cuts to social services.
“They just cut funding for my job, and for my career,” Krantz told The Intercept outside a polling site in Lewiston on Tuesday. “I really voted for my future, but I also voted for every vulnerable child that I work with every single day that really wishes adults would vote for them over money.”
Speaking to a crowd of supporters on the eve of the election, Jackson toasted the grassroots organizing that has powered his rapidly assembled campaign into the most serious challenge yet to Collins’s hold on her seat.
“This government is fundamentally broken, and it only works for the wealthiest people in this country — that’s what we’re up against right now,” Jackson said. “They are going to outspend the hell out of us. There’s no doubt about it. But they don’t have people like you in rooms like this across this state and across the country.”
Jackson, who spent nearly 20 years in the state legislature, ran on a platform focused on lowering costs for working-class families, expanding healthcare access, and combating the influence of wealthy donors and corporate PACs in Washington. He entered the race somewhat hastily in late July, after former Democratic nominee Graham Platner withdrew from the Senate race following a rape allegation, which Platner denied.
The Collins–Jackson race was one of the top targets for national attention this cycle — most of it on purpose. In October, The Intercept reported that Defending Main Street, a Republican-aligned super PAC associated with Collins spent between $20,000 and $25,000 attacking Jackson on topics such as cost-of-living and taxes. The ads mistakenly were targeted to audiences in Portland, Oregon, rather than the intended Portland, Maine.
This developing story has been updated. Noah Hurowitz reported from Lewiston and Portland, Maine.

theintercept.com.title: Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point
theintercept.com.text:
The United States will stop providing $4 billion in annual aid to Israel starting next year, President Donald Trump claimed in an Election Day interview. While the U.S. will continue to sell arms to its closest Middle East ally, Trump’s announcement — should it actually hold true — could represent a seismic shift in American foreign policy.
Still questions remain and experts are dubious that the claim is what it seems.
Trump told Fox News during a phone call on Tuesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him with the idea years ago. He did not state specifically why he waited to announce the decision in the midst of a midterm vote in which his party is expected to lose its lock on Congress, but noted that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point, singling out Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” said Trump.
An August 2026 Fox News poll found 55 percent of Michigan voters oppose continued military assistance to Israel, including 70 percent of Democrats, 66 percent of Independents, and 35 percent of Republicans.
U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats, as Netanyahu’s government has slaughtered civilians with impunity. Almost 75,000 Gazans have been killed and nearly 176,000 wounded, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza. A recent U.N. report said, “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”
Amid the slaughter, sympathy for Israel among all Americans fell from roughly 50 percent to 36, while sympathy for Palestinians rose to 41 percent, according to a February Gallup poll. Among Democrats, support for Israel plummeted from more than 50 percent in 2001 to roughly 17 percent this year. October 2026 polling from the Institute for Middle East Understanding’s D.C.-based IMEU Policy Project and YouGov found a majority of voters in six key swing states — Georgia, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas — support halting the transfer of bombs to Israel.
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Experts cautioned not to take Trump at his word, especially as his administration pushes a pending $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act that would embed Israeli technology within the Pentagon’s programs and supply chain.
“President Trump is a serial liar who has announced over $20 billion in weapons giveaways to Israel since taking office and launched a war at Israel’s request that has already cost every U.S. household over $2,000 — the equivalent of $262 billion,” said Hamid Bendaas, IMEU Policy Project’s communications director. “He and other politicians realize our taxpayer funding for Israel is a liability. That’s why he and his allies in Congress are at this very moment trying to advance legislation to conceal support for Israel by integrating Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon. This is a bait and switch that would result in Americans funding Israeli weapons makers in record amounts.”
Others expressed skepticism about Trump‘s claim of an immediate end of annual aid in 2027. “It’s not plausible there will be a total cut-off starting January 1,” said Josh Paul, who spent more than 11 years as the director of congressional and public affairs at the State Department bureau that oversees arms transfers to foreign nations before resigning in 2023 over U.S. military assistance to Israel, noting that funding is baked into existing and pending legislation. “My guess is that he was speaking off the cuff with the next 10-year memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Israel in mind, but did so in a way that is at best inaccurate or imprecise.”
A decade ago, President Barack Obama signed an unprecedented MOU with Israel to give its military $38 billion between 2019 and 2028, amounting to almost $4 billion a year.
Paul was hopeful, however that Trump’s statement would allow Republicans license to join Democratic colleagues in paring down future funding. He said it was a recognition of the bipartisan demand by the American people for an end to that military aid.
Trump’s announcement did not address the proposal in the National Defense Authorization Act, which would inextricably link the U.S. armed forces and the Israeli military, giving Israel leverage over the Pentagon.
“Initial reporting on Trump’s statement omits a crucial fact: that the National Defense Authorization Act contains a provision intended to protect U.S. tax dollars flowing to Israel from the massive shift in U.S. public opinion against funding Israeli aggression,” Annelle Sheline, who served as a foreign affairs officer in the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, told The Intercept. “The provision would move U.S. funding out of security assistance under the purview of the State Department — which carries legal provisions like the Leahy Laws, transparency requirements, and an annual congressional vote — into the Pentagon procurement process, which has none of these.”
Sheline added, “Insulated from public opinion and away from public visibility, U.S. funding to Israel is likely to grow exponentially.”
With his popularity in free fall in the U.S., Trump teased the possibility of decamping for Israel and taking Netanyahu’s job as the Israeli prime minister battles for his political life after an inconclusive election last week. “In fact, if people ever got tired of me in the U.S., I’ll move to Israel, become prime minister,” Trump declared during his Fox appearance.
The White House did not immediately respond to requests for further details.

theintercept.com.title: Ashley Hinson’s Digital Chief Oversees Firm Paid Millions to Push Israeli Propaganda
theintercept.com.text:
The person in charge of digital strategy for the Senate campaign of Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson helps run a company that received nearly $10 million to influence Americans with pro-Israel propaganda.
In September 2025, Hinson — who is battling Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in a tight race that could decide control of the Senate — tapped Abe Adams to lead her campaign’s digital efforts.
Adams is a co-founder and managing partner of Targeted Victory, a digital consulting firm that has been used by high-profile Republican candidates such as Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio. Targeted Victory shares an address and much of its staff with Targeted Communications Global — a related company with no discernible online presence. Both are subsidiaries of marketing company Stagwell Global.
Israel awarded Targeted Communications a $9.9 million contract in March 2025 focused on social media and paid advertising, documents show. By October 2025, the firm was at work pitching news content and guests on Fox News and CNN, and creating YouTube ads suggesting young Iranians have been educated to believe the “most sacred thing they do is stab a Christian in the heart.”
Hinson is endorsed by both President Donald Trump and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and has been supportive of Trump’s war in Iran.
A June 2026 Department of Justice FARA filing from Targeted Communications details much of the firm’s work for Israel. The document lists 10 registered foreign agents working on the Targeted Communications contract for Israel. Six of them are identified as Targeted Victory employees on the company’s website or their LinkedIn accounts. Adams is not named in the filing.
Hinson, Adams, and Targeted Victory did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Adams is not the only Hinson campaign adviser with ties to Targeted Victory and the Israel lobby. Hinson’s current deputy campaign manager, Addison Lavis, worked at Targeted Victory before serving as Hinson’s campaign manager in her 2023 congressional run. Lavis was previously an intern at AIPAC. Lavis did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Hinson has received more than $100,000 from AIPAC and related pro-Israel PACs in 2026, and as an Iowa state representative supported legislation that prohibited the state from working with any companies that boycott Israel.
Hinson’s political action committee has paid Targeted Victory more than $1.6 million this election cycle for digital consulting and ads — 27 percent of its total expenditures, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Israel’s deal with Targeted Communications is part of a major public relations push that has pumped more than $100 million into swaying public opinion, particularly among young conservatives, back toward Israel.

theintercept.com.title: If Democrats Win, Thank the Left
theintercept.com.text:
Democrats are on the verge of reversing their political fortunes. The party is heading into the midterm elections Tuesday under the kind of conditions campaign consultants dream of, after two years wielding hardly more power than a strongly worded letter.
Donald Trump has spent the erratic waning years of his presidency leading his party into a political wilderness by waging a deeply unpopular war on Iran and driving the cost of living ever higher. Republicans who enjoy a governing trifecta have tried to distance themselves from the party’s decision-making and its leader, a once-animating force who has turned himself into a liability. Poll after poll says the same: Democrats are poised to take control of one or both houses of Congress — and spend the next two years thwarting Trump’s agenda.
But after a primary season dominated by an ascendant left wing and a broader rejection of centrist politics, the question isn’t just whether Democrats win on Tuesday. It’s what kind of Democratic Party emerges on Wednesday morning.
“I really like the socialism aspects,” said Gibrel Said, a supporter of Abdul El-Sayed at his closing rally in Detroit Monday night. In the marquee contest serving as a referendum on the Democratic Party’s future, the Michigan Democratic Senate nominee espouses progressive politics and has often been associated with the the left’s agenda-setting socialists, though he doesn’t identify as one. His race has been rocked by the kind of left-versus-right identity crisis that presents a perennial challenge for Democrats.
“One, Medicare for All; two, how do we fund things that help us as constituents,” Said told The Intercept, ticking off things he appreciates about the candidate. Said, who lives in the Arab enclave of Dearborn, Michigan, especially praised El-Sayed’s willingness to buck party leadership and speak out on U.S.–Israel policy. “Instead of tiptoeing around the subject, he very adamantly says, hey there’s a genocide happening here, we shouldn’t send our money.”
Cycle after cycle, in state after state, an insurgent band of Democrats critical of the political establishment’s ties to corporate interests and its unflinching commitment to Israel has had to overcome the barriers erected by its own party’s centrist leadership. Both sides present themselves as the true representatives of working people: the centrists by arguing that more transformative ideas will scare off lower-information voters, the left by saying they represent the masses.
How much of this trickles down to actual voters? On Monday, The Intercept followed canvassers and spoke to voters in Michigan, Maine, and Texas, asking about which issues had permeated and taking the temperature of voter enthusiasm. Some rolled their eyes at the spats that have dominated the headlines, dismissing the idea that eleventh-hour backstabbing would make a difference. Others regurgitated right-wing misinformation. Many complained of too many campaign mailers.
“They’re wicked mean,” said Sharon McDonnell, a supporter of Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine. Speaking to The Intercept in the town of Yarmouth, she described one mailer that included a photo of Jackson chomping a cigar and describing him as “evil.” “It’s just nasty.”
In Maine, the party’s left flank seized power in the nominating process for the Democratic Senate candidate — then fought to hang onto it after onetime rising star Graham Platner flamed out after a sexual assault allegation (which he denies). With Jackson, a former state Senate leader, Maine now offers progressives one of two opportunities to test their message at the Senate level, where a candidate has to secure appeal statewide, not just in deep-blue House districts.
The other is Michigan, where the intraparty battle is still raging. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., demolished her past attempts at fence-mending when she endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday and abandoned El-Sayed, who beat Stevens in a Michigan primary that saw $30 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
The dustup has had Democrats biting their nails and moderate party leaders making the cable news circuit to demand party discipline — this time, to scold a centrist. The party leads in the polls for 218 of the 435 seats up for grabs in the House of Representatives, but they need to perform well in seven key states — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas, in addition to Maine and Michigan — if they want to win the Senate.
“I think she’s counterintuitively, perhaps, given people a reason to rally some more,” said Kathleen Britton, an El-Sayed supporter at the Detroit rally on Monday, of Stevens. “I really don’t think it’s gonna help Mike Rogers.”
Earlier that day, in a predominantly Black neighborhood of Detroit, a prominent Black supporter of El-Sayed preparing to knock on voters’ doors described Stevens’s endorsement as an “ego-driven statement.”
Mike Bland, the executive director of the Black Men Vote PAC, highlighted that Stevens made her public endorsement of Rogers in a Black church in Detroit. He doubted that Stevens, whose criticism of El-Sayed centers primarily on his skepticism of the U.S. relationship with the state of Israel, would be able to pull Black voters to Rogers, a conservative former House representative whose campaign has repeatedly peddled anti-Muslim tropes against El-Sayed.
“How can I say this without cursing? She used a Black church as a prop, and we have seen that time and time again,” Bland said. “Black folks aren’t stupid.”
Over the past month, El-Sayed has rallied with Barack Obama and Kamala Harris, the two most prominent Black politicians in America — and hardly radicals estranged from the establishment power center. At the same time that Stevens was making her endorsement of Rogers public, El-Sayed was attending a get-out-the-vote event at another church in Detroit. The two primary foes were supposed to appear together that day with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C.
One of the Democrats’ most coveted Senate pickups didn’t present much of an opportunity for the left in the primary, but it has still been characterized by intraparty animosity.
In Texas, where both Democratic Senate primary contenders espoused relatively moderate politics, outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, has declined to campaign with state Rep. James Talarico, though she endorsed him after he beat her in the state’s March Democratic primary.
Talarico has been performing well with Latino voters, a massive voting bloc that helped fuel his primary victory. But Crockett — who, unlike Stevens, is Black — has suggested that Talarico has not done enough to excite Black voters, a demographic she carried in the primary. On a canvassing operation targeting Black voters in the Dallas–Fort Worth area on Monday, few Black Texans who spoke to The Intercept expressed excitement for Talarico. But most had already voted for him, saying they were motivated to do their civic duty.
Black voters frequently discussed concerns over affordability, gas prices, and homelessness. Canvassers told The Intercept they had heard some of those voters express concerns over their perception of Talarico’s policies toward transgender children, at times espousing blatant misinformation, such as the idea that Talarico supported arresting parents who refused to give their children gender-affirming surgeries.
“ I don’t stand for that,” said voter Jermiah Robinson, referring to her belief that Talarico pushed “sex-change” surgery for minors. Like many voters, she cited the cost of living as her most pressing issue. Robinson said she would “want to vote for him if he stands by his words, and he’s actually like ‘Yeah, I’ll help out as far as prices and everything.’”
Talarico appears to have improved his margins with Black voters in the final stretch. According to the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas, Talarico is leading with 79 percent of the Black vote, signaling a significant increase in support from Black voters from just last month. The conventional wisdom suggests that he could barely ask for a better opponent than the scandal-plagued Republican candidate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
In 2015, Paxton was indicted on felony securities fraud charges in Texas, in a case that dragged on for roughly nine years, and ended with Paxton being required to do community service and pay restitution. And in 2023, the Texas House of Representatives voted across party lines to impeach him as attorney general for alleged corruption and retaliation against whistleblowers.
Scandal kept rocking the race for Senate in Maine, where longtime Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins faces her toughest reelection challenge yet from Jackson. Before Jackson, who lost a race this cycle for the state’s Democratic nomination for governor, there was Platner, hailed early as a working-class champion who faced a series of personal scandals in his successful primary campaign. There was the revelation of a Nazi tattoo that he claimed not to understand until last October. There were crudely worded Reddit posts and stories of cruelty from women he’d dated. One former girlfriend’s allegations of sexual assault ultimately ended his campaign — and set off a scramble to find a replacement that progressives ultimately won by elevating Jackson.
By Monday, Mainers who spoke to The Intercept appeared exhausted by the lengthy, contentious, and expensive Senate race that has dominated the state.
“There’s a lot of fatigue. People are tired of it,“ said Charlie Dingman, who chairs the state Democratic Party. “I have had some conversations at doors with people that have led me to think that the extremely negative and extremely untruthful ads may be backfiring.”
Tyler Echard, in Norway, said he’d already cast an absentee ballot for Democrats down the ticket. He was disgusted with a deluge of political mailers and eager to stop seeing them pile up on his doorstep.
“The amount of mailers we get — just mailers, not just handed at the door but in the mail — especially from the Republican side, the amount of money is probably more than I will make in my lifetime, spent in this election,” Echard said. “At some point, we gotta get legislation because money’s just gonna run everything into the ground. I ain’t got it, so I can’t influence it.”
Frustration with the status quo in Congress could spell the end for Collins’s 30-year career in the Senate. On Monday, a University of New Hampshire poll found Jackson leading Collins by 4 percentage points. And in September, Collins found herself thrust into a scandal of her own, when ProPublica revealed that the FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating an alleged pay-to-play scheme between Collins and a donor eager to secure government contracts.
The Intercept later exposed that, alongside a series of campaign donations, defense contractors cozy with Collins had received lucrative carveouts in defense spending. (Collins has denied wrongdoing in all cases.)
But the incumbent senator has faced controversy and come out victorious before. And some Mainers doubt they’ll see change either way.
“I can’t vote for either side,” said a man, who declined to share his name with The Intercept, walking down a rural road in Norway with a hunting rifle slung over his shoulder. “You can’t trust neither of them.”
Noah Hurowitz reported from Yarmouth and Norway, Maine; Akela Lacy reported from Fort Worth, Texas; Matt Sledge reported from Detroit, Michigan.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Faced with SpaceX dominance, Europe races to build independent access to space
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Since the summer of 2026, Europe has faced a new source of concern: Will it have full and autonomous access to space by 2030? In anticipation of the rise of its super-heavy Starship rocket – whose commercial life began on September 28 – SpaceX, the company founded by American billionaire Elon Musk, stopped selling flights aboard its standard Falcon-9 launcher beyond 2028. As a result, many European companies and institutions that thought they could rely on this rocket, capable of launching every two days, wondered whether they would have a solution to place their satellites in orbit.
This question has become even more pressing because, by 2030, European needs are expected to rise sharply. These include the sovereign IRIS² telecom constellation, which will comprise 330 satellites in low Earth orbit and 18 in medium orbit; the German military constellation (initially over 100 satellites); 12 new satellites for Galileo (Europe's satellite navigation system), six for Copernicus (Earth observation network); and many other private projects.
"If all these launches take place simultaneously in 2029, we will not have enough capacity," admitted Christophe Bruneau, executive chairman of ArianeGroup – the prime contractor for the Ariane-6 rocket, Europe's main launcher in service alongside the smaller Italian Vega-C – in Le Figaro on October 21. The shortage of rockets could be damaging: It might delay the launch of IRIS² or the modernization of Galileo, forcing Europe to remain dependent on American services such as Starlink, Elon Musk's satellite telecom constellation.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Trappes attack: When does one stop being an 'immigrant' in France? That depends on one's origins
lemonde.fr/en.text:
A racist terrorist attack left one dead and seven injured in Trappes and La Verrière (in the suburbs of Paris). Yet the city of Trappes continues to be portrayed on television through the lens of Islamism. On CNews, commentators discussed the attack by questioning the mayor's alleged ties to Islamist movements. Leaders of the far-right Rassemblement National (RN) reiterated that Trappes was a "miniature Islamic Republic," even though some admitted they had never set foot there. Residents fell victim to racist terrorist violence, but their city was still portrayed as a problem for "the Republic."
In an interview with Le Monde, Trappes' mayor, Ali Rabeh, denounced this contradiction. His criticism targeted not only the far right but also political leaders who, while claiming to uphold the Republic, have adopted its vision of immigration, Islam, and national identity. The role of the media was also called into question.
Little now remains of the "republican front" of 2002 against the far right, when Jacques Chirac brought together 82.21% of the vote against Jean-Marie Le Pen in the second round of the presidential election. In a quarter of a century, the republican ideal has changed dramatically.
Today, equal rights for citizens do less than ever to ensure equal recognition of their belonging to France. And therein lies the problem: How can we claim to defend citizens against racism while allowing a conception of the nation to flourish that uses French people's “origins” as a basis for discrimination, all while invoking the principles of the Republic?
The past 25 years have crystallized a new narrative of "two Frances." Some French people are presumed to adhere to republican principles on the basis of their supposed cultural and moral qualities ("real French people"), to whom everyone else must answer. Others, meanwhile, must "constantly prove themselves": They have to demonstrate what is taken for granted for others – that their commitment to the Republic is not as weak as some claim. Yet their voices are not truly heard: The questions carry more weight than their answers.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Democrats win control of Senate in stunning rebuke for Trump
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Democrats seized control of the Senate on Tuesday, November 3, and are well-positioned to take the House of Representatives as well, with a landslide of upsets that delivered a crushing rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. The vote reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump's war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.
Trump struck a conciliatory note despite his history of questioning election results, telling The New York Times: "I am absolutely willing to accept those results" and promising to "work with the Democrats." But minutes later on social media the 80-year-old signaled how he intends to deal with Democratic attempts to pass laws, posting a picture of a red baseball cap emblazoned: "VETO."
Democrats charted an extraordinary path to Senate victory. Midterm elections are typically difficult for the president's party, but Republicans had originally expected that their Senate majority was safe. Instead, Democrats marched through some of the most conservative states in the nation. The Democrats' decisive breakthroughs came in Kansas and Iowa, the fifth and sixth Republican-held seats to fall in the extraordinary "blue wave" election night.
In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932.
Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008, again illustrating the scale of party's inroads into Republican strongholds.
The upsets followed victories in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio, where voters rejected Republican candidates despite Trump's intensive efforts to rally his supporters.
Texas was a political bombshell. Democrat James Talarico ousted a Trump-backed Senate candidate, while Gina Hinojosa unseated Republican governor Greg Abbott, ending decades of Republican control of the state's top office.
Democrats also protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff's in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire. Republicans had held a 53-47 Senate majority.
Democrats are also set to capture the House of Representatives after flipping Republican-held districts in states stretching from Pennsylvania and New Jersey to Kentucky, Arizona and North Carolina.
Some victories came in territory Trump had carried comfortably in 2024, despite Republican attempts to shore up House seats by redrawing electoral boundaries.
One bellwether was Indiana, where Democrat JD Ford defeated Republican congresswoman Victoria Spartz in a district Trump won by 17 points. Analysts had identified an upset there as a warning of a much wider Democratic advance.
In Georgia, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in US history, while other Democratic gains extended to statehouses across the country.
Republicans had some bright spots in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds won the governorship, becoming the state's first Black governor, and Ashley Moody kept a Senate seat.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump's MAGA movement "on the run from sea to shining sea." Jeffries is also positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January, if elected by his colleagues.
The results were a major blow to Trump, who visited roughly two dozen states over the last month in a pre-Election Day blitz that was meant to energize Republicans but was unable to stop a wipeout.
Democrats have signaled they'll use a foothold in Congress to ensure Trump's final two years in office feature a series of investigations against top members of his administration and deeper scrutiny of how he's enriched his family.

lemonde.fr/en.title: In Ukraine, Russia intensifies strikes on civilian targets
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Hospitals in Kharkiv and Kherson, a humanitarian center in the Zaporizhzhia region, the Dnipro train station, and shopping malls, gas stations and residential buildings across the country… Russia is increasingly intensifying its attacks on sites in Ukraine that have nothing to do with the war effort of the country it invaded four and a half years ago, with an ever-growing death toll.
The latest and deadliest bombing, on Monday, November 2, targeted a school in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, that serves as a humanitarian aid distribution center every Monday. The attack, which killed at least 33 people and left around 50 missing, according to the latest figures, shocked the country, as did the October 29 strike on Dnipro train station, which killed 15 people.
In Komyshuvakha, nine guided bombs weighing three metric tons each hit in several waves, first targeting those receiving humanitarian aid, then the survivors who had taken refuge in a shelter. Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, said “the timing and location of the humanitarian distribution was well publicized” and that “this attack seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law.”

lemonde.fr/en.title: PSG thrash Villarreal 6-0 in Champions League
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Reigning champions Paris Saint-Germain scored four times in the first 17 minutes on their way to a 6-0 demolition of Villarreal in Spain in the Champions League on Tuesday, November 3, as the French side shrugged off injuries to key players to maintain their perfect record in the competition this season.
João Neves, Désiré Doué, Senny Mayulu and Fabián Ruiz all struck at the Estadio de la Cerámica as PSG set a record for the fastest team to score four times in a match in Europe'e elite club competition. Ruiz added another early in the second half and teenager David Boly completed a comprehensive demolition of the side that finished third in La Liga last season.
"I obviously wasn't expecting that but you get matches where you start in that way," PSG's Spanish coach Luis Enrique told broadcaster Canal Plus. "We were impressive throughout and we are really pleased even if it is very difficult PSG fly out of blocks to hit sorry Villarreal for six in Champions Leaguefor Villarreal – but it is hard when you play against a team like us that presses constantly."
PSG have probably lost star winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia for the rest of the campaign after he suffered a torn ACL in his right knee in last month's win over Barcelona, while Ousmane Dembélé, captain Marquinhos and Nuno Mendes are also missing just now. Despite that, the Ligue 1 leaders made it 10 straight wins in all competitions, including four in the Champions League as they aim to lift the European Cup for a third season running.
They are the only team to have maximum points after four matches in this year's Champions League – Liverpool, Real Madrid and Real Betis all have maximum points from three games before playing on Wednesday – and Luis Enrique's prolific side have now scored 20 goals on that run.
Like all matches in the Champions League on Tuesday, a minute's silence was held prior to kickoff in tribute to Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife player who died following a collision in a Spanish second-division game on Monday. The poignant silence here was also held to remember the victims of last week's deadly train crash in Spain, in which 69 people were killed.
Record home defeat
Neves opened the scoring from close range in the ninth minute, and PSG netted three more goals in under eight minutes following that. Doué swept in as the hosts were punished for calamitous defending, and Villarreal collapsed under the intensity of PSG's pressing as Mayulu made it 3-0.
Spain World Cup star Ruiz rounded off the stunning opening salvo, and the same player finished in style for 5-0 early in the second half after latching onto a ball over the top. The 17-year-old full-back Boly came on for Achraf Hakimi and almost immediately got his team's sixth goal – his first senior strike coming on his Champions League debut.
Villarreal have now lost three of their four games in Europe this season, after collecting just a single point in eight matches in last season's league phase. More than that, this was the worst home defeat ever for a Spanish outfit in the Champions League, but PSG march on before taking on Roma and then Aston Villa in their remaining European fixtures before the end of the calendar year.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Spain's transport minister resigns after deadly train crash that killed 69 people
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Spain's transport minister handed in his resignation on Tuesday, November 3, following a train crash that killed 69 people, one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century and a blow for Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez ahead of a snap poll this month. Oscar Puente, who had earlier pledged to work "tirelessly" to restore confidence in the world's second-largest high-speed rail network, also said he was withdrawing from the November 29 general election. Last week's crash, along with another disaster earlier this year, have overshadowed campaigning for the ballot, in which Sanchez is trailing in opinion polls.
"A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of such seriousness in less than a year, however different they may be, whether or not I bear direct responsibility," Puente told members of parliament, referring to the latest tragedy and a January crash in Andalusia that claimed 46 lives. "I made my decision about my future in the first few minutes after the tragedy, as soon as I learned about it," he said. "Today I am making that decision public, in the place where it is most appropriate to do so."
Puente said he was withdrawing as a candidate in the November 29 snap polls. Hours earlier, at a press conference during which he presented measures to improve safety, the minister had said the government would "work tirelessly to achieve and regain the public's trust in high-speed rail."
The right-wing opposition, which had demanded Puente's resignation, and unions have criticized him for appearing to pin all the blame for the disaster on one control center operator. The accident happened when a train operated by the state-owned Renfe plowed into the back of a stationary train belonging to the private Spanish company Iryo on Wednesday outside the village of Urda, around 130 kilometers (80 miles) south of Madrid. The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63-kilometer stretch of track, but a control center nonetheless authorized the Renfe service to resume its journey.
Among the measures announced at the earlier press conference by Puente was the creation of software for control centers that would issue automatic alerts and make it easier to spot anomalies in traffic. Puente said an AI agent would be created to oversee the system and "minimize the possibility of human error," describing the proposal as unprecedented. In scenarios where a control center operator took a decision while the automatic safety system was down, a second operator would have to confirm it, Puente added.
Safety under scrutiny
The train drivers' union Semaf, which has called strikes at Renfe for November 10 and 12, has denounced a worsening of working conditions and the use of "degraded systems." Critics say investment in maintenance has not kept up with the increase in passenger numbers since the 2021 liberalization of Spain's rail network, which allowed private companies to break Renfe's decades-long monopoly.
In an apparent recognition of the unions' demands, Puente said the working conditions of control center operators would be reformed, including their breaks and monitoring their fatigue levels. Puente also announced an aid package of 30 million euros ($33.5 million) for the families of the dead and the scores of people who were injured in last week's accident. Another collision in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people on the same key line connecting Madrid with the city of Seville, Spain's first high-speed route when it opened in 1992.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Trump says US military aid to Israel will be 'cut off at the end of the year'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Made during a phone interview on Fox News on Tuesday, November 3, Donald Trump announced that military aid to Israel, which he described as "a very thriving country," would be "cut off at the end of the year." The timing reflected both his nervousness and improvisation, coming on midterm election day. The decision, lacking any specifics, remains largely symbolic.
Nonetheless, the announcement by Trump, made during a phone interview with Fox News, could have significant consequences. This aid is part of a non-binding, decade-long support plan, first agreed to under the Clinton administration (1999-2008). The current memorandum, which covers 2019 to 2028, sets US military aid at $3.8 billion annually.
Trump made no secret of the reason: Close ties with Israel were hurting his party in public debate. He cited "slings from lunatics like an (Abdul) El-Sayed," the Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan. "It's a bad talking point because when you say, 'Why don’t we give everybody $4 billion?' Israel’s our number one; we give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it." According to Trump, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggested this historic break, saying he understood "this is one of their points of contention." The joint decision was reportedly made several months ago.

lemonde.fr/en.title: UK tightens policy on legal immigration
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Amid tensions within its own ranks, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Labour government confirmed on Monday, November 2, that it would tighten the conditions for obtaining permanent residency in the United Kingdom. Most foreign nationals with legal status will now need to have spent 10 years in the country – up from five years previously – before they can apply for this status, which grants access to social benefits and housing assistance. They will also be required to have a clean criminal record, a strong command of English and no outstanding tax payments.
Criticized by some government colleagues, who see it as yet another crackdown on foreigners, and by the opposition, which claims the measures do not go far enough, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said, "Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest." The reform aimed to limit legal immigration, discourage illegal arrivals and save some billions of pounds. While not providing a precise figure, the minister acknowledged the savings would fall short of the "£10 billion" previously announced.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Video investigation October 24 protests: How did police respond to the far right?
lemonde.fr/en.text:
In at least 10 cities across France on Saturday, October 24, members of the far right took to the streets on the sidelines of protests over the cost of living crisis and French high school demonstrations, according to footage verified by Le Monde. Some even targeted demonstrators.
In Montpellier, in southern France, men assaulted participants in the protest in front of riot police, who then restrained the victims but let the men leave.
Similar incidents occurred in other cities. "At no point, obviously, did the police protect them. At no point did they work in coordination with police officers and gendarmes," said Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Several judicial investigations have been opened into aggravated assault.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Philippe Jaenada wins Prix Goncourt for 'L'Inconnue du quai de Javel'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
A lifelong horse racing enthusiast, Philippe Jaenada admitted in August that the literary prize season reconciled the writer and the horse-betting fan within him. He also noted that betting is an excellent way to learn to lose gracefully, which no doubt has allowed him to embrace the "playful competition" within the literary world with joy. Previously shortlisted for the Prix Goncourt four times but never a finalist, the 62-year-old author won France's best-known literary award for L'Inconnue du quai de Javel ("The Unknown Woman of the Quai de Javel") with six votes to three for Sylvain Prudhomme, as announced by the Académie Goncourt on Tuesday, November 3, from the Drouant restaurant in Paris.
The other contenders were La solitude des professeurs est infinie ("The Solitude of Teachers Is Infinite") by Yannick Haenel, Choses que je croyais perdues ("Things I Thought Were Lost") by Clémentine Mélois and De l'autre côté du lac ("On the Other Side of the Lake") by Prudhomme. All four books were published by houses under the Madrigall group, the family-run holding chaired by Antoine Gallimard, which won the prize in 2025 with La Maison vide ("The Empty House") by Laurent Mauvignier.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Achille Mbembe, historian: 'We must counter the misconception that democracy is anti-African'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
In the face of democratic crises spreading across the globe, where does the African continent stand? Despite successful transitions of power in several countries, the "long cycle of tyranny," reinforced by the colonial era, is far from over, according to Cameroonian historian and philosopher Achille Mbembe, director of the Innovation Foundation for Democracy. In an interview with Le Monde, he discusses the future of democracy in light of the continent's unique history, major global challenges and the rise of conservatism and far-right voting in liberal democracies in Europe and the United States.
What do you see as the major challenges of our time that are forcing us to rethink democracy?
To break free from the dead ends into which fossil-fuel capitalism has plunged the world, it is no longer possible to separate democracy from environmentalism. The metabolic interaction between humans and all living things has now become the foundation from which we must reimagine democracy. We need to put an end to the race toward the destruction of the commons, driven by social media and artificial intelligence. Our capacity for critical thinking, deliberation and reasoning has increasingly been replaced by automated processes that give rise to a narcissistic self. The relationship to the world generated by machines and algorithms does not allow us to meet the normative expectations required by democracy.

spiegel.de/international.title: Minority Rights in the Midterms: A Democratic Recoil from Transgender Rights
spiegel.de/international.text:
It wasn’t a secret that the attacks on the transgender community were coming. In early 2025, US President Donald Trump, still high on the November 2024 election victory that put him in the White House for the second time, essentially instructed the Republican Party to bring up the issue of transgender rights on the eve of the midterms.
Speaking in the White House on March 13, 2025, Trump said: "I tell the Republicans, don’t bring that subject up, because there is no election right now. But about a week before the election, bring it up because you can’t lose.”
DER SPIEGEL relies on support from its readers. To enjoy the rest of this story, please consider signing up for a subscription to The German View, our English-language channel on Substack. Our Substack channel can be found here . Alternatively, you can sign up for a SPIEGEL+ subscription below.
Throughout the midterm campaign, which has now drawn to a close, it became abundantly clear that the Republicans were listening. GOP campaigns and political action committees (PACs) spent tens of millions of dollars on ads targeting the transgender community in this election cycle, including an ad-buy in early September of more than $100 million by Elon Musk through the America PAC, much of which has been heavily focused on transgender messaging.
